title: Madison officials demand end to Williamson Street occupation as demonstrators vow to stay - WMTV 15 NEWS
text: MADISON, Wis. (WMTV) - The mayor of Madison is calling for an end to the occupation of Williamson and South Baldwin Streets, but protesters at the site say they are not leaving. What began as a vigil for Corey Ruiz has grown into an ongoing demonstration that local leaders say they can no longer manage. Protesters on the ground maintain the gathering has been peaceful and will remain so. “This protest started as a peaceful protest and it’s gonna end as a peaceful protest,” said Maleyk Mason, a member of the protest’s security. Mason said he has been at the site since the first day. In a statement, Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said the occupation of Williamson and Baldwin Streets needs to end. “Please join us in finding long-term solutions. That starts with removing the barricades, taking down the tents, and ending the occupation,” wrote Rhodes-Conway in her latest statement . The Mayor also stated that tow notices have been issued to vehicles blocking the intersection, and citations and impoundment will follow. Mason pushed back on that position, calling on the mayor to visit the site directly. “And if the mayor really, really wants to do anything about it, how about she come out here and see what’s going on for her own two eyes, instead of hiding behind two doors?” Mason said. “Well, if she comes down here and sees what we’re doing, maybe her whole saying of tear the barricades down, do this, do this, maybe that would change. But you know, she’s hiding.” Other community leaders are echoing the mayor’s call for the site to be cleared. Dane County Board District 6 Supervisor Yogesh Chawla said the process should be community-led. “What we need right now is a voluntary, peaceful, community-driven process to take the barricades down,” Chawla said. Chawla warned the current situation at the site is becoming increasingly unstable. “We’re feeling like that fragile peace could shatter at any moment,” Chawla said. Chawla also cited concerns about the sustainability of ongoing de-escalation efforts at the site. “Facilitating that with angry residents around and with a loosely organized situation, there was a real call for constant de-escalation. And I’m just afraid that we can’t have the resources to do that de-escalation 24-7,” Chawla said. Madison District 6 Alder Davy Mayer and Dane County Board District 6 Supervisor Yogesh Chawla are working together at the site. Mayer described the range of community sentiment. “It’s very mixed the way people are looking at it, but generally it’s that people saw what happened there, this horrible police violence, but also understanding the people needing time and space to grieve, but also wanting to have access to their homes and businesses and trying to return to a bit of normalcy there,” Mayer said. Mayer said the absence of a single point of contact has made communication difficult, and described his role as meeting with as many people as possible to gather perspectives and connect those seeking change with resources. Mason said he has noticed Mayer’s presence at the site as he walks around talking with people. “He’s been doing an excellent job. He’s even seen what we do here. We’re not violent people,” Mason said. Mason said despite pressure to leave, demonstrators intend to remain. “We’re here for everybody. We’re not here just for ourselves. We’re here for everybody,” he said. City leaders said they want to work with community members to establish a permanent and safe memorial for Corey Ruiz. “We want the city to help facilitate it but not lead that project. Looking at either retaining items from the memorial, there’s a manhole cover that people decorated and painted really nicely, and we want to keep that,” explained Mayer. Mason said if the roads need to reopen, the city must ensure the current memorial can remain in place. “I mean, if they want to come through, then come through. Just don’t drive on the memorial. That’s all I’m asking for,” said Mason. On concerns about traffic and bus routes, Mason said the city has managed similar disruptions before and can do so again. “You have the Farmers Market on the square. You have Maxwell Street Day. When those events happen, what do the buses do? They detour. So have them detour,” Mason said. The Mayor’s latest statement said plans for a permanent memorial cannot be made until the occupation ends. It has been 11 days since Mayor Rhodes-Conway has spoken publicly with media in an on-camera interview. Her last public appearance was Thursday, July 23 — the day after the shooting. WMTV has asked for an interview with the mayor for the past week to discuss the memorial zone and next steps, and has repeatedly been told no, that she is not available for media, or that she is busy. title: Madison begins clearing protest encampment at site of deadly police shooting - WTMJ
text: MADISON, Wis. — City crews began clearing the protest encampment at the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin streets early Tuesday, nearly two weeks after the fatal police shooting of 38-year-old Corey Ruiz. According to our partners at WISC-TV in Madison , city trucks and Wisconsin State Patrol units arrived before 5 a.m., with workers giving people in the encampment verbal warnings to leave the area. The intersection has remained closed since July 22, when a Madison police officer shot and killed Ruiz during a struggle with authorities. In the days that followed, the site became both a memorial and a protest encampment, with demonstrators erecting barricades and blocking traffic. Madison Police tell WISC-TV at least four people were taken into custody this morning. In recent days, Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway repeatedly called for the encampment to end, saying it was disrupting nearby businesses and residents while urging a peaceful transition that would preserve the memorial and allow the community to continue healing.

title: Madison city crews move in to clear out protest encampment - WMTV 15 NEWS
text: MADISON, Wis. (WMTV) -City of Madison crews are starting to clear out the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin streets, nearly two weeks after a Madison police officer shot and killed 38-year-old Corey Ruiz at the location. WMTV journalists on scene observed city trucks, along with the Wisconsin State Patrol arriving around 4:45 a.m. to streets around the intersection. Initially, Madison Police told our crew on scene it was a city operation right now and police will help if it gets violent. Around 5:00 a.m. crews gave people in the encampment a verbal warning to remove their things and leave. Then around 5:15 a.m. a flames could be seen in the middle of the intersection of Williamson Street, near Fire Station 3. Fire trucks and the Madison Police Department Special Events team in riot gear could be seen responding to the fire. WMTV’s Tabitha Bland confirmed with an official the three fires were started and they were started by protestors throwing memorial candles in the air. Those fires have since been put out. Drone video from WMTV shows there is a group of protesters standing and blocking the middle of the intersection of Baldwin and Williamson Street protecting the memorial for Corey Ruiz preventing city crews from clearing it. Police officers in riot gear are surrounding the intersection. Police told WMTV a total of 10 people have been arrested as of 6:50 a.m. Tuesday. City officials said people who are unhoused and have been staying in the encampment will be taken by city bus to hotels where they can stay. Items that were in the street and removed by city crews, are being taken to Demetral Park on N. 6th Street, not far from Madison East High School. People will be able to go there to retrieve their items. For drivers heading out the door for the morning commune, additional streets around the Williamson and Baldwin Street intersections are closed. The area has remained closed since the deadly MPD shooting on July 22. In the immediate aftermath, the intersection became a place for protesters to gather and build a memorial, until demonstrators starting making barricades and creating an encampment. City leaders have made several calls in the past week for this encampment to be cleared, including statements from Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway. title: Who’s behind Wisconsin’s anti-police ‘autonomous zone’ taking over city streets? - washingtonexaminer.com
text: Activists from at least a dozen leftist groups are organizing or promoting the “autonomous zone” protest in Madison, Wisconsin, that officials say is harming the neighborhood. Protesters began setting up an encampment on July 22 that has since blocked traffic and business after a police-involved shooting that day that killed convicted felon Corey Ruiz, according to the city. Social media posts from those involved show activists coordinating funding and erecting construction site equipment as a blockade, a Washington Examiner analysis found. The protest has also featured a “mental health support tent,” a taxpayer-funded nonprofit group that advocates abolishing police , and a list of criminal justice reform “demands” to the city. Groups posting on-site footage or instructions for protesters include the 50501 Movement, Supply the Siege, Madison Worker Cooperatives, Madison Trans Resistance Action Committee, Freedom Inc., the Party for Socialism and Liberation , Freedom Road Socialist Organization , Feeding the Youth, Wisconsin Bail Out the People Movement , Wisconsin Sapphics , Deflock Dane , and Trans Advocacy Mission . The organizations brand themselves around numerous leftist causes but are now joining to condemn Madison police for killing Ruiz, whom officials claim resisted arrest and pulled a knife on officers. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway called out protesters for continuing to block roads on Sunday and demanded that they stop their “occupation,” but did not announce any action to force their dispersal. The city’s fire department must now take emergency vehicles “around the encampment, potentially adding minutes to a call,” Madison Councilman Alder Evers said Sunday. “There is real harm being done to local businesses and residents in the Marquette Neighborhood,” the mayor said Sunday. “We are hearing from neighbors who are losing income and even jobs, and who will not be able to make rent. We are hearing from employees who are being laid off and businesses that are on the verge of closing permanently.” Rhodes-Conway noted that the so-called Corey Ruiz autonomous zone resembles Seattle Black Lives Matter rioters’ Capitol Hill autonomous zone , or CHAZ, which resulted in shooting and deaths after its occupants kicked out police . The mayor’s office did not provide comment in response to a Washington Examiner inquiry. Several posts ask supporters to donate for supplies at the protest zone, such as food and clothing, using a Venmo account belonging to Feeding the Youth leader Jazzman Brown. Her group got its start providing food for anti-police protesters after George Floyd ‘s 2020 death in Minnesota and helping them travel to Washington, D.C. , demonstrations, according to media outlet Madison365. Brown claims to have known Ruiz personally and organized a candlelight vigil in Madison on the encampment’s second day. “Please let me know if out of state protesters need support with travel or hotel expenses!” Brown wrote in a Facebook post that day. Activists claim they will compensate workers whose lives they are disrupting. Madison Worker Cooperatives, whose stated mission is to “build the solidarity economy,” also opened an online fundraiser through which employees “negatively impacted by the ongoing demonstrations” can apply for funds. The funding is for “employees only,” not business owners, as long as they show proof of lost wages, Madison Worker Cooperatives said in a Saturday Instagram post. The group is coordinating the fundraiser with the Williamson-Marquette Business Alliance, which promised to match up to $5,000 in donations. In addition to Brown, other veteran protesters described participating in the Madison encampment. 50501 Movement member Emily Phillips posted footage of her comrades blocking Madison’s roads with tents, wood, construction cones, and other items. She previously joined protests against Immigration and Customs Enforcement in New Jersey’s Delaney Hall and Minnesota earlier this year, according to media reports and her public comments . Phillips was arrested outside St. Paul’s Cities Church during a January anti-ICE protest that disrupted a church service and led to federal charges for dozens involved, MPR News reported. Phillips’s local misdemeanor charges were dropped. The activist also claimed to have personally worked alongside Minnesota protesters who now face federal charges alleging an antifa-linked conspiracy to harm and impede ICE agents. “Stay safe, f*** ICE, and have a great day,” she told her audience last week in an Instagram video announcing she was traveling to Madison. The 50501 Movement also posted a video purportedly from the autonomous zone featuring a woman who described participating in 2020 Black Lives Matter riots . “Six years ago, I was a big, big, big part of the organizing of the protests after George Floyd passed away, and I am a comrade of yours, Minnesota,” said the woman, identified as Ebony. “I was there when your police station [was] burning and we were rioting,” she said, apparently referring to when the mobs burned down a Minneapolis police precinct in 2020. She also gave a shoutout to allies in Washington, D.C., mentioning how “we all got trapped on Black Lives Matter Drive.” Another group spreading Brown’s donation instructions is Supply the Siege, created in May to support Minnesota’s anti-ICE demonstrators , its website and Instagram account show. “Whether during civil unrest or simply neighbors helping neighbors, we will be there,” the website says. Protesters are petitioning the city for policy changes written on postcards in tandem with Ruiz’s family and the nonprofit Freedom Inc., according to on-site coverage from Freedom Road Socialist Organization’s media arm , “Fight Back! News.” The demands include arresting the police officer who killed Ruiz, defunding the police, and more “community control” over law enforcement. Images from other protest participants show a Freedom Inc. tent and its “abolish police” signage in the protest zone. “Freedom Inc. has set up a tent to carry out a four-day educational series where they will discuss in detail their demands to get justice for Corey and create change in Madison,” the Freedom Road Socialist Organization said Thursday. Madison Trans Resistance Action Committee also told activists to follow Freedom Inc.’s lead on demonstrations. “Our only enemy is the state,” Freedom Inc. said in a Saturday post . “The state murders us in the street. The state occupies our neighborhoods through policing. The state separates families through deportation. The state abandons our communities while funding punishment over care.” FBI STILL SEARCHING FOR 2020 RIOTER WHO HELPED DEMOLISH ICE FACILITY “Our responsibility is to build political clarity, deepen our relationships, organize our communities, and build institutions that answer to the people instead of the state,” the nonprofit group continued . Freedom Inc. reported more than $4.8 million in government funds between 2021 and 2024 on tax filings .

title: Legislative Primaries to Watch in August Elections
text: Key primary races could help decide which party controls both the state Assembly and Senate. The Wisconsin Assembly chamber. Elections in August and November will determine who fills these seats and those in the state Senate. (File photo by Melanie Conklin/Wisconsin Examiner) While Wisconsin’s governor’s race is drawing national attention, control of the state Legislature could determine whether the next governor can enact their agenda. Legislative primaries will shape the handful of Assembly and Senate races that could decide control next year. Republicans are seeking to defend their majorities, which they’ve held since 2011. Democrats are seeking to flip two Senate seats and five Assembly seats while maintaining all the seats they hold currently to win majorities in both chambers. The outcome will determine how much of the next governor’s agenda — from Medicaid expansion to tax cuts and investing in education — can become law. There is sparse polling on state legislative races, although a survey in July from Marquette Law School found that 46% of Wisconsin voters said they would vote for Democrats in legislative races, while 42% said they’d vote for Republicans. The poll could not deliver detailed information on specific districts at play. Republicans are gearing up financially to defend their majorities, with the Republican Assembly Campaign Committee reporting $6.5 million raised in the first half of the year and a total of $11.5 million cash-on-hand. The Committee to Elect a Republican Senate raised nearly $5 million and had $5.3 million on-hand. The bulk of that fundraising came from billionaires Diane Hendricks , who gave $2.5 million to RACC and $2 million to the Senate GOP committee, as well as Elizabeth Uihlein , who gave $3 million to the Assembly committee and $2 million to the Senate committee. The contributions have given the Republicans organizations deeper pockets than their Democratic counterparts. According to recent campaign finance reports, the State Senate Democratic Campaign Committee, the fundraising arm of the Senate Democratic caucus, raised about $2.8 million over the first six months of the year, while the Assembly Democratic Campaign Committee raised $3 million and ended with nearly $2.4 million cash-on-hand. The primary is scheduled for Aug. 11. Here are seven primary elections the Wisconsin Examiner is keeping an eye on in the lead-up to Election Day. The general election is Nov. 3. A four-way Republican primary is taking place in the race to replace Sen. André Jacque in Senate District 1, which represents Door and Kewaunee counties. Nic Cravillion is an Army combat veteran and small business owner from New Franken who is campaigning on lowering taxes and promoting “responsible spending” as well as expanding workforce and affordable housing opportunities. For the last five years, Cravillion has also worked as the district director for Jacque. He reported raising $75,911 and having $62,264 on hand — more than any of the other candidates — at the end of the period. He also reported taking out $62,100 in personal loans. Barbara Bittner serves as the chair of the Calumet County Republican Party. She is running to reduce property taxes, protect “parental rights,” get “tough on crime” and uphold the “sanctity of life and traditional values.” Bittner reported raising $17,180.00 and having about $16,945 on hand at the end of the period. Katie Baney , a De Pere mother, currently works as the managing director of government affairs at Delta Defense, where she advocates for gun owners, and promises not to support any legislation that restricts the Second Amendment, according to her campaign website. Baney reported in July raising $46,772 and having $43,662 on-hand. Jacob VandenPlas , a veteran and farmer who founded DC Farm for Vets, a rehabilitation farm that provides education and services to veterans entering agriculture. No Democrat is running for the seat in the red-leaning district, though the winner of the Republican primary will face Mark Becker , a small business owner who was formerly the chair of the Brown County Republican Party and is now running as an independent. Becker left the party after Trump’s election in 2016 due to disagreements over the direction of the GOP. He reported raising $20,233 and having $15,078 cash-on-hand. He has received contributions from Adam Kinzinger , the former Republican Congressman from Illinois who left the party due to his opposition to Trump, and the campaign account of state Sen. Kristin Dassler-Alfheim (D-Appleton). Three Democrats are competing to win a spot on the ballot to take on Sen. Howard Marklein (R-Spring Green) in November. Marklein was first elected to the Senate in 2014, and has been the co-chair of the powerful Joint Finance Committee since 2021. The district includes Crawford, Grant, Green, Iowa and LaFayette counties as well as the southwestern corner of Dane County . Marklein won the district with 60% of the vote in 2022, but Senate District 17 changed considerably under the new maps. The district leaned Democratic by 1 percentage point in the 2024 presidential election and by over 4 percentage points in the 2024 U.S. Senate race, according to an analysis by John Johnson , a fellow at Marquette Law School. Marklein’s incumbency status gives him an advantage in the district, and he is also raising more than the other Democratic candidates combined. In his most recent campaign finance reports, Marklein reported raising $300,195 and ending the reporting period with $1.01 million in the bank. He received $100,000 — or about a third of his total contributions — from the Committee to Elect a Republican Senate . Rep. Jenna Jacobson (D-Oregon), who has served in the state Assembly since 2023, launched her campaign for the Senate seat in July 2025 with the backing of the State Senate Democratic Campaign Committee. The endorsement has provided her some advantages over her opponents, as she has campaigned with current Senators, including Senate Minority Leader Dianne Hesselbein , and received financial assistance from the SSDC. According to her latest campaign finance reports, Jacobson has raised about $109,277 and has about $201,177 in the bank. About $45,450 of her total contributions this year came from in-kind contributions from the SSDC in the form of campaign staff. title: City of Madison removes encampment - In Business Madison
text: City of Madison crews removed the protest encampment at the intersection of Baldwin and Williamson streets early Tuesday morning. In a statement explaining the decision for the removal, Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway decried the lack of focus on the original subject of the protest — Corey Ruiz, the 38-year-old Madison man who was fatally shot by a Madison police officer — and said an “illegal occupation” of the streets is not the way to solve complex systemic issues. In an Aug. 3 letter to the community, Rhodes-Conway said she is “deeply troubled” that Ruiz is no longer at the center of the current crisis the city faces. “We’ve provided the time and space to allow the community to grieve Corey and the loss of other community members by police hands in the Marquette neighborhood,” she wrote. “We hope to work with Corey’s family and the community to continue to have a space for people to visit a memorial. “Plans for a permanent memorial cannot be made until the occupation ends.” Ruiz was fatally shot on July 22 during an attempted arrest at the intersection. As the protest unfolded, complaints by residents and businesses mounted, and with public health and safety being undermined, the situation became unsustainable, the mayor contends. An investigation into whether the officer was justified in using deadly force continues at the state and local levels. The full text of Rhodes-Conway’s Aug. 3 letter to the community is as follows: “For almost two weeks now, City of Madison staff and elected leaders have been on the ground and communicating to and through community leaders to peacefully resolve extremely complex, emotionally fraught circumstances that started with the police taking the life of Corey Ruiz. Countless efforts have been made to convince people that the occupation of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street is counterproductive. A huge amount of patience has been given because the last thing Madison needs is a large-scale police operation. That’s why those occupying the area need to leave immediately. I’m deeply troubled that Corey is largely no longer at the center of the current crisis our city faces. We’ve provided the time and space to allow the community to grieve Corey and the loss of other community members by police hands in the Marquette neighborhood. We hope to work with Corey’s family and the community to continue to have a space for people to visit a memorial. Plans for a permanent memorial cannot be made until the occupation ends. There are too many residents and local businesses suffering because of the occupation, and it’s become increasingly clear that unsheltered people are being used as leverage for demands that, frankly, the City of Madison cannot deliver because we do not have the power to deliver them. As we and others have repeatedly explained, the City cannot make an arrest or bring criminal charges — that authority rests with the Dane County District Attorney following an independent investigation by the Wisconsin Department of Justice. The City does not control this timeline. I’m increasingly alarmed that those supporting the occupation at the intersection of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street are either purposefully ignoring the harm being done, or deliberately hoping that the situation spirals further out of control. The City has already issued tow notices to vehicles blocking the intersection, and citations and impoundment will follow. At no point did the City pay for porta-potties, and the company that supplied them has been asked to remove them or risk being cited and fined. For those concerned for our unsheltered neighbors and friends, enabling the illegal occupation of city streets is not helping. The City cannot — alone — solve our nation’s failure to provide for people’s basic needs. The faith community, nonprofits already engaged in this work, and individual community members can help the City and the County combat homelessness. But it is naive to think such a systemic problem can be solved overnight, or that maintaining an encampment in the middle of a street will do anything to hasten a solution. As we have outlined in past messages, efforts to provide services to the unsheltered currently at the site are being made by outreach workers and Community Development Division staff. Those suggesting this is a safe location for a homeless encampment are wrong and are actively inviting more trauma and harm. Please join us in finding long-term solutions. That starts with removing the barricades, taking down the tents, and ending the occupation.”

title: Police clear encampment on Williamson and Baldwin streets in Madison - Spectrum News
text: MADISON, Wis. — Police cleared the encampment on Williamson Street and Baldwin Street on Tuesday morning. The occupation of the streets began after police shot and killed Corey Ruiz less than two weeks ago. Authorities came in with bobcats and other heavy machinery to begin clearing barricades, furniture and tents at the site around 4:30 a.m. The city said it did not want to get law enforcement involved but some protesters refused to clear, with some throwing objects at vehicles and lighting fires in the street. That's when the Madison Police Department stepping in. It corralled protesters in the center of the intersection and arrested several people who were trying to prevent the memorial for Ruiz from being taken down. According to the city, the streets were officially back open as of 9 a.m. All city barricades and signage were removed from the area. Supporters of the encampment and memorial criticized the city for how the entire situation was handled. “They could have just been direct and said we’re going to give you 48 hours to move out and then everybody could’ve been given a timeline, nobody was ever given a clear timeline, all they kept doing was throwing vouches, hotel vouchers at the houseless community, less than half of the people here were houseless," said Shadayra Kilfoy-Flores. The latest development comes after Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway called for an end to the encampment, with leaders saying a peaceful end was the best path forward. Rhodes-Conway issued a new video message on Tuesday following the encampment being cleared. She said the city is fully cooperating with the investigation. "As soon as we are allowed to under state law, the police department will provide all relevant materials to the Office of the Independent Monitor for their investigation,” she said, addressing claims last week by the Monitor that MPD was not cooperating with turning over materials. The mayor said the decision to clear the encampment was not made lightly, but there was much to consider, with local businesses and residents caught in the middle of what she called "an increasingly volatile situation." "I ask that if you truly care about building a better future, you allow local businesses to stay open, residents to freely access their homes, and the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin Streets to stay open. Let's focus our energy on the hard work of sustainable change. Holding government accountable for progress should not mean harming the community we all share," she said in the video. Police remained at the scene on Tuesday. The city has also sectioned off a portion of the sidewalk on Baldwin Street as a designated memorial site for Ruiz. The city said those looking to pick up their belongings could do so at the parking lot of Demetral Park; city staff will be there until midnight. As of Tuesday afternoon, about one third of the items had been picked up. Kaitlynn Rouse was one of several people who helps people sift through the various items taken from the encampment. She said she thinks what the city did Tuesday showed a lack of respect.  “I think there should have been a lot more care and empathy when it came to, at the very least, the people and the people’s resources and items," she said. Both Rouse and Kilfoy-Flores said this was just another example of the growing rift between city leaders and the people of Madison. “They’re against the community members who are grieving, in pain, and just seeing it as a nuisance instead of people who just care about their community," said Rouse. "We were starting to get past the anger part, and then there’s healing, but now we’re back to square one,” said Kilfoy-Flores. While the encampment may be gone, protesters said they won't stop fighting for accountability in Ruiz's death.

title: UPDATE: Protestors return to former encampment site in Madison - WTMJ
text: UPDATE 8/4/26 at 4:00p.m. – Protestors have returned to the intersection of Willy and Baldwin Streets in Madison hours after police had cleared out the encampment in the street. The barricades that had blocked off the street have not returned but protestors could be seen walking in circles around the intersection while police monitored close by. This is a developing story; more information will be added as it becomes available. MADISON, Wis. – A protest encampment blocking off a Madison intersection for nearly two weeks is cleared for traffic once again. But those occupying the site at Willy and Baldwin Streets where police last month shot and killed 38-year-old Corey Ruiz did not leave quietly. Police made at least 10 arrests as protestors hurled rocks and lit multiple fires near the encampment that formed in the street in the days following Ruiz’s death. At least one protester was injured and taken to a hospital, while a Madison Fire Department said one city employee experienced a “medical event” but declined to elaborate. The clear-out order came after Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway had for days called for a peaceful end to the encampment, while stressing the street needed to be cleared out. “Multiple efforts and calls to end the occupation peacefully were made but ultimately ignored,” said Rhodes-Conway in a video release August 4. “The decision to invoke this option was not made lightly and was only made after almost two weeks of trying to resolve the situation peacefully, and voluntarily, with the people occupying the site.” Roughly 50 homeless individuals onsite were given the option to stay in hotels and were offered transportation there, says Rhodes-Conway. PREVIOUS COVERAGE: Madison begins clearing protest encampment at site of deadly police shooting Rhodes-Conway added dialogue with occupiers was difficult because there was not one singular individual with which to communicate. The clear-out followed growing concern from people living near the site that tensions were escalating, as well as from area businesses impacted financially by the street closure. Objects from the site are available for pickup at Demetral Field for an undetermined period of time. The officers involved in the Ruiz shooting remain on leave as the state Division of Criminal Investigation continues looking into his death. TOP STORIES FROM THE WTMJ NEWSROOM:

title: Video Message from Mayor Rhodes-Conway - City of Madison, WI
text: For Immediate Release August 4, 2026 "Good morning, I'm Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway.  I want to start by saying that the death of Corey Ruiz is, tragically, another wake up call for Madison. Even one community member killed during interactions with the police is too many. The grief, anger, and frustration are real and I feel it, too. I want to be clear that the City is fully cooperating with the independent investigation conducted by the Wisconsin Department of Justice, and will respect whatever decisions the District Attorney makes regarding charges for the officers involved. As soon as we are allowed to under state law, the police department will provide all relevant materials to the Office of the Independent Monitor for their investigation.   There is more work to be done at the City level to prevent this from happening again - work to build on the success of our CARES program in diverting calls away from police, work on police policy and training, and more. We need reform at the state level as well. I know it's unsatisfying to hear that change takes time, and that these investigations and processes require patience. But these things do take time and many of the changes needed are not in City government's control.   For nearly two weeks, I and City staff have been working day and night to peacefully resolve the occupation of Williamson and Baldwin without law enforcement intervention. The City has committed to maintaining space for members of the community to gather and grieve, and we stand ready to do that work in collaboration with the family and the community. But that work could not begin while city streets were occupied, local businesses were on the verge of closing, and residents in the Marquette neighborhood were caught in the middle of an increasingly volatile situation.   A challenge of the last two weeks was that there was not one leader, one group, or one coalition that represented the people occupying the intersection. What is deeply regrettable is that many vulnerable people were caught in the middle, which is why the City spent considerable time and effort finding emergency solutions — efforts that succeeded in helping dozens of unsheltered people and families. We were doing this work before the occupation, and we will continue to do this work moving forward.  This morning, the City of Madison opened the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin. The work was led by non-law enforcement staff from multiple City agencies. Our goal was to clear the barricades, preserve personal belongings and memorial materials, and open the street up to normal traffic. The CARES Team and members of the Violence Prevention Unit were there from the beginning to assist.  Unfortunately, as City staff cleared the area, rocks and other items were thrown at City employees and two fires were set; as a result, law enforcement was called in to stabilize the scene, and a small number of individuals were arrested. Again, multiple efforts and calls to end the occupation peacefully were made but ultimately ignored.  The 50 or so unsheltered individuals who were onsite were given the option to stay in hotels and were offered transportation there. A significant majority decided to do so and around 10 people were also placed in hotel rooms yesterday. This effort was done with as much compassion as possible under less-than-ideal circumstances. Those with personal belongings left at the site can pick them up at Demetral Field.   Again, the decision to invoke this option was not made lightly and was only made after almost two weeks of trying to resolve the situation peacefully, and voluntarily, with the people occupying the site.  There are many hard conversations to come and I look forward to us coming together as a community to have them. I ask that if you truly care about building a better future, you allow local businesses to stay open, residents to freely access their homes, and the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin Streets to stay open. Let's focus our energy on the hard work of sustainable change. Holding government accountable for progress should not mean harming the community we all share.   Thank you, Madison. We are a strong and compassionate community. Together, we can support each other. Together, we can work towards change. Together we can get through this. title: Madison officials, cops clear protesters from encampment at police shooting site - wisconsinexaminer.com
text: Protesters began their occupation of the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin Streets after Corey Ruiz was shot and killed July 22. On July 23, a vigil was held in honor of Ruiz and protesters remained barricaded on the streets until city officials cleared the intersection August 4. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner) Madison city workers, police and state patrol officers cleared protesters from the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin Streets early Tuesday morning, putting an end to the encampment that had blocked off the major east side intersection since a Madison police officer shot and killed Corey Ruiz there July 22. Starting around 5 a.m., officials announced through loudspeakers that the barricades blocking the streets would be removed and the gathering dispersed. Videos posted to social media show a chaotic scene at which police grappled with protesters and deployed pepper spray. City officials also towed away the replica George Floyd fist statue that was brought to the intersection last week. Dylan Brogan, a spokesperson for the city, said the city planned to let non-police city staff lead the effort. “The plan was for this to be led by non-law enforcement city agencies,” he said, adding that the unhoused people staying at the site would be given the opportunity to stay in a hotel and that people’s belongings would be available for pickup at Demetral Field, located about 2 miles northeast of the protest encampment site. “The message was delivered loudly that people had to get their things together.” The city announced that the intersection was open to traffic at 9 a.m. In a statement released Monday evening, Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway warned that the encampment would be shut down on Tuesday — stating that Ruiz was “no longer at the center of the current crisis our city faces.” “For almost two weeks now, City of Madison staff and elected leaders have been on the ground and communicating to and through community leaders to peacefully resolve extremely complex, emotionally fraught circumstances that started with the police taking the life of Corey Ruiz,” Rhodes-Conway stated. “Countless efforts have been made to convince people that the occupation of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street is counterproductive. A huge amount of patience has been given because the last thing Madison needs is a large-scale police operation. That’s why those occupying the area need to leave immediately.” She added that the protesters at the site were making demands that city officials have no authority to meet, only extending the closure of the intersection which had begun to take a toll on the businesses in the culturally important Willy Street corridor. “There are too many residents and local businesses suffering because of the occupation, and it’s become increasingly clear that unsheltered people are being used as leverage for demands that, frankly, the City of Madison cannot deliver because we do not have the power to deliver them,” Rhodes-Conway said. “As we and others have repeatedly explained, the City cannot make an arrest or bring criminal charges — that authority rests with the Dane County District Attorney following an independent investigation by the Wisconsin Department of Justice. The City does not control this timeline.” “I’m increasingly alarmed that those supporting the occupation at the intersection of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street are either purposefully ignoring the harm being done, or deliberately hoping that the situation spirals further out of control,” she continued. title: Editorial | Madison officers must wear body-worn cameras - captimes.com
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom. Sign up for the Opinion Roundup newsletter for weekly Madison and Wisconsin viewpoints. During a mayoral debate at the Madison Public Library in February 2023, Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway and challenger Gloria Reyes butted heads on issues ranging from housing to public safety. Rhodes-Conway expressed doubts about body-worn cameras preventing both police misconduct and police violence then, and has continued to be indecisive on the matter. Reyes pushed for more urgency on the topic, telling the Cap Times at the time, “Some will say we cannot afford the implementation of body cameras. After watching the murder of Tyre Nichols, I say we can’t afford not to have them.” Nichols was beaten to death by five officers in Memphis a month earlier during a traffic stop. The gruesome footage captured by their body-worn cameras did not save Nichols, but it led to seven officers being fired and three suspended. It was also crucial in both state and federal trials years later. A year before that, on Feb. 3, 2022, state Department of Justice agents shot Quadren Wilson five times in the back on the east side of Madison. None of the agents involved wore body cameras and the Madison Police Department reported no city officers witnessed the shooting — facts that left more questions than answers and further drove a wedge between law enforcement and the community. Less shrouded in mystery is the death of Kevin Price by Fitchburg officer Peter Johnston. We know the nature of his death and every moment leading up to it upon the Fitchburg officers’ arrival at Price’s apartment. Media outlets, including the Cap Times , obtained footage from body-worn cameras and scrutinized every detail of the 40-minute encounter. Researchers who study use of force were able to review the videos and conclude the officers created a dangerous and fatal situation, even if, frustratingly, Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne declined to file criminal charges against the officer. The city of Madison has dragged its feet for years on body-worn cameras, even after green-lighting a pilot program in April 2022. Then, last year in a 17-3 decision, the Madison City Council rejected a proposal to fund a body camera program. But in the aftermath of Corey Ruiz’s death, the only video evidence the Department of Justice has in its investigation comes from bystanders’ cellphone footage, which may not cover the angles necessary to fairly assess the details of what happened and where the knife was in the seconds before Ruiz’s death. We believe it’s incumbent on all City Council members and the mayor to make a decision on this crucial accountability tool. Madison remains one of the only major metropolitan cities in the United States to not require department-wide cameras. It’s high time to change that and to add one more layer of accountability and transparency to public safety.

title: City clears Willy Street encampment, dozens jailed or issued citations - captimes.com
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. Layla Lowe said she had a dream early Tuesday that something was going to happen. She was sleeping at the encampment at the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin streets with other protesters who have been there since the July 22 fatal police shooting of Corey Ruiz, 38. Lowe said she was on edge. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway had been warning for days the encampment would need to be removed. Authorities arrived around 5 a.m. Tuesday and alerted people with a megaphone that they would start cleaning up the site and people could pack their own belongings, according to Madison police spokesperson Stephanie Fryer. Some protesters then started three fires and threw objects at city staff, she said. Bystander videos show a chaotic scene where protesters were arrested and officers used pepper spray while clearing the encampment. Uniforms identified the officers as Madison police and State Patrol officers. “It was scary,” Lowe said. “If these people want to stand here and protest, let them protest. Let them do what they want. You all took an innocent boy's life. He didn’t deserve that. He deserved his justice, though. And we’re going to get it, some way, somehow.” Madison police officers stand near the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin streets following the removal of a memorial for Corey Ruiz on Tuesday. Fryer said 17 people were arrested and it was unclear how many people were pepper sprayed. Three people were injured in the clash: two protesters and one city employee. One of the protesters was taken to a hospital. The city employee suffered a “medical event” and was also taken to a hospital, Fryer said. Later, the Police Department clarified that 16 people were arrested and booked into the Dane County Jail, and 10 others were issued citations and released. By mid-morning, dozens of officers remained at the scene while belongings were being boxed up and loaded into trucks, and street sweepers began moving through the area. Spray paint and chalk writings were left behind on the streets, sidewalks and buildings. Some remnants of the encampment like food and belongings also remained. “Demetral Park” was written on the sides of some boxes. Fryer said the items were being taken to the park, about a mile north of the intersection, for individuals to retrieve. She said city officials went tent by tent and tried to package individuals' possessions together. City buses were on site Tuesday morning to give rides to people experiencing homelessness who had agreed to be part of a hotel voucher program, Fryer said. Two residents around 9:30 a.m. asked whether the city was distributing free bus passes to get off-site. City Council member Davy Mayer, who represents the area, said nearly 30 of the roughly 50 unsheltered individuals who had gathered at the encampment took the city up on its hotel voucher offer. Amy Basel was at the site around 8 a.m. retrieving metal shelves she had brought to support the protesters. Basel, an east side resident, said she had volunteered at the encampment several times, helping to serve food, clean up and provide supplies. She was planning to visit again Tuesday and bring snacks and tomatoes. The city could have rallied volunteers to help clean up the site, Basel said. She described the intersection as not “the neatest place,” especially after a recent bout of rain. “But there was love. There was even hope in the face of all this pain and hatred,” Basel said. Memorial items such as flowers and candles for Ruiz remained at the site Tuesday morning, and were placed alongside a building on South Baldwin Street. The city plans to preserve the memorial items, Fryer said. Flowers and other items from a memorial for Corey Ruiz sit beside stacked traffic barriers after being removed Tuesday. By about 9 a.m., cars and bikes were once again traveling through the intersection. Some drivers slowed or stopped to take photos or video on their phones, while others joined in chants with protesters as they drove by. By early evening, the number of protesters had grown by the dozens. Equipped with signs, megaphones and some masks, the protesters occupied the four corners of the intersection, being kept to the sidewalks by police officers as cars drove through during rush hour. Tensions were high and some protesters splashed water on passing police cars and verbal altercations broke out. At one point, protesters attempted to move into the street near the intersection of Baldwin and Wilson streets but police on foot, by car and on horseback quickly moved in to intervene. Protesters chanted, "We control the traffic." As the City Council met virtually for its regular meeting Tuesday night, a small group of protesters gathered outside the municipal building downtown. While city leaders initially supported barricading the intersection so people could mourn and protest Ruiz's death, they have increasingly raised concern about its safety and impact on the neighborhood in recent days. Tensions in the neighborhood were on display Tuesday morning. During an interview between a witness to the event and the Cap Times, a resident near the corner of Baldwin and Jenifer streets popped out of her door and said she was “sick of this” and asked that the conversations go “somewhere else” away from her yard. Several businesses displayed signs demanding justice for Corey Ruiz, and several dozen protestors remained at the site, chanting phrases including “What’s his name? Corey!” and “The whole damn system is guilty as hell.” On Saturday, Rhodes-Conway issued a statement saying the city was “preparing for a respectful transition” but didn’t indicate the encampment would be cleared Tuesday. On Sunday, the mayor said towing notices had been issued to vehicles blocking traffic. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway issues a recorded video statement on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, addressing the city's decision to clear out an e… Late Tuesday morning, Rhodes-Conway issued a new statement and a recorded video in which she said “there is more work to be done” to prevent future police shootings. “I know it’s unsatisfying to hear that change takes time, and that these investigations and processes require patience,” the mayor said. “But these things do take time and many of the changes needed are not in city government's control.” Rhodes-Conway said she and other city staff had been “working day and night to peacefully resolve the occupation of Williamson and Baldwin without law enforcement intervention,” but their efforts were stymied by a lack of a single person or organization to negotiate on behalf of protesters. Mayer shared a statement from the mayor's office to City Council members, which said the city couldn't provide a schedule publicly to clear the encampment because it would have “compromised the unprecedented amount of planning it took to avoid having law enforcement lead this action.” “We learned from 2020 (George Floyd protests in Madison) that when police are being protested, having the department at the frontlines produces even more negative outcomes,” the statement says. “Setting a deadline or timeline for this action would have made keeping law enforcement away impossible.” A Madison police officer stands near the site as items from a memorial for Corey Ruiz are removed Tuesday. As officers stood at the intersection Tuesday, some residents shouted “it's not over” and “we will be back.” Protesters had been discussing ways to shrink the memorial so the protest could continue and the intersection could reopen, according to Ashzianna Alexander, a protester who left the encampment minutes before city officials arrived and returned later. “We wanted it to be peaceful, and you all chose chaos,” Alexander said. Protesters previously called for city leaders to dedicate an official memorial to Ruiz, assist in transporting belongings and resources to temporary housing elsewhere, and coordinate city resources that could help with the transition. Both Alexander and Basel said they hope protesters continue to apply pressure on officials. Wisconsin State Patrol officers stand nearby as city workers remove items Tuesday from a memorial for Corey Ruiz at Williamson Street and South Baldwin Street. Hanah Jon Taylor, owner of Cafe Coda along Willy Street, had backed those gathered at the intersection. Taylor, 76, said his support was in solidarity with “people who are fighting against the same type of legitimate police brutality and killings” as he saw growing up in Chicago. “I don't believe that there's such a thing as justifiable homicide,” Taylor said. “Especially when you're supposed to have the training and the experience to deal with somebody with a knife.” He decried the shooting of Ruiz, saying police should have seen and treated him as “a neighbor” rather than “the enemy” after being called to the area July 22 on a report that a person was looking into cars along the street. “I work with a lot of kids, and the first thing you learn as an educator is there's no such thing as a bad child,” he said. A Madison police officer stands nearby as city crews remove items from a memorial for Corey Ruiz on Tuesday. Disproportionate treatment of communities of color will continue, he said, without a broader cultural shift alongside police reforms. “Everybody seems to be expecting someone else to do something about it, other than white people. White people should be talking to white people,” Taylor said. “My kids want to get along with your kids. We need to be congenial as a country, but if the law treats us differently based upon our race, it's always going to be a problem.” A state Department of Justice investigation into the fatal shooting of Ruiz is ongoing. Police Chief John Patterson has said Ruiz was shot during a struggle to arrest him and the officer who shot Ruiz had been injured by a knife. The struggle and shooting were recorded on video by bystanders, and then spread on social media, drawing national attention and immediate protests. Rhodes-Conway has questioned the shooting, while City Council President Sabrina Madison and protesters have called for the officer’s arrest. Rhodes-Conway said the city cannot arrest the officer during an ongoing state investigation and that any decision to charge an officer rests with Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne. Authorities have not released the name of the officer who shot Ruiz or three other officers who were involved in attempting to arrest Ruiz. All four officers are on paid administrative leave amid the state investigation, according to Patterson. Democratic state Rep. Francesca Hong, who represents the neighborhood and is running for governor this fall, said in a statement that she was “deeply disappointed” by how the incident was handled Tuesday. She joined protesters at the intersection the day of the shooting, but similarly called for a transition away from the encampment in recent days. “While the intersection has been reopened, we cannot move on from Corey Ruiz’s death,” she said. By early afternoon, organizers, city staff and protesters were gathered at Demetral Park parking lot to reset. The boxes of individuals' belongings were being unloaded onto pallets and the wooden fist-shaped statue that had previously been positioned at the center of the intersection was newly stationed at the edge of the parking lot at the park. A raised fist sculpture, delivered from Minneapolis as a show of solidarity with those protesting the fatal police shooting of Corey Ruiz, was moved from Williamson and South Baldwin streets to Demetral Park on Tuesday. The city said in a statement that city officials will be on site until midnight to assist individuals with collecting their belongings. Items won't be left unattended, the statement said. Brittany Guy, who is related to Ruiz's daughter, said the new location was “perfect,” noting that it had a bathroom for people to use. The park is a large grassy plot near East High School and includes a dog park, shelter and several softball fields. “This isn’t hurting anybody. It's a parking lot,” Guy said as she hung a string of colorful bug lights on a pop-up tent designated for mental health services at the park. “I feel like this should be perfect for them.”

title: Multiple arrests as Madison police clear protest encampment - WTMJ
text: UPDATE 8/4/26 at 4:00p.m. – Protestors have returned to the intersection of Willy and Baldwin Streets in Madison hours after police had cleared out the encampment in the street. The barricades that had blocked off the street have not returned but protestors could be seen walking in circles around the intersection while police monitored close by. This is a developing story; more information will be added as it becomes available. MADISON, Wis. – A protest encampment blocking off a Madison intersection for nearly two weeks is cleared for traffic once again. But those occupying the site at Willy and Baldwin Streets where police last month shot and killed 38-year-old Corey Ruiz did not leave quietly. Police made at least 10 arrests as protestors hurled rocks and lit multiple fires near the encampment that formed in the street in the days following Ruiz’s death. At least one protester was injured and taken to a hospital, while a Madison Fire Department said one city employee experienced a “medical event” but declined to elaborate. The clear-out order came after Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway had for days called for a peaceful end to the encampment, while stressing the street needed to be cleared out. “Multiple efforts and calls to end the occupation peacefully were made but ultimately ignored,” said Rhodes-Conway in a video release August 4. “The decision to invoke this option was not made lightly and was only made after almost two weeks of trying to resolve the situation peacefully, and voluntarily, with the people occupying the site.” Roughly 50 homeless individuals onsite were given the option to stay in hotels and were offered transportation there, says Rhodes-Conway. The clear-out followed growing concern from people living near the site that tensions were escalating, as well as from area businesses impacted financially by the street closure. Objects from the site are available for pickup at Demetral Field for an undetermined period of time. title: How the charity behind Madison, Wisconsin’s ‘autonomous zone’ raked in taxpayer money - Washington Examiner
text: A Wisconsin nonprofit group leading an illegal protest encampment that blocked traffic enjoys lavish federal, state, and local funding. The city of Madison awarded Freedom Inc. at least $149,/000 this year for initiatives such as “[Southeast Asian] and Black Youth Programs” after years of similar community-focused grants , records show. The city’s awards offer a glimpse of the more than $5 million in government funds that flowed to Freedom Inc. since 2020, including from the Department of Justice and state officials. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway is now condemning protesters reacting to a July police shooting after they camped out in the street for days, forcing shuttered businesses to lose money and emergency vehicles to detour. Online posts from those involved show Freedom Inc. pitching a tent inside the so-called “autonomous zone,” handing out supplies to protesters, and forming their “demands” to the city for policy change, the Washington Examiner reported. The city cleared the encampment on Tuesday morning after Rhodes-Conway spent days pleading with protesters to disperse on their own, according to media reports and Rhodes-Conway’s Tuesday comments . Rioters threw rocks and other debris at city workers during the dispersal, leading to “a small number” of arrests, she said. “Again, multiple efforts and calls to end the occupation peacefully were made but ultimately ignored,” the mayor said. Freedom Inc. stood firm on Tuesday, posting a joint Instagram post with other groups that declared “shame” on the arresting officers. The charity is organizing a “Mass Mobilization” protest for Tuesday evening at Wisconsin’s state capitol in Madison. Rhodes-Conway’s office and Freedom Inc. did not respond to the Washington Examiner’s requests for comment. Madison requires funding recipients to sign contracts explaining that they will comply with all relevant laws, ordinances, and regulations. Freedom Inc. is not currently accused of illegal activity. The Madison protests happened against the backdrop of a competitive Democratic primary election for governor on Aug. 11. Socialist candidate Francesca Hong , a state lawmaker who worked with Freedom Inc. on an education bill, told supporters in a July 22 statement that the group was “on the scene supporting community members” at the Madison demonstration. Like other leftist tax-exempt charities , Freedom Inc. attracts public funds for seemingly charitable programs while directing its overall resources toward political advocacy. The group described its mission in IRS filings as “to achieve social justice through coupling direct services with leadership development and community organizing.” Madison’s stated reasons for bankrolling Freedom Inc. since 2024 included “Older Adult Services,” “Family Strengthening” for black and Southeast Asian women, youth, and LGBT people, as well as a “Nkauj Hmoob Hmong Girls Group” and a “Black Girls Matter” program. Rhodes-Conway’s administration also announced $50,000 in 2020 for the nonprofit group to help foreigners overcome “obstacles such as immigration status and lack of documentation that prevent or make it more difficult” to obtain COVID-19 welfare funds. Former President Joe Biden’s DOJ also awarded Freedom Inc. $475,000 in 2024 “to enhance culturally specific services for victims of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking,” federal records show. Between 2023 and 2026, Wisconsin’s Department of Justice awarded the charity hundreds of thousands of dollars in federal DOJ funds related to crime victim programs . Freedom Inc. reported a separate $548,863 from the state’s Department of Children and Families in 2020 for “Immigrant and Refugee” work, “Under-represented Populations,” “Pandemic Shelter,” and other purposes. The DOJ and the two Wisconsin departments did not respond to requests for comment. WHO’S BEHIND WISCONSIN’S ANTI-POLICE ‘AUTONOMOUS ZONE’ TAKING OVER CITY STREETS? Though Rhodes-Conway described the recent encampment as disorganized, Freedom Inc. assumed a leading role by hosting educational sessions, providing “abolish police” signs and other gear, and serving as a contact point for planning protest “actions,” according to activists’ online posts. Freedom Inc. also worked with the family of Corey Ruiz , who was killed in the July shooting, to write down and distribute demands that Madison defund its police, the Freedom Road Socialist Organization said. “OUR ONLY ENEMY IS THE STATE,” Freedom Inc. declared on Saturday during the encampment.

title: Mayor explains why police cleared Willy Street: ‘You cannot please everyone’ - The Cap Times
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. In the two weeks since a Madison police officer fatally shot Corey Ruiz, Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said she’s heard from many community members with differing opinions about how the city should respond to the vigil and encampment that formed at the intersection where Ruiz was shot. At a press conference Wednesday, Rhodes-Conway said some residents wished the city had “come in on day one and stopped all the protests,” never allowing an encampment to form at Williamson and South Baldwin streets. Others wanted the city to allow the encampment to “go on for months and months and months.” A day after city officials and law enforcement decided to clear the intersection, Rhodes-Conway said there are “a lot of people who don’t think that we’ve done the right thing, but they all think that we’ve done the wrong thing for different reasons.” “I think few folks recognize the constraints that we operate under,” she said. “This is part of the business of being in government. You cannot please everyone, and so we collectively have to do our best to, yes, listen to our community, but also make the best decisions we can in the moment with the information that we have, prioritizing following the law, public safety, and then trying to do the best we can to take care of our community.” The press conference marked the mayor’s first after authorities removed the encampment . Police reported arresting or citing dozens of people as the intersection was being cleared. After protesters returned to the intersection Tuesday evening and began to block it again, police returned and cleared it again, arresting more people into Wednesday morning, according to police . Police Chief John Patterson said 22 people were arrested from Tuesday morning to Wednesday morning, though he didn’t provide details of when people were arrested or the charges. There was also one minor arrested who had a firearm, Patterson said. Police Chief John Patterson said 22 people were arrested between Tuesday morning and Wednesday morning where police cleared out an encampment and subsequent protests where Corey Ruiz fatally was shot by a police officer on July 22. Ruiz’s family issued a statement Wednesday thanking protesters while noting they “did not organize or authorize” the encampment. Ruiz’s family said they aren’t affiliated with any particular group. They said individuals “do not need our approval to demand accountability.” "To the activists who have shown up for Corey, thank you. Keep fighting for justice, peacefully and together,” the family wrote. “We ask everyone at that corner (Williamson and Baldwin streets) and everyone wearing a badge to keep this peaceful. No one else should be hurt in Corey’s name.” City leaders initially allowed protesters to barricade the intersection after the July 22 shooting so people could mourn and protest, but they increasingly raised concern about its safety and impact on the neighborhood. Over the last week, Rhodes-Conway issued a series of escalating statements about the city's response to the encampment. On Aug. 1, she said the city was “preparing for a respectful transition” and the next day said towing notices had been issued to vehicles blocking traffic. Dozens of city officials, Madison police officers and Wisconsin State Patrol officers converged on the site around 5 a.m. Tuesday to clear the encampment and reopen the intersection to traffic. After a clash with protesters, the city announced the street opened at 9 a.m. Hours after Madison police fatally shot Corey Ruiz, community members gathered near Williamson Street and erected a memorial encampment. City officials moved memorial items off the street. Other belongings were packed up in boxes and taken to Demetral Park about a mile north for people to pick up. By 11:30 a.m. Tuesday, police reported arresting 16 people and booking them into the Dane County Jail, mostly on charges of unlawful assembly and obstructing a police officer. Ten other people were cited and released. “The decision to invoke this option was not made lightly and was only made after almost two weeks of trying to resolve the situation peacefully and voluntarily with the people occupying the site,” Rhodes-Conway said Wednesday. Asked what led the city to remove the encampment, the mayor said the decision came down to “a balance of resources available and the time to make the plans that we needed to make.” Rhodes-Conway said input from business owners in the area about the encampment’s impact “definitely was a factor.” “Perhaps even more importantly,” she added, residents’ concerns about “how unsafe the situation was” drove the city’s response. She said an “increasing number” of people experiencing homelessness were showing up at the site, noting they continued to come “even after we had provided some of them with other options,” such as hotel vouchers. Before officials cleared the encampment Tuesday, Rhodes-Conway said city staff provided emergency assistance to dozens of individuals at the site, adding “most people left voluntarily.” From the start of the encampment to its clearing, about 70 people accepted vouchers to local hotels from the city, Jim O’Keefe, the city’s community development director, said at the press conference. “I felt like when we tipped over into ‘we are now just attracting more and more folks who are experiencing homelessness to come camp in the middle of the street,’ it was clear that the situation was increasingly dangerous for everybody, and having a huge toll on the neighbors who are in the immediate vicinity,” Rhodes-Conway said. “And I felt like that was not something that could continue.” A Madison police officer stands near the site as items from a memorial for Corey Ruiz are removed Tuesday. Around 8 p.m. Tuesday, protesters regathered at Williamson and South Baldwin streets with tents, according to police. Rhodes-Conway said protesters “briefly” blocked traffic at the intersection and where East Washington Avenue intersects with South Baldwin Street during the night. Police left Williamson and South Baldwin streets at one point in the evening Tuesday in an “attempt to de-escalate the situation,” according to police . Protestors “emptied dumpsters and trash cans throughout the intersection, rendering it impassable,” and protesters set five fires in the streets, which were extinguished by the Fire Department, police said. Patterson said Wednesday he “overall” supported the way police handled the protests. He said officers at the site Tuesday “never used tear gas.” He was aware of one incident where an officer deployed pepper spray. “I think they maintained professionalism. They maintained discretion. Frankly, they showed de-escalation when appropriate,” the chief said. Patterson acknowledged trust with the Police Department is “very fragile right now” and said there is a “tremendous amount of work to do.” “I said this last year when I applied for this job. I think it's an incredible Police Department. I think it's filled with incredible people. But we're not perfect,” he said. “I identified some areas that I think we're going to make immediate progress on, hopefully, or immediate steps to do some restructuring to help us get there.” Police Chief John Patterson and Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway spoke to reporters Wednesday morning for the first time since the city cleared the Willy Street encampment that formed where police fatally shot Corey Ruiz. Madison officers and other city employees had a physical altercation with Aeiramique Glass, the city’s interim independent police monitor, on Tuesday afternoon. The Police Department released drone footage of the encounter, which captures multiple officers surrounding Glass after she is grabbed by one officer as she turned away from them. Patterson said the altercation is being reviewed by investigators. In a video posted to social media and circulated by several local news outlets, Glass says after the encounter that “they've been wanting to do this to me” and “I will burn this city down.” The video appears to show blood on one of Glass’ hands. The attorney for the independent police monitor’s office told Madison 365 that Glass’ remark was a “figurative, idiomatic expression.” “It's disturbing any time a city employee is calling for violence,” Rhodes-Conway said Wednesday in response to Glass’ comments. “But as the (City Council) has made clear time and time again, they want that office to be independent of my office, and it is. So I think I would ask council leadership what they think the path forward is there.” The city’s Office of the Independent Monitor is overseen by the Police Civilian Oversight Board. The office provides oversight of police separate from that of the city’s Police and Fire Commission. Rhodes-Conway said the city is cooperating with a state Department of Justice investigation into Ruiz’s death and will fully cooperate with any investigation by the Office of the Independent Monitor. A few protesters were at Williamson and South Baldwin streets Wednesday morning with police officers nearby. Traffic was flowing through the intersection and remnants of the previous night were evident, including what appeared to be a large burn mark on the pavement near South Baldwin and Wilson streets. Patterson said police will continue to staff the intersection for “the foreseeable future.” “I’m hopeful that we’re not visible, or we don’t need to be visible,” Patterson said, noting the Police Department is working with city partners to have them “be at the forefront whenever possible.” “We recognize that to some people in the area, we are what's causing the agitation, our presence,” he added. “So we don’t want to do that.” The Cap Times welcomes tips from readers to help us inform our community. Email tips@captimes.com or visit captimes.com/tips for more options. Rhodes-Conway said the city will continue monitoring the intersection. People had until noon Wednesday to collect personal belongings at Demetral Park. Remaining items will be held by the city’s Parks Division and can be retrieved through the division’s typical process for lost belongings. Rhodes-Conway expressed a desire to coordinate with Ruiz’s family and community leaders on building another memorial site, noting the city has identified areas in a nearby parking lane. Ruiz’s family said in their statement that they welcomed a memorial that ”honors the man he was.” “Corey was quiet, soft-spoken and giving. He thought about other people before he thought about himself. He had a family who loved him. He was not alone in this world, and he was not without help,” the family wrote. “We ask that he not be reduced to a label he never carried.” While Rhodes-Conway emphasized she wanted to “center” the desire of Ruiz’s family first, she acknowledged a “broader community desire” to be a part of the next steps forward. The mayor said she is hearing “many conflicting things” from the community that she hopes the city can reconcile through continued conversations. “We have heard in my office from so many people expressing pain for so many different reasons. We hear you. I acknowledge that pain, and I just ask that we continue to work together in a peaceful way,” she said. “There is so much work to do to support each other in this community and to make a more just Madison and a more just society. I still believe that we will do better working together than causing more harm and destruction.”
