title: Arrest count at Madison encampment site climbs to 22 after overnight skirmishes - WPR
text: Twenty-two people have been arrested since the city of Madison began clearing out a protest encampment on the city’s near east side, officials said Wednesday after a night marked by clashes between protesters and police. Madison Police Chief John Patterson could not offer a breakdown of how many arrests occurred during overnight skirmishes compared to arrests from throughout the day Tuesday, when the city began forcibly clearing an encampment at the site where police fatally shot Corey Ruiz on July 22. But Patterson said between 30 and 40 protesters remained in the streets for hours overnight, setting fires and expanding the footprint of their nearly two-week-old protest. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. “I saw things last night that I haven’t seen in years,” he said.   Patterson said the city had issued 10 citations, and a minor was detained after being found with a firearm. He did not say whether the juvenile is facing charges. Wednesday’s press conference comes after a fraught 24 hours that began in the early hours of Tuesday when city workers — including parks and sanitation workers and law enforcement from multiple jurisdictions — began removing items from the Williamson Street intersection where protesters and, later, people without homes had established a blocked-off protest and camping zone. Tensions continued throughout the day. After the site reopened to traffic, protesters attempted to block it off again. A city council meeting scheduled for the evening — in virtual format-only, with city spokesperson Dylan Brogan citing threats made against elected officials — ran for almost eight hours, concluding at about 2:30 a.m. Wednesday. During the evening and into the night, some people returned to the site, starting fires and clashing with law enforcement, according to dramatic video of the scenes posted on social media. “Many in this community are angry and grief-stricken over Corey Ruiz’s life being cut short by the police. Those feelings are completely legitimate, and I feel them, too,” Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said at Wednesday’s press conference. “But as mayor of Madison, I will not condone or accept that the solution is to further divide our community by causing harm to your neighbors and local businesses, harassing bystanders or setting fires in city streets.” Rhodes-Conway said she and the city have weathered criticism from every side over how they have handled the presence of the encampment over nearly two weeks . The street where Ruiz, a 38-year-old Black man, was killed by police had been converted into a makeshift memorial with artwork and messages on the street, but also grew to include tents, grills and mattresses. “There are people who wish that we had come in on day one and stopped all of the protests and never let an encampment happen. And then there are people who wish that we would let that encampment go on for months and months and months,” she said. “There are a lot of people who don’t think that we’ve done the right thing, but they all think that we’ve done the wrong thing for different reasons.” Along with protesters, the site had also become a gathering point for people without housing. Jim O’Keefe, Madison’s Director of Community Development, said Wednesday that about 70 people had accepted city vouchers to stay in hotels for up to a week, and that the city had also provided transportation to hotels or other locations. Belongings from the encampment were brought to Demetral Park, on the city’s east side. The mayor said that items not claimed by Wednesday can be retrieved by going through the city parks department. Rhodes-Conway said that the city would continue to monitor the intersection and ensure traffic could continue back through the site unimpeded going forward. She also said the city is “ready to coordinate with Corey’s family” to establish a memorial to Ruiz. “We are absolutely committed to allowing space for some sort of memorial,” she said. “It just can’t be in the middle of the traffic lights.” On Wednesday afternoon, Ruiz’s family released a statement through civil rights attorney Ben Crump. “Our family did not organize or authorize the encampment at Williamson and Baldwin streets,” the family’s statement reads. They disavowed a statement circulated by some activists that purported to come from the family and included a list of demands, saying, “We were never asked, and we never agreed to the statement released in our name.” “The city cleared that intersection yesterday,” the statement concludes. “We ask everyone at that corner and everyone wearing a badge to keep this peaceful. No one else should be hurt in Corey’s name.” Video taken overnight show chaotic scenes over a few blocks. In one, a line of police officers in riot gear block off an intersection at East Washington, a major thoroughfare extending to Madison’s interstates. The Madison Fire Department responded to five fires , according to that agency, set around the intersection in city dumpsters and trash cans. At the start of Tuesday’s meeting of the Madison Common Council, Alder Barbara Harrington-McKinney asked if leaders could suspend the meeting and reconvene later “because there is craziness in the streets.” The meeting continued, with about eight hours of public comment while chaos raged on Williamson Street. No action was taken. Among those involved in altercations with police was the city’s interim police monitor, Aeiramique Glass. In drone video released by the city, she is seen confronting officers at the site. She appears to push one of them before a group of officers subdues her. In a social media video posted after the altercation, she shows a bloodied hand and says, “I will f—— burn this city down.” Rhodes-Conway on Wednesday called it “disturbing” for a city employee to call for violence. Patterson praised how his agency has handled the protests and ensuing flare-ups throughout the day and into the night. He said that neighboring Sun Prairie and the state police were also involved. Patterson said no tear gas or projectiles had been deployed and one officer used pepper spray. The protest zone was erected almost immediately after Ruiz was shot dead in the street, after being apprehended by police officers. Police say he brandished a knife, cutting one police officer, before he was killed. The shooting was captured on video, sparking days of community protest that culminated in a barricaded encampment on the commercial thoroughfare affectionately referred to as Willy Street. For days leading up to Tuesday’s clearance actions, Rhodes-Conway had been calling for an end to the encampment, which she said was straining local businesses and disrupting residents’ daily lives. On Wednesday, she said there was no inciting incident that made Tuesday the day. She said the city had tried to involve other agencies foremost, using police as a last resort. “Often the presence of police officers is part of the escalation, and so we have tried very hard to limit police response to what’s necessary and to use other city staff,” she said. Patterson said city agencies would “staff the intersection for the foreseeable future” to ensure that residents and businesses can return to regular life. “We recognize that for some people in the area, we are what’s causing agitation — our presence — and so we don’t want to do that,” Patterson said. Ruiz’s death is under investigation by the state Department of Justice. Separately, Madison operates an independent police oversight board, with an individual police monitor. Glass, the interim independent monitor involved in the altercation Tuesday, has called on the city to release its records to her office now, instead of after the DOJ investigation concludes. “I should not have to wait,” she said in a July 28 interview with WPR’s “ Wisconsin Today .” On Wednesday, Patterson said that’s not his call to make. “I’ve had discussions literally every single day, multiple times a day, with (the Division of Criminal Investigation) about what updates can be shared. … I’m assured they continue to progress in their investigation,” he said. “I feel it’s really my job to allow the investigating agency to do their work and make some of these decisions on records as well. I don’t want to be a chief that’s going to try to influence decisions one way or the other.” At Tuesday night’s city council meeting, Madison City Attorney Mike Haas said the city’s official position is that those records cannot be provided to the police monitor until the Wisconsin DOJ investigation is over. Editor’s note: WPR’s Sarah Lehr contributed reporting. title: Madison police clear encampment at shooting site, arrest 16 - WXPR
text: This story comes from the  Wisconsin News Collaborative , a partnership of Wisconsin public media newsrooms, including WUWM, Wisconsin Public Radio, and WXPR. Madison police arrested 16 people Tuesday morning as officials moved to clear an encampment at the site where a Madison police officer shot Corey Ruiz on July 22 . The city released the latest arrest totals Tuesday evening. After city workers approached the encampment around 5 a.m. and some of those occupying the space did not leave, a police spokesperson said the demonstrators threw rocks and set fires. Police moved in, and the street reopened to traffic just after 9 a.m. For close to 13 days, the area had been blocked off by a memorial to Ruiz, a 38-year-old Black man. That memorial morphed into an encampment spanning several city blocks, as people brought tents, mattresses and grills to the site at South Baldwin and Williamson streets, known as Willy Street to Madison residents. After the street reopened, protesters attempted to block it intermittently throughout the day, a city spokesperson confirmed Tuesday evening. Traffic continued through the day, although demonstrators at times swarmed back into the intersection. By the time the sun was up Tuesday, garbage and city pick-up trucks were carting things away as police in riot gear stood by. Bulldozers and forklifts rolled through the street. Some residents watched from the sidewalk as officials worked to restore the intersection. A small group of protesters remained, with one person shouting through a bullhorn and some chanting, “No justice, no peace” and “no racist police.” The tents that had made up the encampment were gone. Around 8 a.m., city street sweepers moved in to clean the area. City workers placed memorial objects into boxes that were later taken to Demetral Field, a nearby park. Items include a sculpture of a raised fist that had been part of a memorial for George Floyd in Minneapolis and was brought to the Madison site. “For nearly two weeks, I and city staff have been working day and night to peacefully resolve the occupation of Williamson and Baldwin without law enforcement intervention,” Madison Mayor Satya-Rhodes Conway said in a video message on Tuesday , adding that city officials plan to work with the Ruiz family and other community members to create an ongoing space to grieve. “But that work could not begin while city streets were occupied, local businesses were on the verge of closing and residents in the Marquette neighborhood were caught in the middle of an increasingly volatile situation,” she added. Madison police officers stand in an intersection where a memorial for Corey Ruiz had been set up and maintained by protesters in an encampment Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, in Madison, Wis. The city used street sweepers to clean up the area and re-open it to traffic. Angela Major/WPR Madison Police Department spokesperson Stephanie Fryer told WPR the city initially sent in non-police staffers to tell people to clear the area. She said the city sent its Community Alternative Response Emergency Services or CARES team, and that street division workers walked through the encampment with a megaphone “essentially telling people now is the time to begin grabbing your belongings and leave.” Fryer said police got involved after people began starting fires and throwing objects at Streets Division workers. “We also had been told that they were taking candles that were lit for the memorial and also throwing those in the air, trying to start fire that way,” Fryer said. The mayor’s on update on Tuesday specifically mentioned two fires. It also said that people threw rocks. Two people protesting were injured while the encampment was being cleared, according to Fryer. One person was evaluated by medical staff and taken to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, and the other refused treatment. Fryer said a city employee was taken to the hospital after suffering a “medical event.” Fryer emphasized that no one’s personal property from the site was being thrown away. “The only things that were removed and actually thrown away were the items that obviously were started on fire or actual trash in the area,” Fryer said. Samuel Brooks of Portage was among those cited. He said he was handcuffed, given a court date and later released by police after being at the encampment early Tuesday. Brooks said he previously spent more than a decade living in the Willy Street neighborhood and had been at the encampment overnight. “We saw city vehicles moving around, and then we got word that the police were massing nearby, and yeah, they just circled up,” Brooks said. Brooks said city officials arrived some time before dawn. When that happened, he said he was among the people trying to wake up a homeless couple who were sleeping in a tent. “Bulldozer was coming straight for their tent,” Brooks said. “People were trying to get things under his wheels so we could get these people out of the way before they came through.” Protesters comfort each other as a memorial for Corey Ruiz, a man who was shot and killed by Madison police, is moved out of the intersection where the shooting occurred Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, in Madison, Wis. City workers and police also removed an encampment in the area. Angela Major/WPRBrooks’ citation report showed he was apprehended on suspicion of obstruction and resisting arrest. It listed a $449 fine from the city. He said he wasn’t worried about the citation. “I’ve got resources,” said Brooks, who is white. “I think my skin is a shield against police violence in a lot of situations.” Chaous Riddle of Madison said she was also at the encampment when it was forcibly cleared early Tuesday. “The whole thing was actually horrific,” Riddle said, as she recalled seeing heavy machinery and construction equipment plowing through the area. “They came in with their ToolCats. They barely missed people because it was dark.” In an update Sunday, Rhodes-Conway said the city partnered with local agencies to provide hotel vouchers to roughly  “25 to 30” who were homeless  and staying at the encampment. According to the mayor’s latest update , another 10 people were placed in hotel rooms on Monday. “The 50 or so unsheltered individuals who were onsite were given the option to stay in hotels and were offered transportation there. A significant majority decided to do so,” Rhodes-Conway said on Tuesday. “This effort was done with as much compassion as possible under less-than-ideal circumstances.” Alyse Weber of Madison lives just four blocks from where the encampment took place. For days, she says people were bringing items to the encampment, including food, electrolyte drinks, diapers and medical supplies. After the encampment was cleared, Weber broke down in tears as she described people looking through boxes for their items. “I was looking for my unhoused neighbors — people that I ignored, people that I’m sure my neighbors ignored out of fear of the unknown,” Weber said. “And, for the last two weeks, we’ve seen them and loved them, and been in community with them. And I certainly hope that part continues.” The encampment started as a protest site following the death of Ruiz in a struggle with police. It has blocked a busy thoroughfare and shut down traffic to businesses and residences in the neighborhood since. Police said Ruiz, who was homeless, produced a knife during a struggle with police, injuring one officer. Police used a Taser that they said was unsuccessful, and then an officer fatally shot Ruiz. The shooting, which was captured on video by bystanders, is being investigated by the state Department of Justice. Protesters have called for a permanent memorial to Ruiz as one of their demands following the shooting. Devon Snyder, a civil rights activist who is part of Madison’s Police Civilian Oversight Board, said he found the city’s move to clear the site “hypocritical.” “This is disheartening,” Snyder told a WPR reporter at the scene. “Something that was a tragedy, built a beautiful community. And they come and do this? … They want to call this an unlawful assembly. If this was an unlawful assembly, then why did the city support this for the last week?” Following the shooting of Ruiz, demonstrators dragged trash carts to block off the area. There were also homemade barriers around the encampment, including nails hammered into a strips of wood that was placed on the pavement. City officials also put up official barricades and announced on July 23 that the area of the encampment would be blocked off “until future notice.” At times throughout the last two week, the city has also parked salt tracks around the encampment to help block it off. A private company supplied port-a-potties to the site, and Rhodes-Conway has refuted reports that the city provided any portable toilets to the encampment. The move to clear the encampment comes after days of escalating warnings by Rhodes-Conway . On Sunday, she said the city would issue tow orders for vehicles blocking the street. On Monday, she signaled city action was imminent. “Countless efforts have been made to convince people that the occupation of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street is counterproductive,” Rhodes-Conway said in a statement Monday. “A huge amount of patience has been given because the last thing Madison needs is a large-scale police operation. That’s why those occupying the area need to leave immediately.”Kilfoy Flores, former chair of Madison’s Police Civilian Oversight Board, criticized the mayor for not being seen at the encampment before it was forcibly broken up. “I think that she should have come and mourned with her constituents,” Flores said. “Coming and mourning somebody’s death doesn’t mean that you’re choosing a side. It means that you’re coming to support your community who’s in pain.” Madison Alder Davy Mayer and Dane County Supervisor Yogesh Chawla were at Demetral Field on Tuesday morning as people sorted through boxes from the encampment. “They’re also being very careful because there were a large number of sharps found on site,” Mayer said. “So a lot of people have protective gloves that are going through things.” Mayer and Chawla represent the near east side neighborhood where Ruiz was shot. Chawla noted that rain could be coming and said there’s a plan to cover memorial items with tarps if that happens. “(We wanted) to make this difficult process as orderly and efficient and as compassionate as possible,” Chawla said. Mayer said he did not have an estimate early Tuesday of how much clean up would cost the neighborhood. After street sweepers went through, graffiti messages remained, including on sidewalks and the Baldwin Corners apartment building. Going forward, Mayer said the plan is to create a memorial not solely to Ruiz, but rather to “all the victims of police violence.” In addition to the killing of Ruiz, Madison’s Willy Street neighborhood has been the site of two other fatal shootings by police, one in 2012 and another in 2015.

text: MADISON, Wis. - Madison police responded to overnight unrest and street fires after the clearing of a protest encampment sparked all-day demonstrations near Baldwin and Williamson. After a lull mid-day, crowds returned Wednesday night. What we know: After all-day chaos Tuesday and overnight, FOX6 News crews in the area of Baldwin and Williamson found a peaceful atmosphere throughout Wednesday morning and into the afternoon.  FREE DOWNLOAD: Get breaking news alerts in the FOX LOCAL Mobile app for iOS or Android A circle of flowers still marks where police shot and killed Corey Ruiz two weeks earlier. There were only a few protesters at the intersection by Wednesday afternoon.  Protesters return to intersection of Baldwin and Williamson in Madison on Wednesday evening, Aug. 5. "I’m bringing flowers to commemorate the death of not just this person but lots of people that have been killed by the police," said Pamela Dempsey, who lives in the area. "I am sad, as a person that was born in Madison, that people couldn’t take the time to have a dialogue. We’re supposed to be advanced mammals. I don’t understand why we are working this way." But later Wednesday, a crowd of protesters returned to the intersection and police lined the corners while trying to keep traffic open. What we know: Demonstrations took place all day Tuesday after city crews cleared a protest encampment that formed at the intersection of Baldwin and Williamson, where police shot and killed Corey Ruiz nearly two weeks prior. The Madison Police Department said protesters occupied Baldwin Street with tents, telling officers that the situation was "about to get bad," at around 8 p.m. Tuesday. Madison unrest on Tuesday night, Aug. 4, 2026. Madison Police Chief John Patterson said a group of between 30 and 40 people yelled profanity and insults at officers for hours on Tuesday. "Our police officers, frankly, for hours stood there and took profanity, insults, yelling, really challenging moments," he said. "I am very proud of how they handled the situation. I think they maintained professionalism. They maintained discretion, and they, frankly, they showed de-escalation when it was appropriate." Demonstrators ignited five street fires as authorities tried clearing protesters from Washington Avenue toward Baldwin Street. Officers re-claimed the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin after midnight.  "There were 22 physical arrests in totality," Patterson said Wednesday. "That includes, you know, the initial efforts in the morning (Tuesday) through late or early this morning (Wednesday) I guess, and then 10 individuals were cited." What they're saying: Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway, Police Chief John Patterson and other city officials held a news conference at 11 a.m. to provide an update Wednesday. "I saw things last night that I haven't seen in years. I feel like our trust is very fragile right now. We have a tremendous amount of work to do," Patterson said. "I think this is an incredible police department. I think it's filled with incredible people, but we're not perfect. We have work we need to do. I've identified some areas that I think we're going to make immediate progress on, hopefully, and immediate steps to do some restructuring to help us get there, but that takes time into the mayor's point. It's near impossible to do it when you're in the middle of a crisis." Madison officials held a news conference Wednesday following protests and overnight unrest. Rhodes-Conway reiterated that the streets cannot stay closed and people need to be able to access their homes and businesses. She added that the city is "committed" to allowing space for some sort of memorial, just not in the middle of traffic. "I know that there's work that the police chief has already identified that needs to happen. It's very hard to do any of that work when we're in immediate crisis response," Rhodes-Conway said of starting to work on things the community has asked for, such as a memorial and policy change at the local and state levels.  "I would ask our community to, let's keep the streets open, and let's, certainly, we invite people to exercise their First Amendment rights, but we need to be able to shift to that longer-term work right now." The backstory: Madison Police Chief John Patterson said officers responded to calls about a man stealing bicycles and checking car doors and confronted him on July 22, but he rode away on a bicycle. Police later encountered the man again, at Baldwin and Williamson, and the man "fell or was pulled off the bicycle." There was a struggle in the middle of the intersection, and police said the man pulled out a knife and injured an officer. title: 'Our community is in pain': Madison leaders defend response to protests - spectrumnews1.com
text: MADISON, Wis. — The encampment on Madison's Williamson Street may be gone , but unrest continues in the city. Madison leaders came together for a press conference Wednesday two weeks after 38-year-old Corey Ruiz was shot and killed by a Madison police officer. Mayor Satya-Rhodes Conway said the feelings of anger by the community are legitimate, but she believes the “ illegal encampment ” that developed from Ruiz’s memorial was not the way to enact change. “I felt like when we tipped over into, we are now just attracting more and more folks who are experiencing homelessness to camp in the middle of the street, it became clear that the situation was becoming increasingly dangerous for everybody,” Rhodes-Conway said. The mayor said the intent of the city was to reach a peaceful and mutual end to the occupation . Rhodes-Conway said when that didn’t develop, the city moved to clear the encampment Tuesday morning without the use of law enforcement. She said police only got involved after protesters began throwing objects at city employees and lit multiple fires in the street. Police Chief John Patterson said protests continued late into the night Tuesday after the encampment was cleared, with 22 people being arrested at that time. Patterson said law enforcement presence will continue on Williamson Street for the foreseeable future, while also trying to give space to the community. “We recognize that for some people in the area, we are what’s causing agitation, and so we don’t want to do that,” Patterson said. “We’re trying very hard to work with our partners, city streets employees, parks employees, to have them be at the forefront whenever possible.” Looking back at everything that’s transpired over the last two weeks, Patterson acknowledged there’s a growing rift between the Madison Police Department and the people of Madison. “I feel like our trust is very fragile right now; we have a tremendous amount of work to do,” Patterson said. “I think this is an incredible police department, but we’re not perfect.” Rhodes-Conway said that distrust also extends from community members to city leadership. title: Beyond bodycams: Wisconsin killing reopens debate about police accountability - The Guardian
text: A fter bystander footage of police killing Corey Ruiz – a 38-year-old Black man in Madison, Wisconsin – spread online, many questioned why the officers were not wearing body cameras, a standard practice for more than 80% of police nationwide. Police said Ruiz was wielding a knife and injured an officer; multiple bystander videos showed he was shot while already detained and on the ground . Ruiz’s family called for mandatory body cameras in the city, along with charges for the four officers involved . People across the political spectrum echoed the demand for cameras, including Madison’s police chief. Within days, Madison’s mayor, Satya Rhodes-Conway, announced she would include funding for body cameras in the next city budget. But local organizers say bodycams are just one element of holding police accountable after harm has already been done; some would rather see community control over policing, and policies that reduce police interaction and address underlying issues, such as mental health services and homelessness support. (Ruiz was unhoused at the time of his death.) View image in fullscreen Protesters in downtown Madison, Wisconsin, on 25 July 2026, three days after the fatal shooting of Corey Ruiz by police. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images These tensions came to a head on Tuesday after Rhodes-Conway sent police to take down a community memorial and encampment at the intersection where Ruiz was killed after warning protesters about resident complaints . Nearly two dozen protesters were arrested and another 10 given citations within 24 hours; officers and the city’s independent police monitor also got into a physical altercation . What’s happening in Madison, advocates say, is indicative of how cities are still grappling with what police accountability and intervention should look like six years after millions marched against racist police violence and called for radical changes to policing after George Floyd’s murder. Organizers who spoke to the Guardian said that by focusing on body cameras, the conversation has strayed from the officers facing consequences, let alone reckoning with how to stop police violence from happening at all. According to the Mapping Police Violence project, 2025 was the deadliest year for police killings since 2013 . Even though only 7% of Madison’s population is Black, more than half of the police department’s “use of force” cases were against Black residents last year. “If we wanna really be able to address issues like the killings and harms and surveillance of Black and brown communities, we need to be thinking about, how do we take power away from these institutions and put it into the community?” said Zon Moua, senior director of organizing at the local community group Freedom Inc. In 2020, after the police murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis galvanized millions to protest racism and police violence, cities across the country began listening to local community organizers about possible systemic solutions. Some established more community oversight; others created programs to replace police with mental health workers in crisis situations. While there were calls to defund the police across the country, that demand was quickly overwritten and rejected in the next few years: by the spring of 2022, then president Joe Biden was leading bipartisan cheers to “fund the police” at his State of the Union address, and police funding had actually gone up . Madison is one of those cities that vowed to do better. It had been rocked by two police killings during what were likely mental health crises: of Paul Heenan , a white 30-year-old, in 2012, and of 19-year-old Tony Robinson, who was biracial and shot dead by police in 2015 on the same Madison street as Ruiz. Juliana Bennett was a 21-year-old University of Wisconsin-Madison student and racial justice organizer when she was elected to the city’s common council (Madison’s version of a city council) in 2021. She helped launch a mental health crisis response program that sends a community paramedic and a crisis worker to respond to nonviolent 911 “behavior health” calls. The community-led police-civilian oversight board also created the office of the independent police monitor ; the two work together to review police misconduct and violence cases and make recommendations on police discipline, use of force and other policing issues such as hiring, training and complaint processes. At least three bodycam proposals have also come before the common council since 2020, but each time they were rejected or pushed back for further research, because of estimated costs or in favor of a pilot program. View image in fullscreen Mourners visit the site where Corey Ruiz was shot and killed by police in Madison, Wisconsin. Photograph: Jim Vondruska/Reuters A six-month “ feasibility review ” on mandating body cameras in 2021 found that “some marginalized communities” in Madison were strongly opposed to the cameras over fears of surveillance, among other concerns. When the city launched a body camera pilot program in 2024 , an analysis found the tech did not affect police behavior or community-police relations in the city. Bennett twice voted against bodycams, citing that one of the people commissioned to perform an independent report was on the payroll of a major body camera manufacturer , and that she would rather the costs proposed for the cameras go toward addressing the city’s homelessness crisis, an underlying issue that can lead to police intervention and an important priority for constituents. “When serving on the council, it was a little frustrating to me that most of my colleagues were disinterested in making any real substantive changes to policing,” said Bennett, who is now running for gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong ’s state assembly seat. Read more In the aftermath of Ruiz’s killing, Madison was scrutinized for being the only big city in the state without police bodycams. But research on their effectiveness has been mixed. While body cameras can help with substantiating “use of force” claims against police, particularly in cases brought by people of color, according to a 2025 study, investigations from ProPublica and the New York Times Magazine in 2023 found that the public almost never sees bodycam footage: police departments largely have the discretion to deny requests, redact or edit footage, and refuse to punish officers, sometimes not even following their own “stated policies of transparency”. “We’re under an illusion that body-worn cameras are a good way to stop police violence from happening in the first place,” said Lauren Bonds, executive director of the National Police Accountability Project. “It’s more that they’re helpful if police violence happens and there’s already a program in place limiting police responses.” The 22 July shooting sparked a street protest movement of hundreds of Madison residents and the memorial encampment at the cross streets where Ruiz was shot . Handmade art, chalked messages, bouquets of flowers and signs reading “Justice for Corey” covered the asphalt. A handful of residents slept in tents, weathering the extreme heat, while other community members held cookouts and brought bottled water. Today there’s little sign left of the gathering place. After Rhodes-Conway ordered the encampment to be taken down on Tuesday, citing complaints from nearby residents, 16 people were arrested , 10 people were given citations and others were pepper-sprayed during the shutdown. Protesters overtook the streets on Tuesday night, leading to another six arrests; police again cleared the intersection by the early-morning hours. Both Bennett and Freedom Inc issued condemnations of Rhodes-Conway’s decision to close the encampment, and questioned why the officer who killed Ruiz had not yet been charged. View image in fullscreen A memorial for Corey Ruiz in Madison, Wisconsin, on 24 July 2026. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images The city’s current interim independent police monitor, Aeiramique “Meeka” Glass, also nearly came to blows with nearby police officers at the encampment clear-out. In investigating Ruiz’s killing, Glass has accused the police of denying her evidence and subpoenaed the department. On 4 August, she issued a public statement accusing the mayor’s office, the common council, the city attorney and the district attorney of obstructing, or enabling the obstruction of, the collection of evidence. Glass and the police-civilian oversight board have also called for allocating 1% of the police budget – a little less than $1m – to further bolster the monitor’s office with more personnel; community group Freedom Inc is calling for the board to receive 5% of the police budget. Meanwhile, local organizers who previously expressed opposition or skepticism to body cameras have been harassed by pro-police conservatives. They said Ruiz’s killing – and the current pace of police violence – suggest that at a structural level, things may not have changed much since the 2020 protests. But they will keep pushing for it. “With dozens of witnesses, filmed on camera from multiple angles, why are we [talking about body cameras and] not talking about investing in housing and support systems to make sure people like Corey have their basic needs met?” said Bennett.

text: MADISON (WKOW) -- The family of Corey Ruiz released a statement Wednesday addressing plans for a possible memorial in his honor. Ruiz was shot and killed by a Madison police officer on July 22. In the statement, the family said, "We would welcome a respectful memorial for Corey that honors the man he was." Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway also expressed support for creating a memorial space, but said it cannot interfere with traffic. "I just want to say again, because I think people don't believe this, we are absolutely committed to allowing space for some sort of memorial," Rhodes-Conway said during a news conference. "It just can't be in the middle of the traffic lanes."

title: Arrests at Madison Encampment Site Climb to 22 After Overnight Skirmishes - Urban Milwaukee
text: 30 to 40 protesters of Corey Ruiz killing set fires and clashed with police in early hours of Tuesday. Police Chief John Patterson, left, and Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway address reporters about the Williamson Street protest encampment on Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026 in Madison, Wis. Anya van Wagtendonk/WPR Twenty-two people have been arrested since the city of Madison began clearing out a protest encampment on the city’s near east side, officials said Wednesday after a night marked by clashes between protesters and police. Madison Police Chief John Patterson could not offer a breakdown of how many arrests occurred during overnight skirmishes compared to arrests from throughout the day Tuesday, when the city began forcibly clearing an encampment at the site where police fatally shot Corey Ruiz on July 22. But Patterson said between 30 and 40 protesters remained in the streets for hours overnight, setting fires and expanding the footprint of their nearly two-week-old protest. “I saw things last night that I haven’t seen in years,” he said. Patterson said the city had issued 10 citations, and a minor was detained after being found with a firearm. He did not say whether the juvenile is facing charges. A sign cautions drivers headed toward an encampment Monday, Aug. 3, 2026, in Madison, Wis., which is occupied in response to Madison police shooting and killing Corey Ruiz. Angela Major/WPR Wednesday’s press conference comes after a fraught 24 hours that began in the early hours of Tuesday when city workers — including parks and sanitation workers and law enforcement from multiple jurisdictions — began removing items from the Williamson Street intersection where protesters and, later, people without homes had established a blocked-off protest and camping zone. Tensions continued throughout the day. After the site reopened to traffic, protesters attempted to block it off again. A city council meeting scheduled for the evening — in virtual format-only, with city spokesperson Dylan Brogan citing threats made against elected officials — ran for almost eight hours, concluding at about 2:30 a.m. Wednesday. During the evening and into the night, some people returned to the site, starting fires and clashing with law enforcement, according to dramatic video of the scenes posted on social media. “Many in this community are angry and grief-stricken over Corey Ruiz’s life being cut short by the police. Those feelings are completely legitimate, and I feel them, too,” Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said at Wednesday’s press conference. “But as mayor of Madison, I will not condone or accept that the solution is to further divide our community by causing harm to your neighbors and local businesses, harassing bystanders or setting fires in city streets.” Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway, flanked by city employees including Police Chief John Patterson, far left, addresses reporters about the Williamson Street protest encampment on Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026 in Madison, Wis. Anya van Wagtendonk/WPR Rhodes-Conway said she and the city have weathered criticism from every side over how they have handled the presence of the encampment over nearly two weeks . The street where Ruiz, a 38-year-old Black man, was killed by police had been converted into a makeshift memorial with artwork and messages on the street, but also grew to include tents, grills and mattresses. “There are people who wish that we had come in on day one and stopped all of the protests and never let an encampment happen. And then there are people who wish that we would let that encampment go on for months and months and months,” she said. “There are a lot of people who don’t think that we’ve done the right thing, but they all think that we’ve done the wrong thing for different reasons.” Along with protesters, the site had also become a gathering point for people without housing. Jim O’Keefe, Madison’s Director of Community Development, said Wednesday that about 70 people had accepted city vouchers to stay in hotels for up to a week, and that the city had also provided transportation to hotels or other locations. Belongings from the encampment were brought to Demetral Park, on the city’s east side. The mayor said that items not claimed by Wednesday can be retrieved by going through the city parks department. A statue that had been at the center of the Corey Ruiz memorial is displayed at Demetral Park on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, in Madison, Wis. Angela Major/WPR Rhodes-Conway said that the city would continue to monitor the intersection and ensure traffic could continue back through the site unimpeded going forward. She also said the city is “ready to coordinate with Corey’s family” to establish a memorial to Ruiz. “We are absolutely committed to allowing space for some sort of memorial,” she said. “It just can’t be in the middle of the traffic lights.” On Wednesday afternoon, Ruiz’s family released a statement through civil rights attorney Ben Crump . “Our family did not organize or authorize the encampment at Williamson and Baldwin streets,” the family’s statement reads. They disavowed a statement circulated by some activists that purported to come from the family and included a list of demands, saying, “We were never asked, and we never agreed to the statement released in our name.” “The city cleared that intersection yesterday,” the statement concludes. “We ask everyone at that corner and everyone wearing a badge to keep this peaceful. No one else should be hurt in Corey’s name.” A memorial for Corey Ruiz, a man who was shot and killed by Madison police, fills the Williamson Street intersection where he died Monday, July 27, 2026, in Madison, Wis. Angela Major/WPR Video taken overnight show chaotic scenes over a few blocks. In one, a line of police officers in riot gear block off an intersection at East Washington, a major thoroughfare extending to Madison’s interstates. The Madison Fire Department responded to five fires , according to that agency, set around the intersection in city dumpsters and trash cans. At the start of Tuesday’s meeting of the Madison Common Council , Alder Barbara Harrington-McKinney asked if leaders could suspend the meeting and reconvene later “because there is craziness in the streets.” The meeting continued, with about eight hours of public comment while chaos raged on Williamson Street. No action was taken. Among those involved in altercations with police was the city’s interim police monitor, Aeiramique Glass. In drone video released by the city, she is seen confronting officers at the site. She appears to push one of them before a group of officers subdues her. In a social media video posted after the altercation, she shows a bloodied hand and says, “I will f—— burn this city down.” Rhodes-Conway on Wednesday called it “disturbing” for a city employee to call for violence. Patterson praised how his agency has handled the protests and ensuing flare-ups throughout the day and into the night. He said that neighboring Sun Prairie and the state police were also involved. Patterson said no tear gas or projectiles had been deployed and one officer used pepper spray. A Madison police officer stands near a squad car as protesters approach Wednesday, July 22, 2026, in Madison, Wis. Angela Major/WPR The protest zone was erected almost immediately after Ruiz was shot dead in the street, after being apprehended by police officers. Police say he brandished a knife, cutting one police officer, before he was killed. The shooting was captured on video, sparking days of community protest that culminated in a barricaded encampment on the commercial thoroughfare affectionately referred to as Willy Street. For days leading up to Tuesday’s clearance actions, Rhodes-Conway had been calling for an end to the encampment, which she said was straining local businesses and disrupting residents’ daily lives. On Wednesday, she said there was no inciting incident that made Tuesday the day. She said the city had tried to involve other agencies foremost, using police as a last resort. “Often the presence of police officers is part of the escalation, and so we have tried very hard to limit police response to what’s necessary and to use other city staff,” she said. Patterson said city agencies would “staff the intersection for the foreseeable future” to ensure that residents and businesses can return to regular life. “We recognize that for some people in the area, we are what’s causing agitation — our presence — and so we don’t want to do that,” Patterson said. Ruiz’s death is under investigation by the state Department of Justice. Separately, Madison operates an independent police oversight board, with an individual police monitor. Glass, the interim independent monitor involved in the altercation Tuesday, has called on the city to release its records to her office now, instead of after the DOJ investigation concludes. “I should not have to wait,” she said in a July 28 interview with WPR’s “ Wisconsin Today .” On Wednesday, Patterson said that’s not his call to make. “I’ve had discussions literally every single day, multiple times a day, with (the Division of Criminal Investigation) about what updates can be shared. … I’m assured they continue to progress in their investigation,” he said. “I feel it’s really my job to allow the investigating agency to do their work and make some of these decisions on records as well. I don’t want to be a chief that’s going to try to influence decisions one way or the other.” At Tuesday night’s city council meeting, Madison City Attorney Mike Haas said the city’s official position is that those records cannot be provided to the police monitor until the Wisconsin DOJ investigation is over. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway, with, from left, Madison Police Chief John Patterson and Madison Public Works Director Charlie Romines, speaks at a press conference Wednesday on the decision to clear away an encampment that had taken over the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin streets. People Contact Contests Schedule Marketing Resources Careers Sinclair Cares Weather Watch Live Now 73 ° Fri 85 ° Sat 82 ° facebook icon twitter icon ACCESSIBILITY Police monitor stands by 'burn the city down' comment, criticizes mayor's response by Kyle Jones & Elly Laliberte 2026-08-06 145857.png Share story Share topics: Madison Independent monitor Police oversight Satya Rhodes-Conway Protests Corey Ruiz Pepper spray Wisconsin MADISON, Wis. — Madison’s independent police monitor said she stands by her words after she was seen on video Tuesday saying she “will burn this city down.” The video was posted following an altercation between Glass and Madison police officers during protests that sprung up after the city cleared out an encampment at the site where Corey Ruiz was shot and killed by a police officer. The video, posted by Independent Police Monitor data analyst Greg Gelembiuk, has since been taken down. Independent Police Monitor: 'I will burn this city down' “That comment is a metaphor,” Glass told Fox 47 during an interview Wednesday evening. “So many people have used that comment when they're talking about whether it be fighting against injustice when something is wrong, or when something happens.” Glass went on to say that she made the comment while speaking to people who she trusted, who understood her words. “I don't care that they were recording me,” she said. “I was in pain and had just gotten jumped by a lot of officers.” Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway condemned Glass’ comments while speaking to reporters Wednesday morning, calling the remarks disturbing. Glass criticized the mayor, saying her focus is misplaced. “I think it's really disturbing that over I don't know how many officers jumped me. I think that's disturbing,” Glass said. “Her priorities have continuously been in the wrong place and the wrong perspective. And if anybody who knows me, how I move, how I work, I am not one to ever start anything. But I also believe in defending myself.” Glass also earned condemnation from the Wisconsin Professional Police Association, who said the incident put her independence and neutrality into question. “Independent oversight cannot function effectively when the official responsible for providing it becomes personally involved in an active police operation or is perceived as an advocate or participant,” WPPA executive director Jim Palmer said. Glass maintained that her work has not been tainted and that she will remain impartial. “I have shown up [to the protests] doing de-escalation. There have been city teams out there that could not de-escalate and have asked me to deescalate. There have been city officials who have called me to help deescalate,” she said. “I've been out in my official capacity. Also, I have a duty to monitor the police. So when police are present, or possibly will be present, I have a duty to be out there.” Glass said she wanted to observe Tuesday’s protests after she received calls that people were being arrested and subjected to pepper spray and excessive force. “When I arrived on scene, there was a woman being arrested. I seen her arm being yanked. I began to record immediately,” Glass said. “She was completely limp, and so I began to talk to the officers, coaching them like you need to watch her arm, you need to be careful.” Glass said the officers were antagonistic towards her and told her to go away. When she tried to ask for one of the officer’s badge numbers, things got physical. “Another officer, a woman officer, started to yell and put her arm out. And an officer, I believe a woman officer had a blue helmet on. She came up and used her forearm and shoved [me]. And you see her on camera stepping forward and doing the shove,” Glass said. “Everything happened so quickly. I pushed back, turned around, was walking off. The same officer goes after my arm, and then I was swarmed by officers.” Glass said she suffered a deep cut, and that her comments were made in that context. “People can take it however you know they take it,” Glass said. “But I believe that the majority of people know the context in which that was meant, and that anybody who cares about human life and people will care about me as a human being, and not what I said to trusted people in in a heated situation where I was just harmed by law enforcement.” Glass subpoenaed the Madison Police Department last week for evidence related to Ruiz’s killing, however she said that the department is denying her access. She accused the city attorney, Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne and Rhodes-Conway are helping obstruct her investigation. Rhodes-Conway said the city and department cannot turn over evidence under state law, because the Wisconsin Department of Justice Division of Criminal Investigation is still examining evidence in the case. The DCI will turn over its findings to Ozanne’s office, and he will make a decision on if the officers involved in the shooting will be criminally charged. Glass has since hired independent counsel, William Sulton, to explore next steps. She would not say if that meant filing a lawsuit against the city. “In these cases where we are not getting evidence and the information needed, we are not getting compliance of the ordinance,” Glass said. “We cannot trust the city. We have independent counsel who represents us in all aspects.” Deputy City Attorney Patricia Lauten said Wednesday evening that the city has a process that Glass must follow before she can hire and pay an outside attorney, and that the process is underway. Lauten also pushed back on claims that the City Attorney’s Office was obstructing Glass’ investigation. Glass said she is still working with the city on negotiating a contract for Sulton. Fox 47 contacted Sulton, who confirmed he was being paid by the city but said he did not have a contract that was “acceptable to the city attorneys.” The plan is for Sulton to be paid out of the Office of the Independent Monitor's budget. Asking for more resources Glass has asked for more funding for her office in the wake of Ruiz’s killing. She and members of the Police and Community Oversight Board called on the city last week to re-allocate 1% of the police department’s budget to fund their groups. “We need additional staff. I need to take my current staff who is part time to full time. I need to make sure that he is being provided a livable wage, I need to make sure that we get an investigator,” she said. “The board has trainings, conferences, community engagement is a huge piece. We have been doing a lot of community engagement work, and that costs money.” But the call for more money comes as the city faces a projected $11 million operating budget gap in 2027. Rhodes-Conway earlier this year asked all city agencies to cut their budgets by 2% and not make requests for new positions or additional funding. “The city asked everyone to take a racial equity and social justice approach to the budget, I did so by not making any cuts to our budget,” Glass said. “There are so many complaints coming in, and so many people bringing cases to our office, that if we are going to answer the call in an equitable manner, we must have the resources needed.” The mayor said Wednesday that she would be hesitant to send more resources Glass’ way, given the budget situation. She also said the city has yet to perfect civilian oversight of the police. “I think that is coming from someone who has been a part of stalling the perfection,” Glass said. “I don't think anything becomes perfect, but I do believe that things can become efficient, functional, trusted.” Glass maintained that her office is trusted, and that the work she has put forth is good. The Office of the Independent Monitor, created by the Common Council in 2020, issued one its first major investigative reports earlier this year. It disputed findings that 32-year-old Richard Johnson died from cocaine toxicity while in police custody and instead pinned Johnson’s death on excessive use of force by police. That report came months after an annual report from the office, the second one issued in its history, cast doubt on Glass’ credibility. The report contained blatanly AI-generated imagery, such as a Madison skyline with two Capitol domes, and Madison Police Chief John Patterson disputed the report’s findings on racial disparities in policing. The report has since been revised. “My work has spoke for itself. If folks want to focus on the negative comments every time law enforcement is actually held accountable, I can't do anything about that,” Glass said. “There's always room-not just for improvement, but there's always room to make things operate at its best, and this department, the board is in a completely different positive place than it was before.” Oversight Board stands by Glass In a statement Thursday, the Executive Committee of the Police Civilian Oversight Board defended Glass and said she was acting within her authority. Members of the board said they witnessed Glass’ encounter with officers and claimed they were exposed to pepper spray while monitoring some protests. “If the official charged with independently overseeing police conduct can be physically injured while performing her lawful duties, every member of our community should ask what that means for residents who lack that visibility, authority, or institutional support,” the committee said. “Civilian oversight exists precisely because accountability is most critical especially during moments of crisis.” The committee said scrutiny of Glass’ comments overshadowed questions about how she was injured. “We respectfully disagree with statements suggesting that Monitor Glass incited violence,” the committee said. “Such characterizations fail to account for the context in which her remarks were made and risk diverting public attention from the events that precipitated them.” The committee called for an investigation into Glass’ altercation with police. title: Efforts underway to help Madison businesses and workers amid Ruiz shooting - Spectrum News
text: MADISON, Wis. — Madison city leaders and community groups are pursuing several efforts to help businesses and workers affected by the encampment and cleanup that followed the shooting of Corey Ruiz. Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said this week that the encampment and cleanup have cost the city hundreds of thousands of dollars. PJ Chamberlain, a coordinator with Madison Workers Cooperative and head of outreach at Community Pharmacy, said some workers and business employees were affected both emotionally and financially. “Some people were very impacted the day of because they witnessed it or it was right in front of their business or where they work,” Chamberlain said. He said some workers missed shifts and others lost tips as foot traffic and business activity declined. To help address those losses, Madison Workers Cooperative launched a fund for workers affected by the disruption. The group hopes to raise enough money to provide $500 grants to workers from businesses near the encampment. “Just trying to be there for people… so that they can focus on their lives in other ways,” Chamberlain said. Another fundraising effort has been organized by the Williamson Marquette Business Association to support business owners. At the city level, District 6 Alder Davy Mayer said he plans to push a resolution through the Common Council to establish an emergency fund for affected businesses. “The city… is reaching out to a lot of them to assess how much revenue they’ve lost as we look to do a potential aid for those businesses,” Mayer said. Mayer said the proposal grew out of conversations he had during the protests with demonstrators, residents and business owners in the area. “Just hearing them out and trying to connect them with each other and find solutions,” he said. The proposal could face obstacles because of the city’s already tight budget. Mayer said he remains hopeful that the council can find a way to provide assistance. Chamberlain said he has been encouraged by the community's response. “The response has been just very Madison, very indicative of Madison in general, of how the community has come together to support people,” he said. City officials and community groups are continuing to assess the longer-term impact on businesses, workers and residents in the area.

title: Killing of Corey Ruiz revives calls to shift power from police to communities - The Guardian
text: A fter bystander footage of police killing Corey Ruiz – a 38-year-old Black man in Madison, Wisconsin – spread online, many questioned why the officers were not wearing body cameras, a standard practice for more than 80% of police nationwide. Police said Ruiz was wielding a knife and injured an officer; multiple bystander videos showed he was shot while already detained and on the ground . Ruiz’s family called for mandatory body cameras in the city, along with charges for the four officers involved . People across the political spectrum echoed the demand for cameras, including Madison’s police chief. Within days, Madison’s mayor, Satya Rhodes-Conway, announced she would include funding for body cameras in the next city budget. But local organizers say body cams are just one element of holding police accountable after harm has already been done; some would rather see community control over policing, and policies that reduce police interaction and address underlying issues, such as mental health services and homelessness support. (Ruiz was unhoused at the time of his death.) View image in fullscreen Protesters in downtown Madison, Wisconsin, on 25 July 2026, three days after the fatal shooting of Corey Ruiz by police. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images These tensions came to a head on Tuesday after Rhodes-Conway sent police to take down a community memorial and encampment at the intersection where Ruiz was killed after warning protesters about resident complaints . Nearly two dozen protesters were arrested and another 10 given citations within 24 hours; officers and the city’s independent police monitor also got into a physical altercation . What’s happening in Madison, advocates say, is indicative of how cities are still grappling with what police accountability and intervention should look like six years after millions marched against racist police violence and called for radical changes to policing after George Floyd’s murder. Organizers who spoke to the Guardian said that by focusing on body cameras, the conversation has strayed from the officers facing consequences, let alone reckoning with how to stop police violence from happening at all. According to the Mapping Police Violence project, 2025 was the deadliest year for police killings since 2013 . Even though only 7% of Madison’s population is Black, more than half of the police department’s “use of force” cases were against Black residents last year. “If we wanna really be able to address issues like the killings and harms and surveillance of Black and brown communities, we need to be thinking about, how do we take power away from these institutions and put it into the community?” said Zon Moua, senior director of organizing at the local community group Freedom Inc. In 2020, after the police murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis galvanized millions to protest against racism and police violence, cities across the country began listening to local community organizers about possible systemic solutions. Some established more community oversight; others created programs to replace police with mental health workers in crisis situations. While there were calls to defund the police across the country, that demand was quickly overwritten and rejected in the next few years: by the spring of 2022, then president Joe Biden was leading bipartisan cheers to “fund the police” at his State of the Union address, and police funding had actually gone up . Madison is one of those cities that vowed to do better. It had been rocked by two police killings during what were probably mental health crises: of Paul Heenan , a white 30-year-old, in 2012, and of 19-year-old Tony Robinson, who was biracial and shot dead by police in 2015 on the same Madison street as Ruiz. Juliana Bennett was a 21-year-old University of Wisconsin-Madison student and racial justice organizer when she was elected to the city’s common council (Madison’s version of a city council) in 2021. She helped launch a mental health crisis response program that sends a community paramedic and a crisis worker to respond to nonviolent 911 “behavior health” calls. The community-led police-civilian oversight board also created the office of the independent police monitor ; the two work together to review police misconduct and violence cases and make recommendations on police discipline, use of force and other policing issues such as hiring, training and complaint processes. At least three body-cam proposals have also come before the common council since 2020, but each time they were rejected or pushed back for further research, because of estimated costs or in favor of a pilot program. View image in fullscreen Mourners visit the site where Corey Ruiz was shot and killed by police in Madison, Wisconsin. Photograph: Jim Vondruska/Reuters A six-month “ feasibility review ” on mandating body cameras in 2021 found that “some marginalized communities” in Madison were strongly opposed to the cameras over fears of surveillance, among other concerns. When the city launched a body-camera pilot program in 2024 , an analysis found the tech did not affect police behavior or community-police relations in the city. Bennett twice voted against body cams, citing that one of the people commissioned to perform an independent report was on the payroll of a major body-camera manufacturer , and that she would rather the costs proposed for the cameras go toward addressing the city’s homelessness crisis, an underlying issue that can lead to police intervention and an important priority for constituents. “When serving on the council, it was a little frustrating to me that most of my colleagues were disinterested in making any real substantive changes to policing,” said Bennett, who is now running for gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong ’s state assembly seat. Read more In the aftermath of Ruiz’s killing, Madison was scrutinized for being the only big city in the state without police body cams. But research on their effectiveness has been mixed. While body cameras can help with substantiating “use of force” claims against police, particularly in cases brought by people of color, according to a 2025 study, investigations from ProPublica and the New York Times Magazine in 2023 found that the public almost never sees body-cam footage: police departments largely have the discretion to deny requests, redact or edit footage, and refuse to punish officers, sometimes not even following their own “stated policies of transparency”. “We’re under an illusion that body-worn cameras are a good way to stop police violence from happening in the first place,” said Lauren Bonds, executive director of the National Police Accountability Project. “It’s more that they’re helpful if police violence happens and there’s already a program in place limiting police responses.” The 22 July shooting sparked a street protest movement of hundreds of Madison residents and the memorial encampment at the cross streets where Ruiz was shot . Handmade art, chalked messages, bouquets of flowers and signs reading “Justice for Corey” covered the asphalt. A handful of residents slept in tents, weathering the extreme heat, while other community members held cookouts and brought bottled water. Today there’s little sign left of the gathering place. After Rhodes-Conway ordered the encampment to be taken down on Tuesday, citing complaints from nearby residents, 16 people were arrested , 10 people were given citations and others were pepper-sprayed during the shutdown. Protesters took over the streets on Tuesday night, leading to another six arrests; police again cleared the intersection by the early-morning hours. Both Bennett and Freedom Inc issued condemnations of Rhodes-Conway’s decision to close the encampment, and questioned why the officer who killed Ruiz had not yet been charged. View image in fullscreen A memorial for Corey Ruiz in Madison, Wisconsin, on 24 July 2026. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images The city’s current interim independent police monitor, Aeiramique “Meeka” Glass, also nearly came to blows with nearby police officers at the encampment clear-out. In investigating Ruiz’s killing, Glass has accused the police of denying her evidence and subpoenaed the department. On 4 August, she issued a public statement accusing the mayor’s office, the common council, the city attorney and the district attorney of obstructing, or enabling the obstruction of, the collection of evidence. Glass and the police-civilian oversight board have also called for allocating 1% of the police budget – a little less than $1m – to further bolster the monitor’s office with more personnel; community group Freedom Inc is calling for the board to receive 5% of the police budget. Meanwhile, local organizers who previously expressed opposition or skepticism to body cameras have been harassed by pro-police conservatives. They said Ruiz’s killing – and the current pace of police violence – suggest that at a structural level, things may not have changed much since the 2020 protests. But they will keep pushing for it. “With dozens of witnesses, filmed on camera from multiple angles, why are we [talking about body cameras and] not talking about investing in housing and support systems to make sure people like Corey have their basic needs met?” said Bennett.

title: Independent Police Monitor breaks silence after Madison police confrontation - Spectrum News
text: MADISON, Wis. — Interim Independent Police Monitor Aeiramique Glass said she was still dealing with pain and the emotional impact after a confrontation with Madison police officers. The department released drone footage showing the incident on Tuesday night. Glass spoke publicly Wednesday about the encounter, which happened as officers cleared the Corey Ruiz encampment on Williamson Street. “It was a pretty intense situation,” Glass said. Madison police released the aerial footage, saying it was intended to provide additional context after questions and competing narratives about the encounter circulated. Glass said she was attempting to get an officer’s badge number when the interaction escalated. “I was cut pretty deeply. There is an officer — the officer I was asking for his badge number,” Glass said. Glass said she felt the confrontation represented a larger concern about police accountability. “I wasn’t shocked,” Glass said. “So for me it was unreal, but very real.” The encounter happened as officers cleared the memorial encampment for Ruiz, who was shot and killed by a Madison police officer last month. Glass said she was at the scene in her role as the city’s interim independent police monitor, a position created to provide oversight and accountability. “I am always gonna hold my ground and I think, you know, I come from a background of advocacy, activism, organizing,” Glass said. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway also responded to criticism surrounding comments Glass made after the police confrontation about “burning the city to the ground.” “I think it’s disturbing. Any time a city employee is calling for violence,” Rhodes-Conway said.  Glass said she chose that phrase as a metaphor for standing against injustice. “That is a metaphor that is basically saying, like, I’m not going to allow injustice. I’m not going to — I’ll tear everything up. I’m not going to allow these things to happen to me, not on my watch,” Glass said. The Wisconsin Professional Police Association also weighed in on the confrontation. Executive Director Jim Palmer said the union did not have a formal working relationship with the independent monitor’s office, but said the video raised concerns. “The publicly released video raises serious questions about whether the monitor maintained the independence, neutrality and judgment her position requires,” Palmer said. Palmer said that because the incident remained under review, it would be inappropriate to draw further conclusions. Glass said she understood the significance of the moment but wanted attention to remain focused on Ruiz’s death and the ongoing investigation. “Sad and significant, but I also don’t want to take this away that someone was killed. And I have an investigation to do,” Glass said. “And I now have so many other investigations from what’s happened over the last two weeks.” Glass said her police oversight advisory board was allowing her to remain in her position while the incident was reviewed.
