title: Wisconsin primary election has other big races besides governor - captimes.com
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. All eyes have been on the competitive race for Wisconsin governor, but several other critical races appear on primary ballots for the Aug. 11 election, including those that could help determine control of the state Legislature and Congress. In addition, all Wisconsin ballots feature partisan primaries for lieutenant governor, secretary of state and state treasure. A partisan primary is used for voters to select their party’s nominees to run in the fall general election. Wisconsin has open primary elections, which means voters don’t have to register with a party in order to vote, but they are allowed to vote only for candidates in one party when filling out their ballot. Here is a rundown of the key decisions facing voters — besides who they want to nominate for governor — and the candidates in the running. One of the biggest races in the Dane County area is happening in the 17th Senate District, where three Democrats are competing to take on longtime Republican Sen. Howard Marklein in the fall. After the legislative maps were redrawn in 2024, the district has shifted from a Republican stronghold to a swing district that Democrats have their eyes on flipping. Marklein has represented the district, which dips into the southern corner of Dane County, since 2014. The Democrats in the running are state Rep. Jenna Jacobson of Oregon, former childcare provider Corrine Hendrickson of New Glarus and Potosi business owner Lisa White . Since Jacobson is running for Senate, her Assembly seat is wide open. The 50th Assembly District encompasses all of Green County and parts of southwestern Dane County, including Oregon and Mount Horeb. Three Democrats are hoping to advance to November and challenge Republican candidate Jon Aleckson , a former small business leader who lives outside Mount Horeb. The Democrats running are Albany childcare provider and former nurse Bryna Caves ; Monroe resident and customer service worker Josh Mittness ; and New Glarus School Board President Bill Oemichen . In Madison, a long list of Democrats are hoping to fill the state Assembly seat of Rep. Francesca Hong, who is running for governor. Hong was first elected in 2020 to represent the 76th Assembly District, a deep-blue Democratic stronghold considered one of the most progressive districts in Wisconsin. The Democrats in the running are legislative staffer Isaia Ben-Ami ; former Madison City Council member and state Legislature aide Juliana Bennett ; activist, artist and radio host Tony Casteñada ; Madison City Council Ald. Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford ; and community organizer and journalist Zoe Sullivan . One Republican, Madison resident Nina Chat, is also running. Candidates for Wisconsin's 76th Assembly District participate in a candidate forum at Garver Feed Mill on June 17. Three Democrats are hoping to unseat longtime Republican U.S. Rep. Bryan Steil in the state’s 1st Congressional District, which spans the southeast corner of Wisconsin. The Cook Political Report, a national nonprofit organization that analyzes elections, has it rated as a likely win for Steil. But some analysts have said the district is in play, and Democrats have expressed hope that they can flip the seat, which has been held by a Republican since 1995. Steil is running unopposed in the primary and has represented the district since 2019. The three Democrats hoping to advance to November are: Miguel Aranda , a resident of Whitewater who works for the University of Wisconsin-Whitewater and serves on the local school board; Mitchell Berman , an emergency room nurse who lives in Racine County; and Lorenzo Santos , a Racine resident and U.S. Navy veteran who previously worked as the emergency management director for Racine County. Milwaukee Ald. Peter Burgelis dropped out of the race, but his name will appear on the Aug. 11 ballot. In the state’s 2nd Congressional District, which includes Dane County, longtime Democratic U.S. Rep. Mark Pocan is facing a primary challenge from former teacher and Naval officer Douglas Alexander . Alexander has challenged Pocan before as an independent candidate and he is an advocate for term limits for members of Congress. Pocan has served in Congress since 2013. There is no Republican candidate running for the seat. Democrats have more eager eyes set on flipping the 3rd Congressional District, which has been represented by Republican U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden since 2023. One of the Democrats hoping to unseat Van Orden is repeat candidate Rebecca Cooke from Eau Claire. Cooke is a waitress and a former small business owner, political consultant and nonprofit leader. She challenged Van Orden in 2024 but lost by nearly 3 percentage points. A fellow Eau Claire resident, Emily Berge , is competing against Cooke for the Democratic nomination. Berge is the Eau Claire City Council president and a counselor. The 3rd District represents much of western and southwestern Wisconsin and is seen as one of the most critical battleground districts in the country this fall, as both parties look to take control of the U.S. House. The Cook Political Report has rated the race as a toss-up. Van Orden does not have a Republican challenger in the primary. Republican U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden is seen as vulnerable to a loss in the November general election. Two Republicans are running for a second time to be lieutenant governor, a largely ceremonial job that serves as the first in line to succeed the governor. Will Martin is a small business owner who previously worked in the administrations of former Republican Govs. Tommy Thompson and Scott Walker. When he ran in 2022, he came in fifth, receiving just over 9% of the vote. Former Lancaster Mayor David Varnam is challenging Martin. When Varnam ran in the 2022 primary, he came in seventh, earning just over 5% of the vote. The Cap Times welcomes tips from readers to help us inform our community. Email tips@captimes.com or visit captimes.com/tips for more options. Wisconsin is a state where candidates for governor and lieutenant governor are elected independently, meaning a candidate from either party could win in November and the executive branch could be divided. Martin has been joining presumptive Republican governor nominee U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany on the campaign trail and has outraised Varnam. The winner of the Republican primary will face Secretary of State Sarah Godlewski , the only Democrat in the race for lieutenant governor, in November. Four Republicans hope to succeed Godlewski as secretary of state, a role that is largely in charge of the state’s recordkeeping and maintaining official documents. The Republicans in the running are: small business owner Brayden Myer of Manitowoc; real estate and stock investor Jay Schroeder of Neenah; Dodge County farmer Nate Pollnow ; and Army veteran Cindy Werner of Milwaukee. Pollnow has been endorsed by the Republican Party of Wisconsin. Only one Democrat, Milwaukee Ald. JoCasta Zamarripa , is running for secretary of state. For state treasurer, which is a job that helps oversee the state’s public lands, unclaimed property and various financial documentation, two Democrats are running to unseat current Republican Treasurer John Leiber , who has served in the role since 2023. Dylan Helmenstine is the trustee of the Black Earth Village Board and is an appointed member of the Teachers Retirement Board, which oversees the state’s pension fund. Yee Leng Xiong is a Marathon County Board member and the treasurer of the D.C. Everest School Board. He previously served on the state’s Financial Literacy Council and made an unsuccessful bid for the state Assembly in 2024. Both candidates boast endorsements from Democratic leaders. Helmenstine has been endorsed by U.S. Rep. Mark Pocan and state Senate Minority Leader Dianne Hesselbein, and Xiong has been endorsed by U.S. Sen. Tammy Baldwin.

title: They can destroy a memorial, but they can’t destroy the movement! - Liberation News
text: On July 22nd, the Madison Police Department (MPD) in Wisconsin, murdered Corey Ruiz – yet another Black man executed by racist police terror. MPD targeted Ruiz after responding to calls of someone attempting to enter parked vehicles. In widely circulated videos, MPD is shown tackling Ruiz off a bicycle, beating him and discharging a taser before shooting Ruiz three times in the head at point blank range.  Multiple witnesses captured the horrific execution in real time, and hundreds of people immediately took to the streets in protest, marching to the state capitol and taking over a concert on the square. The next day, the Wisconsin Department of Justice – Division of Criminal Investigation opened a homicide investigation, clearly in response to the righteous anger of the community.  The past two weeks have been marked by daily protests, a growing memorial and encampment at Willy St. and Baldwin Ave. The beloved fist sculpture that was erected at George Floyd Square in Minneapolis made its way to the site in solidarity. For the last several days, Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway and other elected officials made handwringing statements calling the encampment “unsafe and unsustainable,” calling for a “respectful transition” to reopen the streets.  Early in the morning on August 4th, Madison police in riot gear and city workers destroyed the memorial for Corey Ruiz. They plowed through flowers, signs, candles, and art that had been placed in honor of a man killed by one of their own. They arrested 10 people.  Despite this brutality, people remained at Willy and Baldwin for hours in outrage at this blatant repression of a grieving community. As the day went on, the cops continued to harass protesters and attack with tear gas. Independent Police Monitor Aeiramique Glass, who is the head of the Office of the Independent Police Monitor (OIPM), the City’s independent civilian oversight and accountability agency, was also assaulted in an altercation with police.  This comes after evidence related to the killing of Corey Ruiz was requested from MPD and denied. OPIM  issued a subpoena to compel that evidence. The Madison City Attorney, the District Attorney, and the Mayor of Madison are supporting that obstruction. The crowd grew by the hundreds into the evening, and eventually the cops were forced to retreat, outnumbered and overpowered by the people. At the same time, on the evening of August 4th, the Madison Common Council switched their public meeting to virtual in a cowardly refusal to face their constituents. For all their virtue-signalling statements, elected officials like Mayor Rhodes-Conway have done absolutely nothing to move towards justice for Corey Ruiz in a meaningful way. They have not called for the arrest of killer cop Kiel Peterson or even once condemned the brazen, unnecessary use of force. The people continued to hold the intersection overnight, and Willy and Baldwin continues to be an important site of struggle. The intersection has been cleared again as of the morning of August 5. Two weeks later, and Kiel Peterson is still walking free, still getting paid, still enjoying time with his loved ones. Kiel Peterson gets to enjoy all that he stole from Corey Ruiz and his family. The encampment was not a danger to the public. What is truly “unsafe and unsustainable” is a system that produces and protects people like Kiel Peterson, who act as judge, jury and executioner, causing irreversible devastation to families and entire communities. Two weeks later, and Corey Ruiz’s family, community members, and activists continue to fight for these central demands: JUSTICE FOR COREY RUIZ! FIRE, ARREST, CONVICT KIEL PETERSON! END THE WAR ON BLACK AMERICA!

title: Beyond bodycams : Wisconsin killing reopens debate about police accountability
text: A fter bystander footage of police killing Corey Ruiz – a 38-year-old Black man in Madison, Wisconsin – spread online, many questioned why the officers were not wearing body cameras, a standard practice for more than 80% of police nationwide. Police said Ruiz was wielding a knife and injured an officer; multiple bystander videos showed he was shot while already detained and on the ground . Ruiz’s family called for mandatory body cameras in the city, along with charges for the four officers involved . People across the political spectrum echoed the demand for cameras, including Madison’s police chief. Within days, Madison’s mayor, Satya Rhodes-Conway, announced she would include funding for body cameras in the next city budget. But local organizers say body cams are just one element of holding police accountable after harm has already been done; some would rather see community control over policing, and policies that reduce police interaction and address underlying issues, such as mental health services and homelessness support. (Ruiz was unhoused at the time of his death.) View image in fullscreen Protesters in downtown Madison, Wisconsin, on 25 July 2026, three days after the fatal shooting of Corey Ruiz by police. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images These tensions came to a head on Tuesday after Rhodes-Conway sent police to take down a community memorial and encampment at the intersection where Ruiz was killed after warning protesters about resident complaints . Nearly two dozen protesters were arrested and another 10 given citations within 24 hours; officers and the city’s independent police monitor also got into a physical altercation . What’s happening in Madison, advocates say, is indicative of how cities are still grappling with what police accountability and intervention should look like six years after millions marched against racist police violence and called for radical changes to policing after George Floyd’s murder. Organizers who spoke to the Guardian said that by focusing on body cameras, the conversation has strayed from the officers facing consequences, let alone reckoning with how to stop police violence from happening at all. According to the Mapping Police Violence project, 2025 was the deadliest year for police killings since 2013 . Even though only 7% of Madison’s population is Black, more than half of the police department’s “use of force” cases were against Black residents last year. “If we wanna really be able to address issues like the killings and harms and surveillance of Black and brown communities, we need to be thinking about, how do we take power away from these institutions and put it into the community?” said Zon Moua, senior director of organizing at the local community group Freedom Inc. In 2020, after the police murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis galvanized millions to protest against racism and police violence, cities across the country began listening to local community organizers about possible systemic solutions. Some established more community oversight; others created programs to replace police with mental health workers in crisis situations. While there were calls to defund the police across the country, that demand was quickly overwritten and rejected in the next few years: by the spring of 2022, then president Joe Biden was leading bipartisan cheers to “fund the police” at his State of the Union address, and police funding had actually gone up . Madison is one of those cities that vowed to do better. It had been rocked by two police killings during what were probably mental health crises: of Paul Heenan , a white 30-year-old, in 2012, and of 19-year-old Tony Robinson, who was biracial and shot dead by police in 2015 on the same Madison street as Ruiz. Juliana Bennett was a 21-year-old University of Wisconsin-Madison student and racial justice organizer when she was elected to the city’s common council (Madison’s version of a city council) in 2021. She helped launch a mental health crisis response program that sends a community paramedic and a crisis worker to respond to nonviolent 911 “behavior health” calls. The community-led police-civilian oversight board also created the office of the independent police monitor ; the two work together to review police misconduct and violence cases and make recommendations on police discipline, use of force and other policing issues such as hiring, training and complaint processes. At least three body-cam proposals have also come before the common council since 2020, but each time they were rejected or pushed back for further research, because of estimated costs or in favor of a pilot program. View image in fullscreen Mourners visit the site where Corey Ruiz was shot and killed by police in Madison, Wisconsin. Photograph: Jim Vondruska/Reuters A six-month “ feasibility review ” on mandating body cameras in 2021 found that “some marginalized communities” in Madison were strongly opposed to the cameras over fears of surveillance, among other concerns. When the city launched a body-camera pilot program in 2024 , an analysis found the tech did not affect police behavior or community-police relations in the city. Bennett twice voted against body cams, citing that one of the people commissioned to perform an independent report was on the payroll of a major body-camera manufacturer , and that she would rather the costs proposed for the cameras go toward addressing the city’s homelessness crisis, an underlying issue that can lead to police intervention and an important priority for constituents. “When serving on the council, it was a little frustrating to me that most of my colleagues were disinterested in making any real substantive changes to policing,” said Bennett, who is now running for gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong ’s state assembly seat. Read more In the aftermath of Ruiz’s killing, Madison was scrutinized for being the only big city in the state without police body cams. But research on their effectiveness has been mixed. While body cameras can help with substantiating “use of force” claims against police, particularly in cases brought by people of color, according to a 2025 study, investigations from ProPublica and the New York Times Magazine in 2023 found that the public almost never sees body-cam footage: police departments largely have the discretion to deny requests, redact or edit footage, and refuse to punish officers, sometimes not even following their own “stated policies of transparency”. “We’re under an illusion that body-worn cameras are a good way to stop police violence from happening in the first place,” said Lauren Bonds, executive director of the National Police Accountability Project. “It’s more that they’re helpful if police violence happens and there’s already a program in place limiting police responses.” The 22 July shooting sparked a street protest movement of hundreds of Madison residents and the memorial encampment at the cross streets where Ruiz was shot . Handmade art, chalked messages, bouquets of flowers and signs reading “Justice for Corey” covered the asphalt. A handful of residents slept in tents, weathering the extreme heat, while other community members held cookouts and brought bottled water. Today there’s little sign left of the gathering place. After Rhodes-Conway ordered the encampment to be taken down on Tuesday, citing complaints from nearby residents, 16 people were arrested , 10 people were given citations and others were pepper-sprayed during the shutdown. Protesters took over the streets on Tuesday night, leading to another six arrests; police again cleared the intersection by the early-morning hours. Both Bennett and Freedom Inc issued condemnations of Rhodes-Conway’s decision to close the encampment, and questioned why the officer who killed Ruiz had not yet been charged. View image in fullscreen A memorial for Corey Ruiz in Madison, Wisconsin, on 24 July 2026. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images The city’s current interim independent police monitor, Aeiramique “Meeka” Glass, also nearly came to blows with nearby police officers at the encampment clear-out. In investigating Ruiz’s killing, Glass has accused the police of denying her evidence and subpoenaed the department. On 4 August, she issued a public statement accusing the mayor’s office, the common council, the city attorney and the district attorney of obstructing, or enabling the obstruction of, the collection of evidence. Glass and the police-civilian oversight board have also called for allocating 1% of the police budget – a little less than $1m – to further bolster the monitor’s office with more personnel; community group Freedom Inc is calling for the board to receive 5% of the police budget. Meanwhile, local organizers who previously expressed opposition or skepticism to body cameras have been harassed by pro-police conservatives. They said Ruiz’s killing – and the current pace of police violence – suggest that at a structural level, things may not have changed much since the 2020 protests. But they will keep pushing for it. “With dozens of witnesses, filmed on camera from multiple angles, why are we [talking about body cameras and] not talking about investing in housing and support systems to make sure people like Corey have their basic needs met?” said Bennett.

title: Police monitor stands by  burn the city down  comment , says mayor priorities are misplaced | News
text: ​COPYRIGHT 2026 BY CHANNEL 3000. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. THIS MATERIAL MAY NOT BE PUBLISHED, BROADCAST, REWRITTEN OR REDISTRIBUTED. MADISON, Wis. — Madison’s independent police monitor told News 3 Now that she stands by her words after she was seen on video Tuesday saying she “will burn this city down.” The video was posted following an altercation between Glass and Madison police officers during protests that sprung up after the city cleared out an encampment at the site where Corey Ruiz was shot and killed by a police officer. The video, posted by Independent Police Monitor data analyst Greg Gelembiuk, has since been taken down. “That comment is a metaphor,” Glass told News 3 Now during an interview Wednesday evening. “So many people have used that comment when they're talking about whether it be fighting against injustice when something is wrong, or when something happens.” Glass went on to say that she made the comment while speaking to people who she trusted, who understood her words. “I don't care that they were recording me,” she said. “I was in pain and had just gotten jumped by a lot of officers.” Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway condemned Glass’ comments while speaking to reporters Wednesday morning, calling the remarks disturbing. Glass criticized the mayor, saying her focus is misplaced. “I think it's really disturbing that over I don't know how many officers jumped me. I think that's disturbing,” Glass said. “Her priorities have continuously been in the wrong place and the wrong perspective. And if anybody who knows me, how I move, how I work, I am not one to ever start anything. But I also believe in defending myself.” Glass also earned condemnation from the Wisconsin Professional Police Association, who said the incident put her independence and neutrality into question. “Independent oversight cannot function effectively when the official responsible for providing it becomes personally involved in an active police operation or is perceived as an advocate or participant,” WPPA executive director Jim Palmer said. Glass maintained that her work has not been tainted and that she will remain impartial. “I have shown up [to the protests] doing de-escalation. There have been city teams out there that could not de-escalate and have asked me to deescalate. There have been city officials who have called me to help deescalate,” she said. “I've been out in my official capacity. Also, I have a duty to monitor the police. So when police are present, or possibly will be present, I have a duty to be out there.” Glass said she wanted to observe Tuesday’s protests after she received calls that people were being arrested and subjected to pepper spray and excessive force. “When I arrived on scene, there was a woman being arrested. I seen her arm being yanked. I began to record immediately,” Glass said. “She was completely limp, and so I began to talk to the officers, coaching them like you need to watch her arm, you need to be careful.” Glass said the officers were antagonistic towards her and told her to go away. When she tried to ask for one of the officer’s badge numbers, things got physical. “Another officer, a woman officer, started to yell and put her arm out. And an officer, I believe a woman officer had a blue helmet on. She came up and used her forearm and shoved [me]. And you see her on camera stepping forward and doing the shove,” Glass said. “Everything happened so quickly. I pushed back, turned around, was walking off. The same officer goes after my arm, and then I was swarmed by officers.” Glass said she suffered a deep cut, and that her comments were made in that context. “People can take it however you know they take it,” Glass said. “But I believe that the majority of people know the context in which that was meant, and that anybody who cares about human life and people will care about me as a human being, and not what I said to trusted people in in a heated situation where I was just harmed by law enforcement.” Glass subpoenaed the Madison Police Department last week for evidence related to Ruiz’s killing, however she said that the department is denying her access. She accused the city attorney, Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne and Rhodes-Conway are helping obstruct her investigation. Rhodes-Conway said the city and department cannot turn over evidence under state law, because the Wisconsin Department of Justice Division of Criminal Investigation is still examining evidence in the case. The DCI will turn over its findings to Ozanne’s office, and he will make a decision on if the officers involved in the shooting will be criminally charged. Glass has since hired independent counsel, William Sulton, to explore next steps. She would not say if that meant filing a lawsuit against the city. “In these cases where we are not getting evidence and the information needed, we are not getting compliance of the ordinance,” Glass said. “We cannot trust the city. We have independent counsel who represents us in all aspects.” Deputy City Attorney Patricia Lauten told News 3 Now Wednesday evening that the city has a process that Glass must follow before she can hire and pay an outside attorney, and that the process is underway. Lauten also pushed back on claims that the City Attorney’s Office was obstructing Glass’ investigation. Glass said she is still working with the city on negotiating a contract for Sulton. News 3 Now reached out to Sulton, who confirmed he was being paid by the city but said he did not have a contract that was “acceptable to the city attorneys.” The plan is for Sulton to be paid out of the Office of the Independent Monitor's budget. Glass has asked for more funding for her office in the wake of Ruiz’s killing. She and members of the Police and Community Oversight Board called on the city last week to re-allocate 1% of the police department’s budget to fund their groups. “We need additional staff. I need to take my current staff who is part time to full time. I need to make sure that he is being provided a livable wage, I need to make sure that we get an investigator,” she said. “The board has trainings, conferences, community engagement is a huge piece. We have been doing a lot of community engagement work, and that costs money.” But the call for more money comes as the city faces a projected $11 million operating budget gap in 2027. Rhodes-Conway earlier this year asked all city agencies to cut their budgets by 2% and not make requests for new positions or additional funding. “The city asked everyone to take a racial equity and social justice approach to the budget, I did so by not making any cuts to our budget,” Glass said. “There are so many complaints coming in, and so many people bringing cases to our office, that if we are going to answer the call in an equitable manner, we must have the resources needed.” The mayor said Wednesday that she would be hesitant to send more resources Glass’ way, given the budget situation. She also said the city has yet to perfect civilian oversight of the police. “I think that is coming from someone who has been a part of stalling the perfection,” Glass said. “I don't think anything becomes perfect, but I do believe that things can become efficient, functional, trusted.” Glass maintained that her office is trusted, and that the work she has put forth is good. The Office of the Independent Monitor, created by the Common Council in 2020, issued one its first major investigative reports earlier this year. It disputed findings that 32-year-old Richard Johnson died from cocaine toxicity while in police custody and instead pinned Johnson’s death on excessive use of force by police. That report came months after an annual report from the office, the second one issued in its history, cast doubt on Glass’ credibility. The report contained blatanly AI-generated imagery, such as a Madison skyline with two Capitol domes, and Madison Police Chief John Patterson disputed the report’s findings on racial disparities in policing. The report has since been revised. “My work has spoke for itself. If folks want to focus on the negative comments every time law enforcement is actually held accountable, I can't do anything about that,” Glass said. “There's always room-not just for improvement, but there's always room to make things operate at its best, and this department, the board is in a completely different positive place than it was before.” In a statement Thursday, the Executive Committee of the Police Civilian Oversight Board defended Glass and said she was acting within her authority. Members of the board said they witnessed Glass’ encounter with officers and claimed they were exposed to pepper spray while monitoring some protests. “If the official charged with independently overseeing police conduct can be physically injured while performing her lawful duties, every member of our community should ask what that means for residents who lack that visibility, authority, or institutional support,” the committee said. “Civilian oversight exists precisely because accountability is most critical especially during moments of crisis.” The committee said scrutiny of Glass’ comments overshadowed questions about how she was injured. “We respectfully disagree with statements suggesting that Monitor Glass incited violence,” the committee said. “Such characterizations fail to account for the context in which her remarks were made and risk diverting public attention from the events that precipitated them.” The committee called for an investigation into Glass’ altercation with police. The Wisconsin Professional Police Organization said the oversight's board public defense of Glass without any independent review raises additional concerns about whether Madison's oversight structure is capable of holding itself accountable. “The publicly released video raises serious questions about whether the Monitor maintained the independence, neutrality, and judgment her position requires." WPPA said in a statement. "The appropriate response from her supervisory board should be a careful and impartial examination of the incident—not a reflexive defense of the official it is charged with overseeing." ​COPYRIGHT 2026 BY CHANNEL 3000. Add The New York Post on Google Originally Published by: ‘Criminal alien’ duo charged in deadly home invasion as DHS moves to yank green cards Delaware dance teacher arrested for alleged sexual abuse, solicitation GOP senator deals crushing blow to Trump's AG nominee after Alaska lobbying blitz A coalition of communist, socialist and left-wing activist organizations helped drive nearly two weeks of protests and a sprawling encampment in Madison, Wis., following the fatal police shooting of homeless man Corey Ruiz , with the demonstrations later escalating into clashes with police, street fires and blocked intersections, a Fox News Digital investigation has found. Together, the groups have organized demonstrations, maintained a sprawling protest encampment, demanding the officer’s arrest and repeatedly referring to him as a “killer cop.” Freedom Inc. also publicly said it bailed out dozens of protesters following recent arrests. The mobilization reflects a broader pattern in which communist and socialist organizations have used local confrontations with law enforcement to build protest movements and advance broader political agendas, national security experts say. Before city crews dismantled the encampment Tuesday morning, it had expanded to include dozens of tents, four portable toilets, food distribution areas and memorial displays. The initial demonstrations erupted after Ruiz was fatally shot on July 22 after police said officers responded to reports of theft before Ruiz fled on a bicycle. After several officers caught up with him, authorities said Ruiz pulled a knife, injured one officer during a struggle and was fatally shot by another officer. Protesters have accused law enforcement of using excessive force and, during several demonstrations, drawing parallels to the 2020 death of Floyd by while he was being restrained by Minneapolis police. The Madison unrest culminated late Tuesday and overnight into Wednesday when protesters allegedly threw projectiles at city workers, set five street fires and clashed with officers, according to the Madison Police Department. Police said the unrest resulted in at least 22 arrests, while officers also recovered a handgun from a juvenile protester arrested on unrelated charges. Among the organizations helping drive the demonstrations was the Party for Socialism and Liberation, which Fox News Digital has previously identified as a key organizer of nationwide protest movements within the broader activist ecosystem surrounding organizations funded by Marxist tech entrepreneur Neville Roy Singham , who lives in Shanghai. Earlier this year, a  Fox News Digital investigation  documented roughly $285 million flowing from Singham into a global network of nonprofits, activist organizations and media operations. Since the shooting, the Madison chapter of the Party for Socialism and Liberation has used its social media accounts to mobilize supporters with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly referring to the officer involved as a “killer cop.” The group has helped organize demonstrations, urged followers to “take the streets” and pressured elected officials through coordinated phone and email campaigns demanding the officer’s arrest . After city crews dismantled the protest encampment Tuesday morning, the Party for Socialism and Liberation posted an Instagram video showing officers clearing flowers, candles and memorial items from the intersection where Ruiz was shot before urging supporters to attend another evening demonstration outside Madison City Hall. The accompanying caption accused city officials of protecting the officer, stating: “Killer cop … is still walking free. Still on the streets. Still getting paid,” the post read, while identifying the officer by name. The group concluded the post by writing: “You can destroy a memorial, but you cannot destroy a movement.” Hours after the Party for Socialism and Liberation promoted the evening demonstration, protesters returned to the streets , where officers reported multiple arrests, street fires and blocked intersections. While the activist group has repeatedly identified the officer involved and demanded his arrest, Madison police have declined to publicly identify any of the four officers involved in the encounter. All four remain on administrative leave while the Wisconsin Department of Justice investigates the shooting, according to local reports. Another prominent organizer is Freedom Inc., a Madison-based activist nonprofit that advocates abolishing police, defunding law enforcement and broad criminal justice reforms. In an  Instagram post  on Wednesday, Freedom Inc. claimed it had “bailed out 50 people” from the Dane County Public Safety Building following the previous night’s arrests and had “shut down Doty Street directly in front of the jail while working to get people released.” Fox News Digital was unable to independently verify Freedom Inc.’s claim that it bailed out 50 protesters and has reached out to the organization for comment. Fox News Digital also sought comment from the Party for Socialism and Liberation. IRS filings reviewed by Fox News Digital show Freedom Inc. reported roughly $4.9 million in revenue in 2024, including about $1.24 million in government grants, after reporting roughly $4.2 million in revenue in 2023, including about $1.13 million in government grants. The overlap between Freedom Inc. and the Madison chapter of the Party for Socialism and Liberation was evident Wednesday morning, when they jointly published an  Instagram post  calling supporters to another protest outside the Dane County Courthouse. The poster declared, “All out for Freedom, Inc.! Don’t arrest me, arrest the cops!” while the caption urged supporters to attend, declaring: “Jail killer cops! Justice for Corey Ruiz! Dare to struggle, Dare to win!” On social media, Freedom Inc. identified itself as the organizer of Monday night’s “mass mobilization” that saw protesters climb onto Madison City Hall and hang a giant banner reading “Arrest the Killer Cop” across the front of the building. They also threw balloons filled with red liquid at the building, according to local media outlet WKOW . Following the encampment’s removal, Freedom Inc. accused Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway of “sending armed militia to raid the memorial site.” The rhetoric reflected Freedom Inc.’s broader platform. In a  February Instagram post  pinned to its page, the group called to “Abolish Police,” defund police and ICE, end deportations and close jails, prisons and ICE detention centers. The organization wrote that “Police and ICE are tearing families apart, racially profiling our people, criminalizing poverty, and inflicting violence on Black, Brown, immigrant, and working-class communities,” adding that communities deserve “safety without surveillance” and “care without criminalization.” Freedom Inc.’s organizing also drew support from Fight Back! News, which jointly published an  Instagram post  with the group highlighting its organizing at the protest encampment. The post described individuals and organizations traveling to Madison from “around the country” to “help organize on the ground” and highlighted a four-day educational series and postcard-writing campaign by Freedom Inc. demanding the officer’s arrest, defunding the police, strengthening civilian oversight and expanding community control of policing. Fight Back! News openly  states on its website  that some of its writers and staff are members of the Freedom Road Socialist Organization, another far-left organization that has appeared alongside the Party for Socialism and Liberation in previous Fox News Digital reporting on protest movements from Minneapolis to Los Angeles. Freedom Inc.’s organizing also extended nationally. On July 22, the group jointly published an Instagram post with the National Alliance Against Racist and Political Repression and the Milwaukee Alliance Against Racist and Political Repression calling for “Justice for Corey Ruiz” and “Community Control of the Police Now!” Meanwhile, state Rep. Francesca Hong, who is running for governor and has previously called for “abolishing the police,” appeared at the memorial site shortly after Ruiz’s death. Hong does not appear to be affiliated with any of the groups. Madison resident Tom Beck, a retiree who has lived in the city for about 12 years, said city officials allowed the encampment to become entrenched before finally dismantling it. “They should have given them maybe 48 hours and then go in there and just push it out of the way. Instead, they let it grow,” Beck told Fox News Digital. “It’s just become an embarrassment.” Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway defended the city’s response, saying officials first offered shelter and hotel accommodations before clearing the encampment, citing public safety concerns and its detrimental impact on nearby businesses and the surrounding neighborhood.

title: Wisconsin’s partisan primary election is Tuesday. Learn more about who’s on your ballot. - Wisconsin Watch
text: Wisconsin: It’s time to winnow the field.  Tuesday is the state’s partisan primary election, where voters will choose the candidates to represent the major political parties during the general election this November.  There are important races up and down the ballot on Tuesday, but the top contest is Wisconsin’s Democratic gubernatorial primary . Seven names will appear on the ballot, but only four are still running for the party’s nomination after a chaotic summer that saw multiple candidates drop out of the race, a historically rare endorsement from Gov. Tony Evers of Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley and increased momentum for Madison state Rep. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist. Depending on which party voters choose as they cast ballots on Tuesday, there are also competitive primaries for the state’s congressional districts and legislative seats . The stakes of those races are high as Democrats and Republicans battle for majorities both in Washington, D.C., and at the Capitol in Madison this November.  Under Wisconsin’s open primary system, primary voters must select a party and then may only vote for candidates running from that party. So if a voter chooses “Republican Party,” that person can’t vote in the Democratic primary for governor, and if a voter chooses “Democratic Party,” that person can’t vote in the Republican primary for the 7th Congressional District. A voter doesn’t need to be a member of the party to vote in that primary, and a selection does not commit a person to joining that party or voting for that candidate in the November general election. Ballots are secret so which party a voter chooses is not publicly disclosed. As of Friday, the Wisconsin Elections Commission reported more than 234,000 people voted early in person or by mail. In 2022, about 295,000 people voted early when the top races were the Democratic U.S. Senate primary and the Republican gubernatorial primary. Remember: If you already voted, you are not able to spoil your ballot and cast a new one. Polls are open from 7 a.m. until 8 p.m. on Tuesday. You can find out what’s on your ballot, the location of your polling place and more at myvote.wi.gov . Voters must show a valid photo ID and can register at the polls on Election Day with proof of residency .  At the start of the year, the Democratic gubernatorial primary was a sleepy seven-candidate contest. That rapidly changed over the past month. Former Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez dropped out of the race in mid-July following revelations of issues with her campaign finance reports. Rodriguez’s exit led Crowley to restart his campaign with Evers’ endorsement and an effort to position himself as the moderate alternative to Hong. Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, who was Hong’s closest competition in multiple polls, left the race in late July.  The remaining Democrats include former Department of Administration Secretary Joel Brennan, Crowley, Hong and Madison state Sen. Kelda Roys. Brennan and Roys have struggled to garner more than single-digit support in the polls despite Brennan pitching himself as a continuation of the moderate Evers era and Roys’ endorsement from the state’s largest teachers union. The winner of the Democratic primary will take on the GOP nominee. The Republican primary features U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany and 27-year-old medical service technician Andy Manske. Tiffany, who is endorsed by President Donald Trump and the Republican Party of Wisconsin, is expected to cruise to a win Tuesday. Tiffany has nearly $5 million cash on hand, as of late July, far exceeding Manske’s $1,600.  Republicans took control of the U.S. House in 2022 and currently hold six of Wisconsin’s eight seats. Democrats, as they try to take back the chamber, are targeting Wisconsin’s 1st and 3rd congressional districts . Republican U.S. Rep. Bryan Steil has held the 1st District since 2018. The three Democrats vying to unseat Steil are ER nurse Mitchell Berman, Navy veteran Lorenzo Santos and Whitewater Unified School Board Vice President Miguel Aranda. Milwaukee Ald. Peter Burgelis will be on the ballot Tuesday, but ended his campaign in July.  In the 3rd District in western Wisconsin, Republican U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden is running for a third term. 2024 Democratic nominee Rebecca Cooke and former Eau Claire City Council President Emily Berge are competing in the Democratic primary. Political science experts rate the district a toss-up. The 7th District in northern Wisconsin features a heavily contested Republican primary as U.S Rep. Tom Tiffany leaves the seat to run for governor. The Republican candidates include Wausau financial adviser Kevin Hermening, Chippewa County factory worker Jessi Ebben, Crescent business owner Niina Baum, Superior contractor Don Raihala, and Michael Alfonso, son-in-law of former congressman and current U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy . Alfonso is endorsed by Trump. Democrats are seeking to take control of both chambers of the Legislature this midterm cycle, needing to flip two Senate seats and five Assembly seats to secure majorities. The party is using momentum from new legislative maps two years ago that officially ended a decade-plus Republican gerrymander and allowed them to flip 14 legislative seats in 2024 .  There are three Senate district primaries we’re watching Tuesday.  The 1st Senate District, covering the Door County peninsula, features four Republicans competing to succeed Sen. André Jacque, R-New Franken, who is not seeking reelection. Barbara Bittner, Jacob VandenPlas, Katie Baney and Nic Cravillion will compete for a place on the November ballot against independent candidate Mark Becker.  The 17th Senate District has long been a target for Senate Democrats. Sen. Howard Marklein, a co-chair of the Joint Finance Committee, is running for a fourth four-year term. Rep. Jenna Jacobson, D-Oregon, Lisa White and Corrine Hendrickson will face off in the Democratic primary. The Senate Democratic Campaign Committee, which is supporting Jacobson, considers the seat a flip opportunity in 2026.  Two former state representatives, Erik Severson and Angie Sapik, are competing in the Republican primary for the 25th Senate District to determine who will face Democrat Charly Ray in the general election for an open seat left vacant by redistricting.  In the Assembly on Tuesday, David Liners and Daniel J. Bukiewicz will face off in the Democratic primary for the 21st Assembly District to replace Rep. Jessie Rodriguez, R-Oak Creek, who is not seeking reelection. The primary winner will face Republican Dylan Pfaffenbach.  Three Republicans — Tyler Schneekloth, John Belanger and James Brotz — will compete in the Republican primary to unseat freshman Rep. Joe Sheehan, D-Sheboygan, who flipped the 26th District back in 2024.  Democrats Brian Bock, Ben Brist and Lawanda Chambers will face off in the August primary to challenge two-term incumbent Rep. Bob Donovan, R-Greenfield, in the 61st District — a district targeted by Democrats for control of the Assembly.  There is also competition for safe Democratic seats in Milwaukee and Madison. Rep. Ryan Clancy, D-Milwaukee, and Bridget Maniaci will compete for a place on the November ballot in the 19th Assembly District. Clancy hails from the socialist wing of the party, and Maniaci is a former Madison City Council member. The winner faces Republican Yasmine Outlaw.  Assembly District 76 features five Democrats — Isaia Ben-Ami, Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford, Juliana Bennett, Zoe Sullivan and Tony Castañeda — after Hong opted to run for governor. The winner faces Republican Nina Chat in the general election. Depending on which party they select, voters will have the opportunity to pick candidates for certain statewide offices.  Republican primary voters can choose between Will Martin, a Racine consultant, and David Varnam, a Lancaster stay-at-home dad, in the race for lieutenant governor. Secretary of State Sarah Godlewski is the only Democrat running for lieutenant governor. The winning candidates will form a joint ticket with the party’s gubernatorial nominee this November.  They can also choose their nominee in the four-person GOP primary for secretary of state. The candidates include Braden Myer, Jay Schroeder, Nate Pollnow and Cindy Werner. The winner will face Milwaukee Ald. JoCasta Zamarripa, who is running unopposed for the Democratic nomination. Democratic primary voters will determine whether Dylan Helmenstine, of Black Earth, or Yee Leng Xiong, of Wausau, will be the party’s nominee for state treasurer in November. The winner will take on first-term Republican incumbent Treasurer John Leiber in November. Republican attorney general candidate Eric Toney and two-term Democratic Attorney General Josh Kaul are both unopposed in the primary. Voters on Tuesday can also make decisions in local races, including sheriff and clerk of court contests in counties across the state.  For more information about specific local races on your ballot, visit myvote.wi.gov . For more information on statewide and legislative candidates, check out the Wisconsin Watch voter guide. Wisconsin Watch is a nonprofit, nonpartisan newsroom. title: As Madison grapples with police shooting, a dispute over who is in charge - Wisconsin Examiner
text: Madison’s east side responded to the police shooting of Corey Ruiz with a vigil Thursday evening. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner) While Madison attempts to respond to the police killing of Corey Ruiz on July 22, a dispute has emerged within city government over the authority of the city’s independent police monitor to subpoena materials related to the incident from the police department and the Wisconsin Department of Justice. In the weeks since Ruiz was killed, the city has seen the occupation of a major intersection, standoffs with police as the city moved to reclaim the occupied area, a marathon common council meeting and continued tensions between elected officials and the people they’ve empowered to oversee the city’s cops. Aeiramique Glass, the city’s independent police monitor, has drawn criticism for getting into an altercation with police officers while they worked to clear the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin Streets early Tuesday morning and later saying in a now-deleted video posted to social media that she would “burn this city down.” Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said “it’s disturbing anytime a city employee is calling for violence,” while reiterating the independence of Glass’ office. William Sulton, a Milwaukee-based civil rights attorney hired by Glass to represent the office, said she was making a “figurative, idiomatic expression.” Glass’ position was established by the common council in 2020 as part of the city’s response to the widespread police reform protests that summer. The Office of the Independent Monitor and the Police Civilian Oversight Board were established and given independence from the mayor’s office and council. Madison is the only city in the state with such a civilian oversight system, and this is the first time the system has had to respond to a police killing, meaning that as the board and office work to investigate Ruiz’s death, they’re testing the limits of the ordinance granting them those powers for the first time. Within the ordinance establishing the OIM, the city gave the office complete access to MPD documents and the authority to issue subpoenas — so long as those provisions don’t conflict with other laws. “The OIM shall, to the extent permitted by law, have unfettered access to all MPD records, policies, Standard Operating Procedures, data, computer databases, and other information necessary to fulfill the duties of the OIM,” the ordinance states. “The Monitor may, to the extent permitted by law, issue subpoenas for the purpose of compelling testimony or receiving documents necessary to fulfill the duties of the OIM.” Soon after Ruiz was killed, Glass opened her own investigation and issued a subpoena to the police department demanding all records related to the shooting be handed over to her office by July 31. However, under state law , when a police officer kills someone, the investigation must be conducted by an outside agency. In this case, the Wisconsin Department of Justice’s Division of Criminal Investigation is handling the review. DCI’s investigative report will be turned over to Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne, who will determine if the officer who killed Ruiz should be charged with a crime. Glass, members of the oversight board and activists in the community have argued that the ordinance establishing OIM granting “unfettered access” to police department materials and subpoena authority means that the department should hand over its materials related to the shooting — including dash cam videos, 911 call recordings, a list of officers on duty and communications with the chief of police. “We have a mandate and an ordinance that says we are to have unfettered access to all of MPD’s records, databases, video footage, everything,” Glass told the Examiner. “There’s no limit to what we are able to and should have access to.” But the city attorney’s office, MPD and city officials say that limits on the office’s subpoena authority are set under state law. Once the independent investigation started, all of those materials, initially under the purview of the department, are now controlled by DOJ and state law prevents the release of evidence and materials pertaining to an open criminal investigation. Because DOJ is investigating a government employee, state law also prevents the release of “information relating to the current investigation of a possible criminal offense or possible misconduct connected with employment by an employee prior to disposition of the investigation.” “I think the case is clearly made [that] we can’t interfere with a criminal investigation,” Madison Alder Tag Evers told the Examiner. “The concern is the release of that information could compromise the ongoing investigation and if it’s determined prosecution is warranted, complicate or interfere with the prosecution of a crime.” DOJ’s work in these cases can often be slow and clash with the public’s demands for answers . The Examiner has previously reported on the flaws of the independent investigation system. A spokesperson for DOJ did not respond to a request for comment. The argument over the limits of the Madison independent monitor’s subpoena power have resulted in dueling FAQ pages on the city’s website in which the mayor’s office says it is limited in what can be released and Glass accuses the city attorney and mayor of helping the police department obstruct her investigation. This dispute was explicitly predicted when the common council drafted the ordinance in 2020. In a pair of memos to the council, City Attorney Michael Haas wrote that giving the independent monitor subpoena power without explicitly outlining its limits could lead to legal challenges. “It is the opinion of our Office that the Council may enact an ordinance providing subpoena authority to the Independent Monitor,” the memo states. “Where there is no contrary statutory provision or contractual right, we would expect such subpoenas to be enforceable. It is less clear that a subpoena issued in the course of an investigation, or in a case which could lead to a disciplinary decision by the Police Chief or PFC, would be held to be enforceable if challenged.” Haas’ memo also directly addresses the question of officer-involved shooting investigations. “It may also be useful to note that, under [the statute], all officer-involved shooting deaths are investigated in the first instance by an outside law enforcement agency rather than by MPD, and that the Monitor would not be entitled to participate in such investigations,” the memo states. At a meeting of the Police Civilian Oversight Board Executive Subcommittee on Wednesday, Haas and board members continued to debate the issue. “People cannot deny that the words ‘to the extent permitted by law,’ are in the ordinances, and I think that has been consistently overlooked when people simply talk about unfettered access and subpoena authority,” said Haas, whose office is working to release an official opinion on the issue. “Those words were intentionally put in the ordinances, and that means we have to look to existing Wisconsin law.” But members of the board and independent monitor staff suggested that Haas’ office should seek outside legal opinions on the matter and charged that the city attorney’s office has a conflict of interest in the matter. Glass has asserted several times that the ordinance’s grant of independence to her office means that the city attorney doesn’t represent the office — a claim that city officials also dispute. “There’s an inherent structural conflict of interest between city attorney offices and police oversight agencies,” the independent monitor’s data analyst Greg Gelembiuk said at the Wednesday meeting. “You can see this play out again and again and again across cities in the U.S. City attorney’s offices are very enmeshed with police departments, and of course, the mayor’s office. They have a primary role of risk management. Police oversight agencies have a primary role of investigating police, exposing the truth. Those roles are in conflict, and because of that, you have a universal pattern where you cannot rely on the opinions of the city attorney’s office to be accurate and valid.” Glass has hired an outside attorney, Milwaukee-based William Sulton, to represent the office, telling the Examiner that she has “the ability to take full legal action that is available to us.” Sulton did not respond to a request for comment. Glass has previously threatened to sue the city over the limits of her authority, a legal action that itself is in dispute because even though the ordinance grants the office independence, it is still a city department and a city can’t sue itself. “The basic law in Wisconsin is that one city agency cannot sue another city agency. City agencies are all part of the same organization and one arm cannot sue another arm,” Haas told the Madison alternative newspaper Isthmus during the previous episode. “City agencies have the authority delegated to them in the ordinances and cannot file lawsuits independent of the city.” by Henry Redman, Wisconsin Examiner August 10, 2026 by Henry Redman, Wisconsin Examiner August 10, 2026 While Madison attempts to respond to the police killing of Corey Ruiz on July 22, a dispute has emerged within city government over the authority of the city’s independent police monitor to subpoena materials related to the incident from the police department and the Wisconsin Department of Justice. This dispute was explicitly predicted when the common council drafted the ordinance in 2020. In a pair of memos to the council, City Attorney Michael Haas wrote that giving the independent monitor subpoena power without explicitly outlining its limits could lead to legal challenges. “It is the opinion of our Office that the Council may enact an ordinance providing subpoena authority to the Independent Monitor,” the memo states. “Where there is no contrary statutory provision or contractual right, we would expect such subpoenas to be enforceable. It is less clear that a subpoena issued in the course of an investigation, or in a case which could lead to a disciplinary decision by the Police Chief or PFC, would be held to be enforceable if challenged.” Haas’ memo also directly addresses the question of officer-involved shooting investigations. “It may also be useful to note that, under [the statute], all officer-involved shooting deaths are investigated in the first instance by an outside law enforcement agency rather than by MPD, and that the Monitor would not be entitled to participate in such investigations,” the memo states. At a meeting of the Police Civilian Oversight Board Executive Subcommittee on Wednesday, Haas and board members continued to debate the issue. “People cannot deny that the words ‘to the extent permitted by law,’ are in the ordinances, and I think that has been consistently overlooked when people simply talk about unfettered access and subpoena authority,” said Haas, whose office is working to release an official opinion on the issue. “Those words were intentionally put in the ordinances, and that means we have to look to existing Wisconsin law.” But members of the board and independent monitor staff suggested that Haas’ office should seek outside legal opinions on the matter and charged that the city attorney’s office has a conflict of interest in the matter. Glass has asserted several times that the ordinance’s grant of independence to her office means that the city attorney doesn’t represent the office — a claim that city officials also dispute. “There’s an inherent structural conflict of interest between city attorney offices and police oversight agencies,” the independent monitor’s data analyst Greg Gelembiuk said at the Wednesday meeting. “You can see this play out again and again and again across cities in the U.S. City attorney’s offices are very enmeshed with police departments, and of course, the mayor’s office. They have a primary role of risk management. Police oversight agencies have a primary role of investigating police, exposing the truth. Those roles are in conflict, and because of that, you have a universal pattern where you cannot rely on the opinions of the city attorney’s office to be accurate and valid.” Glass has hired an outside attorney, Milwaukee-based William Sulton, to represent the office, telling the Examiner that she has “the ability to take full legal action that is available to us.” Sulton did not respond to a request for comment. Glass has previously threatened to sue the city over the limits of her authority, a legal action that itself is in dispute because even though the ordinance grants the office independence, it is still a city department and a city can’t sue itself. “The basic law in Wisconsin is that one city agency cannot sue another city agency. City agencies are all part of the same organization and one arm cannot sue another arm,” Haas told the Madison alternative newspaper Isthmus during the previous episode. “City agencies have the authority delegated to them in the ordinances and cannot file lawsuits independent of the city.” Wisconsin Examiner is part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity. title: The Badger Herald Editorial Board: A student guide to the August primaries - The Badger Herald
text: Election day is Aug. 11. Here’s what students should know. Statewide Governor Democratic candidates Republican candidates Governor is a statewide position that serves as the chief executive of Wisconsin, overseeing state agencies, proposing the state budget and signing or vetoing legislation. The Democratic primary includes Francesca Hong, Kelda Roys, David Crowley and Joel Brennan. Democratic candidates Mandela Barnes, Missy Hughes and Sara Rodriguez withdrew from the race after qualifying for the ballot. Their names remain on the ballot. The Republican primary includes Congressman Tom Tiffany and Andrew Manske. Francesca Hong has represented Wisconsin 76th Assembly district since 2021 and previously worked as a chef and business owner. Her campaign for governor focuses on universal childcare, universal paid leave, fully funded public schools and affordable healthcare. She is a member of the Democratic Party and the Democratic Socialists of America. She is endorsed by U.S. Representative Ilhan Omar, labor union SEIU Wisconsin and the national and state chapters of progressive organization Our Revolution. Kelda Roys has represented Wisconsin’s 26th Senate district since 2021, and served two terms in the Wisconsin State Assembly from 2009 to 2013. Her campaign focuses on providing affordable healthcare and childcare, expanding housing opportunities, creating clean energy abundance, fighting for reproductive freedom and defending equality for all communities, including BIPOC, LGBTQ+ and disabled individuals. Her endorsements include Former Lt. Governor Barbara Lawton, Former Assembly Speaker Tom Loftus and the Wisconsin Education Association Council, the state’s largest teacher’s union. David Crowley has served as the Milwaukee County Executive since 2020 and is the youngest and first Black person elected in the role. His campaign for governor focuses on improving life for working Wisconsinites through expanding affordable housing, improving healthcare accessibility, increasing access to jobs and creating livable wages. According to an article by The Badger Herald, Crowley dropped out of the gubernatorial race July 8, but reentered July 18 after Lt. Gov Sara Rodriguez dropped out. Crowley’s endorsements include current Governor Tony Evers, Congresswoman Gwen Moore and Milwaukee Mayor Cavalier Johnson. Joel Brennan served as the 18th secretary of the Wisconsin Department of Administration from 2019 to 2021 under Governor Tony Evers. His campaign for governor focuses on improving affordability for Wisconsinites, boosting education and childcare funding, protecting reproductive and voting rights and standing up to President Donald Trump. His affordability and economic sustainability goals are informed by his leadership positions at Greater Milwaukee Committee and Discovery World, the state’s largest science museum. Tom Tiffany has represented Wisconsin’s 7th congressional district since 2020. He is a businessman and member of the Republican Party and House Freedom Caucus. His campaign for governor focuses on fiscal conservatism, enforcing a border-security-style approach to state law enforcement and public order, conservative educational reform and restricting girls’ sports and locker rooms to biological females. He is endorsed by President Trump, former Wisconsin Governor Tommy Thompson and the Republican Party of Wisconsin. Andrew Manske is a medical service technician running as a political outsider (not a career politician) in the Republican primary. His campaign focuses on reforming property taxes, protecting citizens’ housing access and making state elections more transparent and verifiable. He also emphasizes technological and independent governance, proposing to utilize artificial intelligence to reduce the size of government while also restricting it to protect manufacturing and trade jobs. Andrew Manske does not have any political or institutional endorsements for his gubernatorial campaign. Lieutenant Governor Democratic candidate (not contested) Republican candidates Lieutenant Governor is a statewide position that acts as second in command to the Governor. The Democratic primary is not contested, and Sarah Godlewski will advance to the general election. The Republican primary features two candidates, who both ran for the position in 2022. Martin finished in 5th place and Varnam in 8th place. Will Martin served in senior leadership roles under Governors Tommy Thompson and Scott Walker. His campaign focuses on reducing government spending, supporting small businesses and reducing housing costs. His goals as Lieutenant Governor include supporting the police and improving energy production. Martin is a small business owner and is endorsed by the Republican Party of Wisconsin and the Milwaukee Police Association. David Varnam was the Mayor of Lancaster, Wisconsin, from 2016 to 2022 and served in the Grant County Economic Development Corporation. His campaign focuses on lowering taxes, cooperating with federal deportation efforts and supporting Christian values. Varnam is endorsed by Wisconsin Family Action PAC and Pro Life WI Victory Fund. Attorney General (Neither contested) Democratic candidate Republican candidate The attorney general is the highest law enforcement office in Wisconsin, responsible for overseeing the state’s legal offices and litigating on behalf of the people of Wisconsin. Neither primary is contested and both candidates will advance to the general election. Wisconsin Secretary of State Democratic candidate (not contested) Republican candidates The secretary of state oversees records passed by the legislature and keeps them accessible to the public. They do not oversee the elections like many of their counterparts in other states, which has been an issue for some candidates. The Democratic primary is uncontested, and JoCasta Zamarripa will advance to the general election. The Republican primary has four candidates. Brayden Myer entered politics by forming the Moms for Liberty chapter in Manitowoc before winning a seat on the Manitowoc school board. His campaign promises to make the job of secretary of state as transparent as possible by establishing a database of the records that pass through the office and wants to return election oversight to the office of the secretary. Myer is endorsed by Pro-Life Wisconsin Victory Fund PAC. Nathan Pollnow positioned himself as a political outsider, having never held office and coming in 4th in a 2021 special election primary for the 37th Assembly seat in Wisconsin. His campaign emphasizes increasing transparency about Wisconsin’s laws by publishing them in a way that is easily readable. Pollnow is endorsed by the Republican Party of Wisconsin. Jay Schroeder has touted a Wisconsin version of Trump’s SAVE Act, which attempts to suppress voting by raising ID requirements to register and vote in elections. His campaign emphasizes making the office the overseer of elections in Wisconsin, removing that power from the Wisconsin Elections Commission which has administered elections since 2016. He has never held political office, coming closest in 2018 when he lost the general election for Secretary of State. Schroeder is endorsed by Pro-Life Wisconsin Victory Fund and Wisconsin Right to Life. Cindy Werner does not appear to have a campaign website and is running without seeking any endorsements. Her campaign’s Facebook focuses on her role in passing the Wisconsin Citizenship Voting Requirement Amendment. She too has never held political office, coming closest in 2020 when she lost the primary for Congressional House District 4 by 87 votes to her opponent, who came a distant second in the general to Gwen Moore. Wisconsin Treasurer Democratic candidates Republican candidate (not contested) Wisconsin Treasurer is a state wide position that oversees the state’s finances. The treasurer balances spending efficiency while maintaining public investments. The treasurer is a member of the Board of Commissioners of Public Lands which distributes finances for local governments and school districts. The Democratic primary includes candidates Dylan Helmenstine and Yee Leng Xiong. The Republican primary is not contested, and incumbent John Leiber will advance to the general election. Dylan Helmenstine was an auditor and financial analyst for Wisconsin Medicaid programs. His campaign focuses on improving spending transparency and protecting public education funding. He believes in supporting rural communities and working across party differences. Helmenstine is endorsed by Citizen Action of Wisconsin. Yee Leng Xiong is the director of New Beginnings for Refugees and the District 19 Supervisor in Marathon County. His campaign focuses on increasing the Common School Fund and improving financial literacy across the state. He believes in expanding knowledge of the responsibilities of the treasurer and ensuring the office reaches rural communities. Xiong is endorsed by Senator Tammy Baldwin. Congressional WI House District 2 Covers the greater Madison area, Janesville and Beloit Democratic candidates Republican candidates None Wisconsin’s 2nd Congressional District covers much of south-central Wisconsin, including the greater Madison area, Janesville and Beloit. The Democratic primary includes incumbent Congressman Mark Pocan and Douglas Alexander. No Republican candidates are running. Mark Pocan has represented Wisconsin’s 2nd Congressional District since 2013 after serving 14 years in the Wisconsin State Assembly. His campaign emphasizes policies including funding public education, investing in clean energy, raising the minimum wage, protecting voting rights and closing corporate tax loopholes. He is a co-chair of the Congressional LGBT Equality Caucus and Labor Caucus and previously chaired the Congressional Progressive Caucus. Pocan is endorsed by labor union AFL-CIO and progressive groups like Planned Parenthood Action Fund and Fair Wisconsin. Douglas Alexander is a former naval officer, high school teacher and account executive. His campaign focuses on imposing congressional term limits and replacing career politicians with what he calls “citizen legislators.” He supports rank-choice voting and open primaries, regenerative farming and reforms to the influence of money and incumbency in Congress. Alexander does not have any political or institutional endorsements. State Legislature State Assembly Seat 76 The State Assembly is the lower house in the Wisconsin legislature. District 76 comprises the north western area around the Capital and the Tenney-Lapham neighborhood. The Democratic primary has five candidates. The Republican primary is not contested and Nina Chat will advance to the general. Democratic candidates Republican candidate (not contested) Isaia Ben-Ami has spent six years working in the assembly, most recently as the policy director for Representative Kalan Haywood (D-Milwaukee). His campaign focuses on policy solutions for affordable housing, access to transportation and funding the Wisconsin University system. Ben-Ami is endorsed by Assistant Assembly Minority leader Kalan Haywood and District 77 Assembly Representative Renuka Mayadev. Juliana Bennett is a former city Alderwoman running as the DSA candidate in the race. Her campaign proposes policies for affordable housing including a vacancy tax on landlords and rent controls, raising the minimum wage and rescinding Act 10. Bennett is endorsed by AFT-Wisconsin and the Madison Area DSA. Tony Castañeda is a musician and longtime resident of the 76th District. His campaign focuses on repairing the damage he believes Republicans have caused Wisconsin. He touts his immigrant roots in opposing ICE, funding public schools and rescinding Act 10. Castañeda does not have any endorsements. Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford is the current alderwoman for District 15 in Madison, having won elections in 2023 and 2025. Her campaign focuses on her personal experiences with homelessness and being a transgender woman. She advocates for decreasing cost of living, housing affordability and public school funding. Nina is endorsed by Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway and IBEW Local 159. Zoe Sullivan is a journalist and non profit organizer for solar power in Wisconsin. Her campaign focuses on funding for public schools and the UW system, establishing regional transit authorities and making Wisconsin a ranked choice voting state. Sullivan is endorsed by Madison activist Allen Ruff. State Assembly Seat 77 (Neither contested) District 77 comprises the UW-campus, most of State Street and other areas around campus. Neither primary is contested and both candidates, including incumbent Renuka Mayadev, will advance to the general. Democratic candidate Republican candidate
