title: Wisconsin’s partisan primary election is Tuesday. Learn more about who’s on your ballot. - Wisconsin Watch
text: Wisconsin: It’s time to winnow the field.  Tuesday is the state’s partisan primary election, where voters will choose the candidates to represent the major political parties during the general election this November.  There are important races up and down the ballot on Tuesday, but the top contest is Wisconsin’s Democratic gubernatorial primary . Seven names will appear on the ballot, but only four are still running for the party’s nomination after a chaotic summer that saw multiple candidates drop out of the race, a historically rare endorsement from Gov. Tony Evers of Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley and increased momentum for Madison state Rep. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist. Depending on which party voters choose as they cast ballots on Tuesday, there are also competitive primaries for the state’s congressional districts and legislative seats . The stakes of those races are high as Democrats and Republicans battle for majorities both in Washington, D.C., and at the Capitol in Madison this November.  Under Wisconsin’s open primary system, primary voters must select a party and then may only vote for candidates running from that party. So if a voter chooses “Republican Party,” that person can’t vote in the Democratic primary for governor, and if a voter chooses “Democratic Party,” that person can’t vote in the Republican primary for the 7th Congressional District. A voter doesn’t need to be a member of the party to vote in that primary, and a selection does not commit a person to joining that party or voting for that candidate in the November general election. Ballots are secret so which party a voter chooses is not publicly disclosed. As of Friday, the Wisconsin Elections Commission reported more than 234,000 people voted early in person or by mail. In 2022, about 295,000 people voted early when the top races were the Democratic U.S. Senate primary and the Republican gubernatorial primary. Remember: If you already voted, you are not able to spoil your ballot and cast a new one. Polls are open from 7 a.m. until 8 p.m. on Tuesday. You can find out what’s on your ballot, the location of your polling place and more at myvote.wi.gov . Voters must show a valid photo ID and can register at the polls on Election Day with proof of residency .  At the start of the year, the Democratic gubernatorial primary was a sleepy seven-candidate contest. That rapidly changed over the past month. Former Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez dropped out of the race in mid-July following revelations of issues with her campaign finance reports. Rodriguez’s exit led Crowley to restart his campaign with Evers’ endorsement and an effort to position himself as the moderate alternative to Hong. Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, who was Hong’s closest competition in multiple polls, left the race in late July.  The remaining Democrats include former Department of Administration Secretary Joel Brennan, Crowley, Hong and Madison state Sen. Kelda Roys. Brennan and Roys have struggled to garner more than single-digit support in the polls despite Brennan pitching himself as a continuation of the moderate Evers era and Roys’ endorsement from the state’s largest teachers union. The winner of the Democratic primary will take on the GOP nominee. The Republican primary features U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany and 27-year-old medical service technician Andy Manske. Tiffany, who is endorsed by President Donald Trump and the Republican Party of Wisconsin, is expected to cruise to a win Tuesday. Tiffany has nearly $5 million cash on hand, as of late July, far exceeding Manske’s $1,600.  Republicans took control of the U.S. House in 2022 and currently hold six of Wisconsin’s eight seats. Democrats, as they try to take back the chamber, are targeting Wisconsin’s 1st and 3rd congressional districts . Republican U.S. Rep. Bryan Steil has held the 1st District since 2018. The three Democrats vying to unseat Steil are ER nurse Mitchell Berman, Navy veteran Lorenzo Santos and Whitewater Unified School Board Vice President Miguel Aranda. Milwaukee Ald. Peter Burgelis will be on the ballot Tuesday, but ended his campaign in July.  In the 3rd District in western Wisconsin, Republican U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden is running for a third term. 2024 Democratic nominee Rebecca Cooke and former Eau Claire City Council President Emily Berge are competing in the Democratic primary. Political science experts rate the district a toss-up. The 7th District in northern Wisconsin features a heavily contested Republican primary as U.S Rep. Tom Tiffany leaves the seat to run for governor. The Republican candidates include Wausau financial adviser Kevin Hermening, Chippewa County factory worker Jessi Ebben, Crescent business owner Niina Baum, Superior contractor Don Raihala, and Michael Alfonso, son-in-law of former congressman and current U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy . Alfonso is endorsed by Trump. Democrats are seeking to take control of both chambers of the Legislature this midterm cycle, needing to flip two Senate seats and five Assembly seats to secure majorities. The party is using momentum from new legislative maps two years ago that officially ended a decade-plus Republican gerrymander and allowed them to flip 14 legislative seats in 2024 .  There are three Senate district primaries we’re watching Tuesday.  The 1st Senate District, covering the Door County peninsula, features four Republicans competing to succeed Sen. André Jacque, R-New Franken, who is not seeking reelection. Barbara Bittner, Jacob VandenPlas, Katie Baney and Nic Cravillion will compete for a place on the November ballot against independent candidate Mark Becker.  The 17th Senate District has long been a target for Senate Democrats. Sen. Howard Marklein, a co-chair of the Joint Finance Committee, is running for a fourth four-year term. Rep. Jenna Jacobson, D-Oregon, Lisa White and Corrine Hendrickson will face off in the Democratic primary. The Senate Democratic Campaign Committee, which is supporting Jacobson, considers the seat a flip opportunity in 2026.  Two former state representatives, Erik Severson and Angie Sapik, are competing in the Republican primary for the 25th Senate District to determine who will face Democrat Charly Ray in the general election for an open seat left vacant by redistricting.  In the Assembly on Tuesday, David Liners and Daniel J. Bukiewicz will face off in the Democratic primary for the 21st Assembly District to replace Rep. Jessie Rodriguez, R-Oak Creek, who is not seeking reelection. The primary winner will face Republican Dylan Pfaffenbach.  Three Republicans — Tyler Schneekloth, John Belanger and James Brotz — will compete in the Republican primary to unseat freshman Rep. Joe Sheehan, D-Sheboygan, who flipped the 26th District back in 2024.  Democrats Brian Bock, Ben Brist and Lawanda Chambers will face off in the August primary to challenge two-term incumbent Rep. Bob Donovan, R-Greenfield, in the 61st District — a district targeted by Democrats for control of the Assembly.  There is also competition for safe Democratic seats in Milwaukee and Madison. Rep. Ryan Clancy, D-Milwaukee, and Bridget Maniaci will compete for a place on the November ballot in the 19th Assembly District. Clancy hails from the socialist wing of the party, and Maniaci is a former Madison City Council member. The winner faces Republican Yasmine Outlaw.  Assembly District 76 features five Democrats — Isaia Ben-Ami, Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford, Juliana Bennett, Zoe Sullivan and Tony Castañeda — after Hong opted to run for governor. The winner faces Republican Nina Chat in the general election. Depending on which party they select, voters will have the opportunity to pick candidates for certain statewide offices.  Republican primary voters can choose between Will Martin, a Racine consultant, and David Varnam, a Lancaster stay-at-home dad, in the race for lieutenant governor. Secretary of State Sarah Godlewski is the only Democrat running for lieutenant governor. The winning candidates will form a joint ticket with the party’s gubernatorial nominee this November.  They can also choose their nominee in the four-person GOP primary for secretary of state. The candidates include Braden Myer, Jay Schroeder, Nate Pollnow and Cindy Werner. The winner will face Milwaukee Ald. JoCasta Zamarripa, who is running unopposed for the Democratic nomination. Democratic primary voters will determine whether Dylan Helmenstine, of Black Earth, or Yee Leng Xiong, of Wausau, will be the party’s nominee for state treasurer in November. The winner will take on first-term Republican incumbent Treasurer John Leiber in November. Republican attorney general candidate Eric Toney and two-term Democratic Attorney General Josh Kaul are both unopposed in the primary. Voters on Tuesday can also make decisions in local races, including sheriff and clerk of court contests in counties across the state.  For more information about specific local races on your ballot, visit myvote.wi.gov . title: Madison police shooting: Wisconsin DOJ identifies officer who shot Corey Ruiz - FOX6 News Milwaukee
text: Scene of Madison police officer-involved shooting at Baldwin and Williamson on July 22, 2026. (Courtesy WMTV-TV) MADISON, Wis. - The Wisconsin Department of Justice (DOJ) Division of Criminal Investigation (DCI) on Monday, Aug. 10 released the name of the Madison Police Department officer who shot and killed Corey Ruiz.  The Wisconsin Department of Justice identified the officer Monday as Kiel Baitinger-Peterson. Officer Kiel Baitinger-Peterson has 10 years and 10 months of law enforcement service.  The four responding officers have been placed on administrative leave, per the agency’s policy. The backstory: Madison Police Chief John Patterson said officers responded to calls about a man stealing bicycles and checking car doors and confronted him on July 22, but he rode away on a bicycle. Police later encountered the man again, at Baldwin and Williamson, and the man "fell or was pulled off the bicycle." There was a struggle in the middle of the intersection, and police said the man pulled out a knife and injured an officer. FREE DOWNLOAD: Get breaking news alerts in the FOX LOCAL Mobile app for iOS or Android Officers used a taser to try to take the man into custody before the injured officer shot the man, since identified as Corey Ruiz. Ruiz was pronounced dead at a hospital. Madison police said the four officers involved were placed on administrative leave as the Wisconsin Department of Justice Division of Criminal Investigation investigates the shooting as a homicide .  The Madison Police Department does not have body-worn cameras for officers. After prior efforts to fund bodycams were shut down, Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway has said she will include funding for them in her next budget. title: Election Day in Madison: 7 questions today’s vote will answer - The Cap Times
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. Madison voters are back at the polls today for a primary election that will narrow the pool of candidates for several local, state and federal government offices. For some candidates, today’s election will likely ensure victory in the November general election, as well. The Cap Times will track election results tonight and publish preliminary figures from the Dane County Clerk’s Office , as well as monitor statewide results gathered by the Associated Press and other news organizations. Below is a quick primer on what to watch. For more information about the races on your ballot and voting today, including the location of your polling place, visit myvote.wi.gov . With President Donald Trump’s endorsement and the lack of a well-funded or well-known competitor, the likely Republican nominee to seek a four-year term as Wisconsin governor this fall is U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany. Barring an upset, Tiffany is poised to advance today against medical services technician Andrew Manske. But who will face Tiffany from the Democratic ticket? A crowded field narrowed in recent weeks to four candidates: former Department of Administration Secretary Joel Brennan, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, state Rep. Francesca Hong and state Sen. Kelda Roys. READ MORE: How to tell candidates for Wisconsin governor apart, on key issues The Democratic primary has garnered national attention, partly due to Hong leading in polls as a democratic socialist in a state known for tight races. The election has also featured late surprises, such as Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez dropping out amid a campaign finance scandal and Crowley jumping back in with Gov. Tony Evers’ endorsement . Three Democratic candidates who dropped out remain on today’s ballots because of the timing of election deadlines and their decisions: Rodriguez, former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes and former Wisconsin Economic Development Corp. CEO Missy Hughes. Five Democratic candidates are vying to succeed Hong in the Assembly’s 76th District, which stretches from downtown Madison to Stoughton Road and north to Cherokee Park. District voters have historically backed Democratic candidates by wide margins, so whoever wins today’s primary is likely to secure a two-year term in November. READ MORE: Candidates for Francesca Hong's Assembly seat explain their views The candidates are legislative aide Isaia Ben-Ami; former Madison City Council member Juliana Bennett; activist, artist and radio host Tony Casteñeda; Madison City Council member Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford; and community organizer and journalist Zoe Sullivan. Republicans control the state Legislature with majorities in the Assembly and Senate. As Democrats aim to take control in November , one election near Madison to watch will be the Senate’s 17th District. With only half of the Senate’s seats up for election this fall, the swingy southwestern Wisconsin district might be among Democrats’ best options to flip. READ MORE: Wisconsin primary election has other big races besides governor Incumbent Sen. Howard Marklein is running unopposed in today’s Republican primary. The Democratic primary includes three candidates: state Rep. Jenna Jacobson, former childcare provider Corrine Hendrickson and Potosi business owner Lisa White. The winner of the Democratic primary will face Marklein for a four-year term. Two local Democrats are facing primary challengers today. In both races, no Republican qualified for the ballot so whoever wins today’s election is likely to secure the job in November. Mark Pocan is serving a two-year term as the U.S. House representative of Wisconsin’s 2nd Congressional District, which includes all of Dane County and several neighboring counties. Pocan is being challenged in the Democratic primary by Douglas Alexander, whose campaign website calls him a naval officer, high school teacher and account executive. Kalvin Barrett is serving a four-year term as Dane County sheriff. He was previously appointed sheriff by Evers in 2021 after then-Sheriff Dave Mahoney retired. Barrett is being challenged in the Democratic primary by Jack Ordman , a software engineer and activist. The statewide elections today for lieutenant governor, secretary of state and state treasurer each feature contested primaries. Whoever gets the most votes in each race will advance to the November general election and face an opposing party candidate for a four-year term. Business owner and radio host Will Martin and former Lancaster Mayor David Varnam are competing in the Republican primary for lieutenant governor. Secretary of State Sarah Godlewski is unopposed in the Democratic primary. For secretary of state, JoCasta Zamarripa is unopposed in the Democratic primary, while Brayden Myer, Nathan Pollnow, Jay Schroeder and Cindy Werner are competing in the Republican primary. Pete Karas is unopposed in the Green primary. Dylan Helmenstine and Yee Leng Xiong are competing in the Democratic primary, while incumbent State Treasurer John Leiber is unopposed in the Republican primary. Under Wisconsin’s Constitution , the lieutenant governor is first in line to succeed the governor upon death, resignation or removal from office. The secretary of state is next in line. The secretary of state and state treasurer are two members of the state’s Board of Commissioners of Public Lands , which manages funds that distribute millions annually to schools, libraries and local governments. The board’s third member is the attorney general. Madison appointed a new city clerk in August 2025 after the previous one resigned in the wake of an election snafu. In November 2024, the clerk’s office failed to count 193 absentee ballots in the presidential election, prompting a state investigation and a lawsuit by disenfranchised voters. Then in April this year, under new City Clerk Lydia McComas, another election oversight emerged. A carrier failed to deliver 23 absentee ballots to polls by an 8 p.m. deadline on Election Day. State officials ordered the ballots to not be counted, but a Dane County judge later overturned that decision . In June, the nonprofit news organization Votebeat reported that a former deputy clerk who claimed responsibility for the 23 late-arriving ballots had been reassigned within the clerk’s office to non-election tasks. While voter turnout is typically lower in elections without a president on the ballot, primaries with a contested gubernatorial race have prompted more turnout in Dane County than other elections. In August 2018, when Evers advanced from a primary with nine other Democrats on the ballot, about 126,000 ballots were cast in Dane County, according to election clerks. Four years later, when Evers ran unopposed in the primary, about 133,000 ballots were cast. Dane County turnout was about the same in each election: 39% of registered voters in 2018 and 37% in 2022.

title: Wisconsin’s partisan primary election is Tuesday. Learn more about who’s on your ballot. - civicmedia.us
text: Wisconsin: It’s time to winnow the field. Tuesday is the state’s partisan primary election, where voters will choose the candidates to represent the major political parties during the general election this November. There are important races up and down the ballot on Tuesday, but the top contest is Wisconsin’s Democratic gubernatorial primary . Seven names will appear on the ballot, but only four are still running for the party’s nomination after a chaotic summer that saw multiple candidates drop out of the race, a historically rare endorsement from Gov. Tony Evers of Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley and increased momentum for Madison state Rep. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist. Depending on which party voters choose as they cast ballots on Tuesday, there are also competitive primaries for the state’s congressional districts and legislative seats . The stakes of those races are high as Democrats and Republicans battle for majorities both in Washington, D.C., and at the Capitol in Madison this November. Under Wisconsin’s open primary system, primary voters must select a party and then may only vote for candidates running from that party. So if a voter chooses “Republican Party,” that person can’t vote in the Democratic primary for governor, and if a voter chooses “Democratic Party,” that person can’t vote in the Republican primary for the 7th Congressional District. A voter doesn’t need to be a member of the party to vote in that primary, and a selection does not commit a person to joining that party or voting for that candidate in the November general election. Ballots are secret so which party a voter chooses is not publicly disclosed. As of Friday, the Wisconsin Elections Commission reported more than 234,000 people voted early in person or by mail. In 2022, about 295,000 people voted early when the top races were the Democratic U.S. Senate primary and the Republican gubernatorial primary. Remember: If you already voted, you are not able to spoil your ballot and cast a new one. Polls are open from 7 a.m. until 8 p.m. on Tuesday. You can find out what’s on your ballot, the location of your polling place and more at myvote.wi.gov . Voters must show a valid photo ID and can register at the polls on Election Day with proof of residency . At the start of the year, the Democratic gubernatorial primary was a sleepy seven-candidate contest. That rapidly changed over the past month. Former Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez dropped out of the race in mid-July following revelations of issues with her campaign finance reports. Rodriguez’s exit led Crowley to restart his campaign with Evers’ endorsement and an effort to position himself as the moderate alternative to Hong. Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, who was Hong’s closest competition in multiple polls, left the race in late July. The remaining Democrats include former Department of Administration Secretary Joel Brennan, Crowley, Hong and Madison state Sen. Kelda Roys. Brennan and Roys have struggled to garner more than single-digit support in the polls despite Brennan pitching himself as a continuation of the moderate Evers era and Roys’ endorsement from the state’s largest teachers union. The winner of the Democratic primary will take on the GOP nominee. The Republican primary features U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany and 27-year-old medical service technician Andy Manske. Tiffany, who is endorsed by President Donald Trump and the Republican Party of Wisconsin, is expected to cruise to a win Tuesday. Tiffany has nearly $5 million cash on hand, as of late July, far exceeding Manske’s $1,600. Republicans took control of the U.S. House in 2022 and currently hold six of Wisconsin’s eight seats. Democrats, as they try to take back the chamber, are targeting Wisconsin’s 1st and 3rd congressional districts . Republican U.S. Rep. Bryan Steil has held the 1st District since 2018. The three Democrats vying to unseat Steil are ER nurse Mitchell Berman, Navy veteran Lorenzo Santos and Whitewater Unified School Board Vice President Miguel Aranda. Milwaukee Ald. Peter Burgelis will be on the ballot Tuesday, but ended his campaign in July. In the 3rd District in western Wisconsin, Republican U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden is running for a third term. 2024 Democratic nominee Rebecca Cooke and former Eau Claire City Council President Emily Berge are competing in the Democratic primary. Political science experts rate the district a toss-up. The 7th District in northern Wisconsin features a heavily contested Republican primary as U.S Rep. Tom Tiffany leaves the seat to run for governor. The Republican candidates include Wausau financial adviser Kevin Hermening, Chippewa County factory worker Jessi Ebben, Crescent business owner Niina Baum, Superior contractor Don Raihala, and Michael Alfonso, son-in-law of former congressman and current U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy . Alfonso is endorsed by Trump. Democrats are seeking to take control of both chambers of the Legislature this midterm cycle, needing to flip two Senate seats and five Assembly seats to secure majorities. The party is using momentum from new legislative maps two years ago that officially ended a decade-plus Republican gerrymander and allowed them to flip 14 legislative seats in 2024 . There are three Senate district primaries we’re watching Tuesday. The 1st Senate District, covering the Door County peninsula, features four Republicans competing to succeed Sen. André Jacque, R-New Franken, who is not seeking reelection. Barbara Bittner, Jacob VandenPlas, Katie Baney and Nic Cravillion will compete for a place on the November ballot against independent candidate Mark Becker. The 17th Senate District has long been a target for Senate Democrats. Sen. Howard Marklein, a co-chair of the Joint Finance Committee, is running for a fourth four-year term. Rep. Jenna Jacobson, D-Oregon, Lisa White and Corrine Hendrickson will face off in the Democratic primary. The Senate Democratic Campaign Committee, which is supporting Jacobson, considers the seat a flip opportunity in 2026. Two former state representatives, Erik Severson and Angie Sapik, are competing in the Republican primary for the 25th Senate District to determine who will face Democrat Charly Ray in the general election for an open seat left vacant by redistricting. In the Assembly on Tuesday, David Liners and Daniel J. Bukiewicz will face off in the Democratic primary for the 21st Assembly District to replace Rep. Jessie Rodriguez, R-Oak Creek, who is not seeking reelection. The primary winner will face Republican Dylan Pfaffenbach. Three Republicans — Tyler Schneekloth, John Belanger and James Brotz — will compete in the Republican primary to unseat freshman Rep. Joe Sheehan, D-Sheboygan, who flipped the 26th District back in 2024. Democrats Brian Bock, Ben Brist and Lawanda Chambers will face off in the August primary to challenge two-term incumbent Rep. Bob Donovan, R-Greenfield, in the 61st District — a district targeted by Democrats for control of the Assembly. There is also competition for safe Democratic seats in Milwaukee and Madison. Rep. Ryan Clancy, D-Milwaukee, and Bridget Maniaci will compete for a place on the November ballot in the 19th Assembly District. Clancy hails from the socialist wing of the party, and Maniaci is a former Madison City Council member. The winner faces Republican Yasmine Outlaw. Assembly District 76 features five Democrats — Isaia Ben-Ami, Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford, Juliana Bennett, Zoe Sullivan and Tony Castañeda — after Hong opted to run for governor. The winner faces Republican Nina Chat in the general election. Depending on which party they select, voters will have the opportunity to pick candidates for certain statewide offices. Republican primary voters can choose between Will Martin, a Racine consultant, and David Varnam, a Lancaster stay-at-home dad, in the race for lieutenant governor. Secretary of State Sarah Godlewski is the only Democrat running for lieutenant governor. The winning candidates will form a joint ticket with the party’s gubernatorial nominee this November. They can also choose their nominee in the four-person GOP primary for secretary of state. The candidates include Braden Myer, Jay Schroeder, Nate Pollnow and Cindy Werner. The winner will face Milwaukee Ald. JoCasta Zamarripa, who is running unopposed for the Democratic nomination. Democratic primary voters will determine whether Dylan Helmenstine, of Black Earth, or Yee Leng Xiong, of Wausau, will be the party’s nominee for state treasurer in November. The winner will take on first-term Republican incumbent Treasurer John Leiber in November. Republican attorney general candidate Eric Toney and two-term Democratic Attorney General Josh Kaul are both unopposed in the primary. Voters on Tuesday can also make decisions in local races, including sheriff and clerk of court contests in counties across the state. For more information about specific local races on your ballot, visit myvote.wi.gov . For more information on statewide and legislative candidates, check out the Wisconsin Watch voter guide.

On July 22, police responded to a report that a man was checking parked cars in the Marquette neighborhood. Four officers intercepted Ruiz at the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin streets, police said. Officers attempted to use a Taser on Ruiz, who police say pulled out a knife and injured an officer. The injured officer, identified Monday as Kiel Baitinger-Peterson , then fatally shot Ruiz. Ruiz’s death has prompted questions from community members, elected officials and experts about de-escalation tactics and other measures that could’ve potentially helped prevent the shooting. The Madison Police Department’s standard operating procedure recommends officers exercise de-escalation tactics “when safe and without compromising law enforcement priorities.” The guidance provides examples of practices that officers may take before deciding to use force, including creating barriers and communicating from a safe position. “When safe and feasible under the totality of circumstances, officers should attempt to slow down or stabilize the situation so that more time, options and resources are available for incident resolution,” the guidance says. “An officer’s awareness of these possibilities, when time and circumstances reasonably permit, should then be balanced against the facts of the incident facing the officer when deciding which tactical options are the most appropriate to bring the situation to a safe resolution.” A protester raises a fist during a march to demand justice for Corey Ruiz, who was shot and killed by a Madison police officer July 22. John Wallschlaeger, a former Appleton police officer, has helped train officers in de-escalation techniques as part of the Crisis Intervention Team , a partnership between law enforcement and mental health providers through the National Alliance on Mental Illness Wisconsin. The 40-hour de-escalation training aims to improve how officers respond to people experiencing a mental health crisis. “They (officers) go there, and if they make contact, they know how to be nonthreatening in their approach, allowing the person to vent and talk, and ... de-escalating as they go along and interview the subject and figure out what's going on,” Wallschlaeger said. Emilie Smiley, program director for the Crisis Intervention Team, emphasized the importance of the training and de-escalation techniques officers are taught. “We’re focused on ... coming into a situation and learning how to listen to what's going on, take in your surroundings, and use your body language and your words to de-escalate that situation to a safe place,” Smiley said. The Cap Times welcomes tips from readers to help us inform our community. Email tips@captimes.com or visit captimes.com/tips for more options. De Lacy Davis, a former New Jersey police officer who founded Black Cops Against Police Brutality, said the ultimate goal of de-escalation is slowing down a situation. “I often tell young officers that time is on your side,” Davis said. “There is no need to speed up the situation.” In the case of Ruiz, videos from bystanders show the situation escalated in seconds. Yet it remains unclear what exactly happened leading up to the shooting. While many large Wisconsin law enforcement agencies have body-worn cameras, the Madison Police Department doesn’t typically use the devices. Police Chief John Patterson has said body-worn cameras are his top capital budget request for next year. Despite long-standing conversations about body-worn cameras in Madison, city leaders haven’t funded them, citing the cost of fully implementing the devices. City leaders have also raised questions about the effectiveness of body-worn cameras. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway, who is up for reelection next year, has said body cameras alone are not the solution to reduce police misconduct. In 2024, Madison ran a 90-day body camera pilot program , and it expired without renewal. Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said the city is discussing training more city employees in de-escalation tactics following the fatal police shooting of Corey Ruiz. Body-worn cameras could have shown the circumstances leading up to the shooting of Ruiz, said Davis, the former police officer. “I would want to know how this gentleman got separated from his bicycle, which looked to be about 10 or so feet away from him,” Davis said. “I’d want to know if he (was) knocked off the bike, pushed off the bike, jumped off the bike, ran from the bike?” Another benefit of the cameras is training for police officers, Wallschlaeger said. The footage offers opportunities for real-world scenario analysis and post-incident debriefs, and it can help review an officer’s performance, he said. Rhodes-Conway has pledged to propose funding for body-worn cameras next year, but she hasn’t yet provided a specific dollar amount. The mayor also said at a press conference last week that her office would explore further de-escalation training for city employees. “I haven’t really had time to process lessons for the past two weeks yet,” she said, “but I do think we are going to have some conversations about what kind of training that a broader array of city staff need in de-escalation techniques, and make some plans about if we cannot only use a law enforcement response, what our options are.” Arunava Prabhakaran was a member of Youth Press Corps 2026, a one-week student journalism camp held at the Cap Times. title: Justice for Corey Ruiz: Struggle against police terror continues in Madison - Struggle-La Lucha
text: Struggle-La Lucha spoke with Dorothy Brown of the Madison-based Wisconsin Bail Out the People Movement (WiBOPM) about the racist police murder of Corey Ruiz and how the people’s movement there is resisting state repression. Struggle – La Lucha: What happened in Madison after police killed Corey Ruiz? Dorothy Brown: A rainbow of people immediately set up a vigil at what became known as Corey’s Corner, at the intersection of Williamson and S. Baldwin streets, where Corey Ruiz was publicly executed by Madison Police on July 22. The vigil led to the people setting up barricades on each street in every direction leading to the vigil site. The entry points to the barricades were staffed by people’s volunteers. Since then, mass protests have taken place with marches, actions at City Hall and the jails to bail protesters out, and much more. Corey’s Corner became a special community, with contributions of food and water, a People’s Library, barbers and hair stylists giving free cuts, a medical tent, assistance for the unhoused, and much more. The encampment was a place for community members to grieve, meet friends and to develop relationships with those that are horrified and outraged by the killers of Corey Ruiz and many others. Many traveled from across Wisconsin and beyond – including from George Floyd Square in Minneapolis — to pay their respects to Corey and his family. SLL: Who is participating in the movement for Justice for Corey? What are the movement’s demands? DB: A diverse range of participants were at the encampment 24 hours a day, including union members, students, parents, teachers, workers of all kinds, and organizations such as Freedom Inc. Even after the encampment was destroyed by the city on Aug. 4, when many were arrested, people still hold space daily at the site where Corey was murdered by the cops. And the cops continue to menace the people and arrest some at the site. The family of Corey Ruiz is presenting these demands: The family has retained the firm of civil rights attorney Benjamin Crump to represent them. SLL: How have the Madison Police and local government responded to the people’s protests and demands? DB: Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway and the police are in full opposition to the movement. The police in Madison and the surrounding metro area have murdered and brutalized many over the years – mostly Black and Brown people, but also poor white workers as well. The mayor’s attack on Corey’s Corner confirmed her role as the bankers’, speculators’, developers’ and corporations’ representative in City Hall to keep the profits rolling at the expense of the people. Gentrification in Madison is reaching an extreme level. Rents in particular have skyrocketed. There were numerous opportunities for the mayor to visit the site, but she never did. Instead she chose to send in the police, the protectors of the rich. SLL: Why did the police target the memorial at Corey’s Corner last week? DB: The area where Corey Ruiz was murdered by the police is quickly being gentrified, with many forced to move out of this historically student and working-class neighborhood. This neighborhood has been a stronghold of people’s resistance for decades. Despite the challenges in Wisconsin due to capitalism and imperialism, including personal challenges present at times at the Corey’s Corner encampment, there was also a depth of real conversations and relationships building and evolving hour-by-hour and day-by-day. With social media in the hands of many people’s fighters at the site, people around the world were watching. People of all nationalities, genders, sexualities and ages were working together to cook, to have poetry readings, to take notes, share, produce art and to love and grieve with each other – and to organize on a working-class basis. The unhoused had tents and supporters at the encampment. Corey’s Corner also had an international component, with Palestinians and others educating participants about the intimate connections between the Israeli Occupation Forces in occupied Palestine and police of all kinds in the U.S. The potential for future organizing is what scared the mayor, her capitalist backers, and their police servants. SLL: What kind of social and economic conditions are working-class people confronting in the city and state? DB: In Madison, Black and Brown residents face a variety of structurally racist obstacles, including lack of access to living-wage union jobs, adequate and safe housing and public education that meets the needs of oppressed people’s communities. Wisconsin has some of the highest rates of incarceration and infant mortality for Black people. Since the implementation of Act 10 in June 2011, Wisconsin has faced some of the most unrelenting austerity in U.S. history. Act 10 eliminated almost all collective bargaining rights for public-sector workers statewide and stipulated that public workers had to pay for their health care and pension contributions – amounting to big wage cuts. In addition to this, Wisconsin became a right-to-work-for-less state in 2015 when the right-wing legislature and governor signed this Jim Crow-based law into existence. These two anti-worker and racist laws ushered in a period of austerity. Most tenant rights laws were eviscerated. Attacks on the LGBTQIA+ community and women’s rights were rampant. The right-wing Bradley Foundation used Milwaukee as a laboratory for the implementation of charter schools and so-called “welfare reform” in the 1990s, and then Wisconsin as a whole was used as a laboratory for what’s now being done federally. Madison and Milwaukee residents have faced a variety of other racist and anti-worker attacks from the right-wing legislature, including a massive drop in state shared revenue (taxes) sent back to these cities for desperately needed services. This austerity by the rich since 2011 has resulted in the robbery of tens of billions of dollars from working-class communities throughout the state in the form of increasing debt service to the banks, privatization and other IMF/World Bank-type procedures similar to what Wall Street did in Eastern Europe after the collapse of the USSR. SLL: What’s next for the fightback? How can people outside Madison support the struggle? DB: The struggle for justice for Corey is taking place daily in a variety of ways. Many continue to visit Baldwin and Williamson streets to pay their respects and to resist the cops. Those arrested and brutalized after the encampment was raided are healing and getting back into the streets to organize. Educational events and protest events are in the planning stages. Much more is ongoing. We urge people to call the Dane County district attorney and demand action: (608) 266-1221. Supporters can make contributions to Corey Ruiz’ family here: https://www.gofundme.com/f/justice-for-corey-telling-his-story People can also elevate the demands of the family, share information about upcoming protests, join them or hold solidarity ones in their communities, and raise up Corey’s name. For coverage of actions in Wisconsin and more information about the ongoing struggle for justice for Corey Ruiz, follow WiBOPM on Instagram and wibopm.org , Freedom Inc. and Madison 365 .

title: Wisconsin’s partisan primary election is today. Learn more about who’s on your ballot. - VernonReporter
text: Aug. 11, 2026 By Brittany Carloni, Zoey Elwood and Audrey Lopez-Stane, Wisconsin Watch Wisconsin: It’s time to winnow the field.  Tuesday is the state’s partisan primary election, where voters will choose the candidates to represent the major political parties during the general election this November.  There are important races up and down the ballot on Tuesday, but the top contest is Wisconsin’s Democratic gubernatorial primary . Seven names will appear on the ballot, but only four are still running for the party’s nomination after a chaotic summer that saw multiple candidates drop out of the race, a historically rare endorsement from Gov. Tony Evers of Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley and increased momentum for Madison state Rep. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist. Depending on which party voters choose as they cast ballots on Tuesday, there are also competitive primaries for the state’s congressional districts and legislative seats . The stakes of those races are high as Democrats and Republicans battle for majorities both in Washington, D.C., and at the Capitol in Madison this November.  Under Wisconsin’s open primary system, primary voters must select a party and then may only vote for candidates running from that party. So if a voter chooses “Republican Party,” that person can’t vote in the Democratic primary for governor, and if a voter chooses “Democratic Party,” that person can’t vote in the Republican primary for the 7th Congressional District. A voter doesn’t need to be a member of the party to vote in that primary, and a selection does not commit a person to joining that party or voting for that candidate in the November general election. Ballots are secret so which party a voter chooses is not publicly disclosed. As of Friday, the Wisconsin Elections Commission reported more than 234,000 people voted early in person or by mail. In 2022, about 295,000 people voted early when the top races were the Democratic U.S. Senate primary and the Republican gubernatorial primary. Remember: If you already voted, you are not able to spoil your ballot and cast a new one. Polls are open from 7 a.m. until 8 p.m. on Tuesday. You can find out what’s on your ballot, the location of your polling place and more at myvote.wi.gov . Voters must show a valid photo ID and can register at the polls on Election Day with proof of residency .  Wisconsin gubernatorial primaries  At the start of the year, the Democratic gubernatorial primary was a sleepy seven-candidate contest. That rapidly changed over the past month. Former Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez dropped out of the race in mid-July following revelations of issues with her campaign finance reports. Rodriguez’s exit led Crowley to restart his campaign with Evers’ endorsement and an effort to position himself as the moderate alternative to Hong. Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, who was Hong’s closest competition in multiple polls, left the race in late July.  The remaining Democrats include former Department of Administration Secretary Joel Brennan, Crowley, Hong and Madison state Sen. Kelda Roys. Brennan and Roys have struggled to garner more than single-digit support in the polls despite Brennan pitching himself as a continuation of the moderate Evers era and Roys’ endorsement from the state’s largest teachers union. The winner of the Democratic primary will take on the GOP nominee. The Republican primary features U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany and 27-year-old medical service technician Andy Manske. Tiffany, who is endorsed by President Donald Trump and the Republican Party of Wisconsin, is expected to cruise to a win Tuesday. Tiffany has nearly $5 million cash on hand, as of late July, far exceeding Manske’s $1,600.  Congressional primaries Republicans took control of the U.S. House in 2022 and currently hold six of Wisconsin’s eight seats. Democrats, as they try to take back the chamber, are targeting Wisconsin’s 1st and 3rd congressional districts . Republican U.S. Rep. Bryan Steil has held the 1st District since 2018. The three Democrats vying to unseat Steil are ER nurse Mitchell Berman, Navy veteran Lorenzo Santos and Whitewater Unified School Board Vice President Miguel Aranda. Milwaukee Ald. Peter Burgelis will be on the ballot Tuesday, but ended his campaign in July.  In the 3rd District in western Wisconsin, Republican U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden is running for a third term. 2024 Democratic nominee Rebecca Cooke and former Eau Claire City Council President Emily Berge are competing in the Democratic primary. Political science experts rate the district a toss-up. The 7th District in northern Wisconsin features a heavily contested Republican primary as U.S Rep. Tom Tiffany leaves the seat to run for governor. The Republican candidates include Wausau financial adviser Kevin Hermening, Chippewa County factory worker Jessi Ebben, Crescent business owner Niina Baum, Superior contractor Don Raihala, and Michael Alfonso, son-in-law of former congressman and current U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy . Alfonso is endorsed by Trump. Legislative primaries Democrats are seeking to take control of both chambers of the Legislature this midterm cycle, needing to flip two Senate seats and five Assembly seats to secure majorities. The party is using momentum from new legislative maps two years ago that officially ended a decade-plus Republican gerrymander and allowed them to flip 14 legislative seats in 2024 .  There are three Senate district primaries we’re watching Tuesday.  The 1st Senate District, covering the Door County peninsula, features four Republicans competing to succeed Sen. André Jacque, R-New Franken, who is not seeking reelection. Barbara Bittner, Jacob VandenPlas, Katie Baney and Nic Cravillion will compete for a place on the November ballot against independent candidate Mark Becker.  The 17th Senate District has long been a target for Senate Democrats. Sen. Howard Marklein, a co-chair of the Joint Finance Committee, is running for a fourth four-year term. Rep. Jenna Jacobson, D-Oregon, Lisa White and Corrine Hendrickson will face off in the Democratic primary. The Senate Democratic Campaign Committee, which is supporting Jacobson, considers the seat a flip opportunity in 2026.  Two former state representatives, Erik Severson and Angie Sapik, are competing in the Republican primary for the 25th Senate District to determine who will face Democrat Charly Ray in the general election for an open seat left vacant by redistricting.  A sign directs voters to the Olbrich Botanical Gardens polling place during the primary election Aug. 13, 2024, in Madison, Wis. (Joe Timmerman / Wisconsin Watch) In the Assembly on Tuesday, David Liners and Daniel J. Bukiewicz will face off in the Democratic primary for the 21st Assembly District to replace Rep. Jessie Rodriguez, R-Oak Creek, who is not seeking reelection. The primary winner will face Republican Dylan Pfaffenbach.  Three Republicans — Tyler Schneekloth, John Belanger and James Brotz — will compete in the Republican primary to unseat freshman Rep. Joe Sheehan, D-Sheboygan, who flipped the 26th District back in 2024.  Democrats Brian Bock, Ben Brist and Lawanda Chambers will face off in the August primary to challenge two-term incumbent Rep. Bob Donovan, R-Greenfield, in the 61st District — a district targeted by Democrats for control of the Assembly.  There is also competition for safe Democratic seats in Milwaukee and Madison. Rep. Ryan Clancy, D-Milwaukee, and Bridget Maniaci will compete for a place on the November ballot in the 19th Assembly District. Clancy hails from the socialist wing of the party, and Maniaci is a former Madison City Council member. The winner faces Republican Yasmine Outlaw.  Assembly District 76 features five Democrats — Isaia Ben-Ami, Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford, Juliana Bennett, Zoe Sullivan and Tony Castañeda — after Hong opted to run for governor. The winner faces Republican Nina Chat in the general election. State office primaries Depending on which party they select, voters will have the opportunity to pick candidates for certain statewide offices.  Republican primary voters can choose between Will Martin, a Racine consultant, and David Varnam, a Lancaster stay-at-home dad, in the race for lieutenant governor. Secretary of State Sarah Godlewski is the only Democrat running for lieutenant governor. The winning candidates will form a joint ticket with the party’s gubernatorial nominee this November.  They can also choose their nominee in the four-person GOP primary for secretary of state. The candidates include Braden Myer, Jay Schroeder, Nate Pollnow and Cindy Werner. The winner will face Milwaukee Ald. JoCasta Zamarripa, who is running unopposed for the Democratic nomination. Democratic primary voters will determine whether Dylan Helmenstine, of Black Earth, or Yee Leng Xiong, of Wausau, will be the party’s nominee for state treasurer in November. The winner will take on first-term Republican incumbent Treasurer John Leiber in November. Republican attorney general candidate Eric Toney and two-term Democratic Attorney General Josh Kaul are both unopposed in the primary. Other local elections Voters on Tuesday can also make decisions in local races, including sheriff and clerk of court contests in counties across the state.  For more information about specific local races on your ballot, visit myvote.wi.gov . For more information on statewide and legislative candidates, check out the Wisconsin Watch voter guide. ~~~ This article first appeared on Wisconsin Watch and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License . Off On Stream on Wisconsin DOJ releases name of Madison police officer who shot Corey Ruiz Ruiz was shot and killed on July 22. 1:28 Corey Ruiz before he was shot and killed during an incident with police in Madison, Wis., July 22, 2026. Dan Hudec The identity of the Madison, Wisconsin, police officer involved in the fatal shooting of Corey Ruiz was announced by investigators on Monday. The Wisconsin Department of Justice Division of Criminal Investigation (DCI) said Madison police officer Kiel Baitinger-Peterson shot Ruiz on July 22. “At approximately 1:00 p.m., Madison Police Department officers responded to the Marquette neighborhood [in Madison, WI] for a report of a subject allegedly involved in checking parked vehicles and an alleged burglary attempt,” the DCI said in a press release on Monday. “Officers located and attempted to contact the subject, who fled on a bicycle.” Corey Ruiz, as he is being chased by police officers, falls off his bike, July 22, 2026, in Madison, Wis. Mud Lord via Storyful In bystander video, law enforcement can be seen restraining Ruiz after he fell off a bicycle. Officials said Ruiz pulled out a knife during a physical altercation with the officers and injured Baitinger-Peterson. The officer can be seen shooting Ruiz multiple times from close range in video footage. “Mr. Ruiz’s death was tragic, and the use of deadly force must be thoroughly examined," Jim Palmer, executive director of the Wisconsin Professional Police Association, who is representing Baitinger-Peterson, told ABC News in a statement last week. "But fairness requires acknowledging the circumstances that brought officers to the area, the danger they encountered, and their cooperation since the incident." Two other officers allegedly attempted to use a stun gun on Ruiz before shots were fired, according to DCI. A knife was recovered from the scene. ABC News obtained , verified and synchronized three bystander videos showing the shooting. Corey Ruiz before he was shot and killed during an incident with police in Madison, Wis., July 22, 2026. Michael Doubek The videos show a fatal confrontation that lasted just 28 seconds from the point Ruiz fell from a bicycle as he was being chased by officers in Madison until he was shot and killed, according to an ABC News analysis of verified imagery. None of the officers were wearing police body cameras. A spokesperson with the city of Madison told ABC News that the city is one of the few major cities that doesn’t have body cameras for its police officers -- besides its SWAT teams. The DCI said emergency medical services were contacted and life-saving measures were administered on Ruiz, who was transported to a local hospital where he was pronounced deceased. Another officer sustained injuries during the confrontation, according to officials. Both injured officers were treated at a hospital and were released. Ruiz’s family gave emotional remarks at a press conference with their attorneys in July. They said that Ruiz made mistakes in the past, but he wasn’t a violent person. “People, whoever is saying, ‘Oh, but he was a criminal.’” Kh’Liah Omar, Ruiz’s 13-year-old daughter, said at the press conference. “So what? He had a family. He had me. The last time I talked to him, it was for a short period of time, and I wish he'd be longer.” Margery Omar, Kh’Liah Omar’s mother, said that her daughter will have to walk by the location where Ruiz was shot every day that she goes to school because the shooting happened near their home. An officer is seen and heard firing three shots at Corey Ruiz in Madison, Wis., July 22, 2026. Michael Doubek Palmer with the WPPA said that Baitinger is a certified instructor within the department and had never previously been involved in an incident involving deadly force. He also told ABC News that it is important to allow "the evidence -- not isolated images, policial pressure, or public speculation -- to determine the outcome" of the case. The union said Baitinger-Peterson and his family have also been subjected to threats, and appropriate precautions are being taken for their safety. The four responding officers will be placed on paid administrative leave, per Wisconsin law, according to the WPPA. The union said Baitinger-Peterson did not recognize Ruiz or believe he had ever interacted with him before the day of the shooting. DCI said in their statement that they are reviewing the evidence to determine the facts of the case and will turn over their findings to the Dane County District Attorney’s Office when the investigation concludes. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said in a video last week that protests surrounding Ruiz’s shooting at the site of his death quickly turned into an encampment, blocking off street traffic and access to businesses. She said as city workers cleared the intersection, rocks were thrown at them and two fires were set. title: Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford wins Democratic nomination for Madison Assembly seat - The Daily Cardinal
text: Madison Common Council Member Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford won the Democratic nomination for Madison’s 76th Assembly District on Tuesday. Rep. Francesca Hong, D-Madison, left the seat vacant after announcing her campaign for governor.  Martinez-Rutherford won the race with 6,170 votes over four other candidates, according to the Associated Press. The Associated Press called the race at 11:31 p.m. when Martinez-Rutherford had 29.4% of the vote.  Martinez-Rutherford, a democratic socialist, will go on to face Republican Nina Chat, who ran uncontested in the primary, in the November election. Democrats will likely maintain their grasp on the historically bright blue seat.  Before Hong, the seat was held by current Wisconsin Supreme Court Justice Chris Taylor from 2011 to 2020. Hong was elected in 2020 in a landslide election with 88% of the vote after Taylor was appointed to the Dane County Circuit Court by Gov. Tony Evers. Hong then went on to run unopposed for both the 2022 and 2024 elections.  Martinez-Rutherford’s opponents included former State Assembly Policy Director Isaia Ben-Ami, former District 8 Alder Juliana Bennett, activist and musician Tony Castañeda and journalist Zoe Sullivan.  Housing affordability and cost of living in Madison were top issues, according to a City Cast Madison questionnaire sent to all candidates. They agreed to support a yearlong moratorium on data center construction in Wisconsin, according to The Cap Times.  The majority of the candidates like Ben-Ami and Bennett also aligned themselves with democratic socialism.  Cost of living and access to reproductive healthcare were key issues for Martinez-Rutherford, who was endorsed by Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway.  During her campaign, Martinez-Rutherford accrued over $45,000 in campaign money. The general election is set for Nov. 3. Staff writer

Democrats will likely maintain their grasp on the historically bright blue seat.  Before Hong, the seat was held by current Wisconsin Supreme Court Justice Chris Taylor from 2011 to 2020. Hong was elected in 2020 in a landslide election with 88% of the vote after Taylor was appointed to the Dane County Circuit Court by Gov. Tony Evers. Hong then went on to run unopposed for both the 2022 and 2024 elections.  Martinez-Rutherford’s opponents included former State Assembly Policy Director Isaia Ben-Ami, former District 8 Alder Juliana Bennett, activist and musician Tony Castañeda and journalist Zoe Sullivan.  Housing affordability and cost of living in Madison were top issues, according to a City Cast Madison questionnaire sent to all candidates. They agreed to support a yearlong moratorium on data center construction in Wisconsin, according to The Cap Times.  The majority of the candidates like Ben-Ami and Bennett also aligned themselves with democratic socialism.  Cost of living and access to reproductive healthcare were key issues for Martinez-Rutherford, who was endorsed by Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway.  During her campaign, Martinez-Rutherford accrued over $45,000 in campaign money. The general election is set for Nov. 3. Staff writer

People Contact Contests Schedule Marketing Resources Careers Sinclair Cares Weather Watch Live Now 84 ° Thu 76 ° Fri 81 ° facebook icon twitter icon ACCESSIBILITY Middleton-Cross Plains school board approves $34.6M referendum for Nov. 3 election by Samantha Calderon Screenshot 2026-08-12 135938.png Share story Share topics: Schoolboard Operational referendum Property taxes Revenue limit Inflation School funding Staff salaries Wisconsin MIDDLETON, Wis. — The Middleton-Cross Plains Area School District Board of Education on Monday approved placing an operational referendum question on the Nov. 3 ballot, which will eventually reach $34.6 million. If approved by voters, the four-year, nonrecurring referendum would allow the district to exceed the state-imposed revenue limit for operating expenses. The proposal would authorize $24.9 million in 2027-28, with annual increases intended to keep pace with inflation. The authorization would rise to $34.6 million by the 2030-31 school year. District officials said the funding would support competitive class sizes; current curricular and co-curricular opportunities; salaries and benefits needed to recruit and retain staff; sustainability efforts; and facility maintenance. The proposal would continue funding authorized under the district’s 2022 operational referendum while adding annual adjustments to address rising costs over the next four years, officials said. Based on current projections, the estimated tax impact on a property with a fair market value of $100,000 would increase gradually over the four-year period, reaching about $64 a year in the fourth year. "The Board evaluated a range of options before approving a proposal that balances the District's financial needs with the impact on taxpayers," Superintendent Dr. Dana Monogue said. The district operates under a state-imposed revenue limit that determines how much funding districts may receive through state aid and local property taxes. The funding system has not kept pace with inflation or the increasing cost of educating students. About 94% of the district’s operating revenue is determined by the state funding formula, leaving districts with limited flexibility to address rising costs. "While the referendum would not eliminate every financial challenge we face, it would significantly reduce the budget reductions the District would otherwise need to make and help us continue providing the high-quality educational opportunities our community expects," Monogue said. title: Key Wisconsin congressional, state legislative races set for November - The Cap Times
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. In addition to finalizing the matchup for Wisconsin governor this November, voters in Tuesday’s primary election also set the stage for a number of key down-ballot races, from Congress to state treasurer. Here are the results from those races, and responses from some of the candidates: There will be a rematch this fall in the battleground 3rd Congressional District in western Wisconsin after Eau Claire Democrat Rebecca Cooke won her primary on Tuesday. Cooke, a waitress and former small business owner, political consultant and nonprofit leader, beat Eau Claire City Council President Emily Berge by just over 21%. She will now face Republican U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden of Prairie du Chien. Van Orden has represented the district since 2023. He’s a close ally of President Donald Trump and is a former Navy SEAL who had no political experience before running for Congress. Cooke previously ran against Van Orden two years ago but came up short by about 11,000 votes. It is one of a handful of key House seats that Democrats hope to flip this fall to take back control of the chamber. Van Orden has been referring to Cooke online as the "Anointed One,” claiming she was “handpicked” by the Democratic Party. After Tuesday night, Van Orden also cast doubt on the election results online, saying “the fix was in.” In a statement online, Cooke invited supporters of both Berge and Van Orden to support her. “Our tent is big. Our tent is squarely focused on lowering costs, combatting corruption, supporting small business, bolstering agriculture and building an American Dream we can actually grasp,” Cooke said. Wisconsin Democrat Rebecca Cooke speaks to a crowd of supporters in Viroqua on Saturday alongside Vermont Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders. In the 1st Congressional District, Racine County emergency room nurse Mitchell Berman won the Democratic primary and will face Republican U.S. Rep. Bryan Steil in the fall. Berman received just over 44% of the vote against three other Democratic candidates. The race has been ranked by analysts as a likely win for Steil, who has represented the district in Congress since 2019, but Democrats have still been eyeing it as a potential flip. “Tonight proves that when working people stand up, we can make a difference,” Berman said in a statement online. Up north in the 7th Congressional District, voters chose Trump-backed conservative Michael Alfonso as the Republican candidate to try to replace U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany as he seeks the governorship. Alfonso is the son-in-law of U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, a Wisconsin native who previously represented the district. Alfonso earned nearly 49% of the vote after a contentious five-way Republican primary where opponents accused the 26-year-old of nepotism and inexperience. Fred Clark, pictured in 2014 at his small business Baraboo Woodworks, is the Democratic nominee for the 7th Congressional District. Clark previously lived in Baraboo, where he served in the state Assembly, but now resides in Bayfield. The Democratic nominee in the race will be Bayfield resident Fred Clark, a conservationist and small business owner who served in the state Assembly from 2013 to 2015 while living in Baraboo. While the seat is left wide open by Tiffany’s bid for governor, it is a deep-red district and will likely be difficult for Democrats to overturn. And in the 2nd Congressional District, which includes Madison and Dane County, longtime Democratic U.S. Rep. Mark Pocan handedly beat his opponent Douglas Alexander with nearly 88% of the vote. No Republican will be on the ballot against Pocan in November, meaning he has a clear path to his reelection to an eighth term. Voters selected state Rep. Jenna Jacobson of Oregon to take on longtime Republican Sen. Howard Marklein of Spring Green for the 17th Senate District in the fall. Jacobson secured nearly 66% of the vote and beat out two other Democratic candidates. The 17th Senate District is seen as a critical battleground to decide which party controls the Wisconsin Senate next year. Sen. Howard Marklein, R-Spring Green, is running for reelection in the 17th Senate District, a seat Democrats they think they can flip on their way to taking over control of the chamber. “Last cycle, Senate Democrats defied the odds and swept every single battleground district at a time when President Trump carried the state,” said Will Karcz, the communications director for the State Senate Democratic Committee. “Now, with the wind at our backs, we’re out to not just win a razor-thin majority, but a durable one that will deliver for Wisconsinites.” Corrine Hendrickson, a former childcare provider who came in second in the district’s Democratic primary, urged Democrats to unify heading into November. New Glarus School Board President Bill Oemichen will be the Democrat running to fill Jacobson’s seat in the Assembly’s 50th District after winning his primary with just over 49% of the vote. Oemichen will face Mount Horeb Republican and former small business leader Jon Aleckson in November. Bryna Cave, one of the other Democrats in the 50th District race, expressed her support for Oemichen online on Wednesday and said she already donated to his campaign. “He is extremely qualified, much more than I am, and will definitely beat Jon Aleckson in November,” Cave said. In the deep blue 76th Assembly District currently held by Rep. Francesca Hong, who lost her bid for governor on Tuesday, Madison City Council Ald. Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford will likely be the new representative. Martinez-Rutherford earned more than 29% of the vote, eking out a win in a crowded field of five. In 2023, she made history as the first transgender woman elected to the City Council, and if successful in November, she would also become the first transgender member of the state Legislature. Michelle Ellinger Linley congratulates Madison City Council member Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford, right, on her win in the Democratic primary for the 76th Assembly District. They attended state Rep. Francesca Hong’s gubernatorial primary election night watch party at Atwood Music Hall in Madison. “Our community elected someone who has lived the policy failures of our government. Someone who has been homeless, gone without healthcare, and worked for a tipped wage in the service industry. Someone whose rights continue to be debated by politicians in the Capitol,” she said in a statement online. “That’s the perspective that I’ll bring to the Assembly.” While Martinez-Rutherford will be on the ballot in November against Republican Nina Chat of Madison, the district is a Democratic stronghold that will almost certainly go to Martinez-Rutherford. For lieutenant governor, the Republican field had a surprising result when former Lancaster Mayor David Varnam won the nomination with nearly 56% of the vote. Varnam beat small business owner Will Martin, who was endorsed by several state Republican leaders, had outraised Varnam, and was campaigning alongside Tiffany. “Starting tonight, I will do everything I can to get Tom Tiffany across the finish line this November,” Varnam said in a statement . In his own statement , Martin did not address the upset, and instead simply thanked supporters. Varnam will join Tiffany on the ticket to face Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Crowley and lieutenant governor nominee Sarah Godlewski in November. The Cap Times welcomes tips from readers to help us inform our community. Email tips@captimes.com or visit captimes.com/tips for more options. Marathon County Board member and D.C. Everest School Board treasurer Yee Leng Xiong became the Democratic nominee for state treasurer on Tuesday after securing about 58% of the vote. Xiong beat fellow Democrat Dylan Helmenstine, who is a trustee of the Black Earth Village Board and member of the Teachers Retirement Board. Both Democrats had received split endorsements from party leadership in the primary. Xiong will now challenge Republican incumbent John Leiber for the job. Xiong said in a post online that he spoke with Helmenstine on Tuesday night, calling him his friend and thanking him for a strong campaign. “Now that the primary is behind us, we need everyone united this fall to take back the state treasurer’s office,” Xiong said. “For four years, John Leiber has treated (the job of treasurer) like a placeholder. Wisconsin deserves better than a treasurer who simply shows up to collect a paycheck.” And for secretary of state, Jay Schroeder, a Neenah real estate and stock investor, will be the Republican nominee. He won a four-way primary with roughly 47% of the vote. In November, Schroeder will face Democratic Milwaukee Ald. JoCasta Zamarripa, who ran unopposed in the primary.

title: David Crowley caps unlikely comeback with win in Wisconsin Democratic primary for governor - WRJN
text: Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley completed an unlikely political comeback in Tuesday’s primary election, narrowly winning Wisconsin’s Democratic nomination for governor after Gov. Tony Evers gave him a late endorsement . Crowley will face U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany in November, with President Donald Trump backing the Republican nominee. The Associated Press declared Crowley the winner at 2:34 a.m. Wednesday, ending a race that remained unsettled deep into the night. With 98% of the votes tallied, Crowley led Madison state Rep. Francesca Hong by less than half a percentage point — State Sen. Kelda Roys and former Department of Administration Secretary Joel Brennan trailed far behind with percentages in the single digits. Crowley, who served two terms in the Assembly, often highlighted his experience as Milwaukee County executive as the key difference between himself and his primary opponents. He was elected to lead Wisconsin’s most populous county in 2020 and reelected in 2024. On the campaign trail, Crowley pointed to his ability to work with both Democrats and Republicans to help improve lives in Milwaukee County. He frequently highlighted the 2023 shared revenue law that helped Milwaukee County pay off debts from the pension scandal in the early 2000s. Crowley’s revived campaign drew criticism from people who saw his return to the race as efforts by establishment Democrats to stop more progressive candidates, like Hong. Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, who had been Hong’s closest competition in polls before he dropped out of the race in July, at the only televised debate called Crowley “revived by special interests.” Crowley in recent campaign stops has dismissed the “establishment” label and pointed to his early years growing up in Milwaukee where his parents struggled with mental health issues and addiction and his family faced evictions. The 2026 election for governor is an open seat after Evers chose not to run for a third term . It’s the first open governor’s race in the state since 2010 when Gov. Scott Walker ushered in a conservative era during which Republicans dismantled public sector unions, increased pension and health insurance contributions for public employees, cut taxes and enacted gerrymandered legislative maps. Democrats are hoping to take control of the state Legislature for the first time in 16 years after flipping the state Supreme Court to a liberal majority and enacting bipartisan legislative maps. But even with a legislative majority, the ability to enact Democratic legislation would still run through the governor’s office. Hong, a democratic socialist, led in the polls for months, and her primary victory seemed all but assured heading into Tuesday. But the close race mirrored a similar battle between establishment Democrats and left-wing activists in the Michigan U.S. Senate primary. Polls showed the left-wing candidate with a double-digit lead heading into last week’s primary, but he only won by 1 percentage point. Hong had led the Democratic field in five Marquette University Law School polls ahead of the primary. Her rise as a front-runner in the race happened alongside significant democratic socialist candidate wins in states like New York and Colorado. Hong, though, faced questions from some Democrats over whether she could win in November. Republicans in recent weeks also seized on Hong’s old social media posts on positions such as defunding the police, abolishing the U.S. Senate and canceling Thanksgiving. Hong spent time in national news interviews during the final week of the primary attempting to walk back those past comments. Crowley’s strong showing marks a stunning turnaround for a candidate who polled in single digits before he dropped out of the race in early July. Even in the final Marquette Law School Poll before the election, he only mustered 7% support to 38% for Hong, though 34% were undecided. Crowley initially ended his campaign after he said he saw both poll and fundraising numbers show momentum for Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez. But then Rodriguez dropped out of the race after revelations of issues with her campaign finance reports, which led Crowley to return to the race with a historically rare endorsement from Evers. In the final week of the primary, the two-term governor joined Crowley on the campaign trail to champion Crowley as his successor. At the Atwood Music Hall in Madison on Tuesday night, Hong’s supporters waited for the results as the loudspeakers pumped in Stevie Wonder, Spice Girls and Chappell Roan. One Hong staffer estimated that a couple hundred people were in attendance, but didn’t have an official number. Reporters and TV cameras packed the balcony. Supporters cheer as Madison Rep. Francesca Hong takes a short-lived lead over Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley in Wisconsin’s Democratic primary for governor during Hong’s election night watch party at Atwood Music Hall in Madison, Wis. on Aug. 11, 2026. (Jake Piper for Wisconsin Watch) Supporters of Madison Rep. Francesca Hong leave her election night watch party at Atwood Music Hall in Madison at 11:30 p.m. on Aug. 11, 2026, with the Democratic primary for governor still too close to call. (Jake Piper for Wisconsin Watch) Luca Farmer, a 21-year-old Madison resident, cheered and waved a poster reading “Hotties 4 Hong” as CNN results showed the state representative pulling closer to Crowley around 10 p.m. Tuesday. Farmer said he had been following the race since Evers chose not to run for reelection last year. He said he voted for Hong because she is “policy first.” But Farmer said he did not anticipate Hong and Crowley were going to be as close as they were Tuesday night. “My heart is palpitating,” he said. “I did not think it was going to be this close. I was very confident, but I am still confident that we will win.” Around 11:20 p.m., Hong walked onstage to address and thank supporters, who erupted in cheers. She acknowledged that the results were not final, but “the fight continues no matter what.” “In 11 weeks, no matter who’s on the ballot, y’all, we are going to fight to win for one another,” Hong said as the crowd started a chant of “we will win.” “We will win together, united, because everyone who’s running in this race, they know that we can make better possible, and we must make better possible.” At the Hyatt Regency in downtown Milwaukee, at least 250 people were spread among two ballrooms and a reception area. Chatter was loud but, as of 11 p.m., few cheers went up — the vote totals simply remained too tight. Early in the evening, Noel Morales, a 21-year-old Crowley supporter from suburban Milwaukee, expressed confidence about Crowley’s chances. But he worried whether young Hong supporters would back Crowley if Crowley wins the nomination because Crowley has been cast as an establishment Democrat. It’s a very big “it depends” on whether Democrats can find unity, he said. The first sustained cheer at the Crowley gathering went up about 11:15 p.m. when a TV station went live from the party. Minutes later, the party went mostly quiet to listen to remarks made by Hong at her gathering. At that point, Crowley had yet to appear before his supporters. At midnight, Milwaukee election officials said “human error” would delay ballot counting. At the Crowley party, just as supporters appeared ready to claim victory, the news was deflating. “I’m at a loss for words,” said Crowley supporter Angela Hinton of the Milwaukee suburb of Glendale. “With the votes so close, we were on pins and needles. Now this.” U.S. Rep. Gwen Moore told the gathering just after midnight that results were 90 minutes away. “It looks very good, but we have to wait,” she said. In other primary results Tuesday, Rebecca Cooke won the Democratic nomination in the 3rd Congressional District for a rematch with Republican U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden. The seat is rated a toss-up and one of two that national Democrats are hoping to flip to retake control of the House. In the other, the 1st Congressional District in southeast Wisconsin, Mitchell Berman won the Democratic nomination to take on U.S. Rep. Bryan Steil. Michael Alfonso, the son-in-law of U.S. Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, won the Republican nomination in the 7th Congressional District in northern Wisconsin. The Democratic nomination was too close to call, though the seat being vacated by Tiffany leans Republican. Nic Cravillion, a staffer for Sen. André Jacque, R-New Franken, won the Republican nomination for the 1st Senate District to replace Jacque after his two terms in the Senate. Rep. Jenna Jacobson, D-Oregon, won the Democratic nomination in the 17th Senate District to challenge Sen. Howard Marklein in November. Jacobson is supported by the Senate Democratic Campaign Committee, which sees this district as a potential flip opportunity. Case manager Ismael Luna beat incumbent Rep. Sylvia Ortiz-Velez, D-Milwaukee, by a large margin for the Democratic nomination in the 8th Assembly District. Ortiz-Velez had left the Democratic caucus last year after making a gun-related threat to a fellow Democrat. In the 21st Assembly District, Oak Creek Mayor Dan Bukiewicz won the Democratic nomination and will now face Republican Carroll University student Dylan Pfaffenbach in the general election. The winner will replace Rep. Jessie Rodriguez, R-Oak Creek, who won by a narrow margin in 2024. Former Sheboygan Ald. John Belanger won the Republican nomination in the 26th Assembly District and will face Rep. Joe Sheehan, D-Sheboygan. In the 76th Assembly District, Hong’s district, Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford, a former Madison City Council member, won the nomination. She will face Republican Nina Chat in the general election in the solid Democratic district. If elected Martinez-Rutherford would be the first transgender person elected to the Assembly.
